candidate.name: AAPM MATCH markerless lung tracking Grand Challenge (experimental phantom part)
candidate.why_relevant: Marginal. It has real Varian kV intrafraction frames (11 Hz) and CBCT rotations of a 3D-printed patient-derived thorax phantom with bone. The same phantom has a planning 3D CT (0.6 mm), a 4D CT and known motion traces. The kV fields are small and collimated (7x7 or 5.5x7 cm) on lung targets, so the spine is mostly outside them. Only the experimental part is real; Part A is in silico. It is a different dataset from the known SPARE.
candidate.institution: AAPM; Image X Institute (Sydney), Aarhus, Amsterdam UMC and others
candidate.device: Varian TrueBeam-class linac (XIM kV, MV cine)
candidate.anatomy: Thorax (3D-printed from patient anatomy, with bone)
candidate.pose_or_labels: Linac geometry, gantry angle, 3DCT + 4DCT, setup CBCT, motion ground truth
candidate.xray_kind: kV intrafraction frames + CBCT rotations (60 s, 120 s)
candidate.licence: 'Anyone is welcome to use the MATCH Challenge datasets for their research' (cite Mueller et al. 2021)

verdicts.access_now: You can download it now, with no login, request or agreement. The live link on the AAPM MATCH page is a public Google Drive file, "MATCH upload.zip" (id 1yxE07D4KEBWY_p8rb_nbfgoINJwJdlIe). The only thing in the way is a notice that the file is too large for Google to scan for viruses. I checked access without downloading the whole file: a byte-range request came back HTTP 206 with a total size of 12,284,104,646 bytes. I then read the zip's file index from the end of the file, and pulled out and decoded four real files: one kV DICOM frame, two CBCT XIM projections and the README .docx. The page also still has an older "Download the challenge datasets" block, but it is commented out in the HTML. Its two Dropbox links (the in-silico data and the participants' individual results) now return a Dropbox error page, so they are dead. The ground-truth motion is not in the zip. It is in the public GitHub repo MarcoMueller-MCT/AAPM_GrandChallenge_MATCH, as GroundTruth.zip (1.7 MB) and Motion.zip (3.0 MB). These hold MATCH_A_Exp01..04_GroundTruthTargetPos.xlsx, GroundTruth.mat and plots of the motion traces.
verdicts.licence: There is no formal licence. The dataset page says: "Anyone is welcome to use the MATCH Challenge datasets for their research. Any study that makes use of the MATCH Challenge dataset should cite" Mueller et al., Med Phys, doi 10.1002/mp.15418. The zip has no licence file. The GitHub repo reports license: null, which means the analysis code is all-rights-reserved by default. According to the paper, during the challenge the datasets were shared through a data usage agreement with Washington University in St. Louis. Today's Google Drive release has no agreement attached. Commercial use and redistribution are not addressed anywhere.
verdicts.counts:
The zip is 12,284,104,646 bytes (about 12.3 GB) and unpacks to 39,264,691,916 bytes (about 39.3 GB). It holds 21,173 entries: 17,676 .dcm files, 3,466 .xim files and 1 .docx.

What the downloadable (Part A) data contains:
- **kV intrafraction frames:** 6,241 masked DICOM RTIMAGE files, one frame each, 1024x768, 16-bit, SID 1800 mm, SAD 1000 mm, 120 kV, 11 Hz. They cover four deliveries, all acquired on 2020-01-08:
  - Plan1 High Complexity: 1,610
  - Plan1 High Motion Range: 1,610
  - Plan2 Mean Motion Range: 1,510
  - Plan2 Mean Complexity: 1,511
- **MV cine:** 7,197 EPID frames at 12.7 Hz (1,857 / 1,859 / 1,740 / 1,741).
- **CBCT projections:** 3,466 Varian XIM files, 1024x768, 0.388 mm pixels, 125 kV, 15 mA, 20 ms, half-fan (kV detector offset laterally by 16 cm).
  - 3D CBCT: 895 per plan (15 Hz, 360 degrees in 60 s)
  - 4D CBCT: 838 per plan (7 Hz, 120 s)
- **CBCT reconstructions:**
  - 3D: 88 slices per plan
  - 4D: 11 phases x 117 slices = 1,287 per plan
- **Planning CT:** a static 3DCT at 0.6 mm (346 slices) for each of Plan1 and Plan2, each with RS, RP and RD objects.
- **4DCT:** 780 slices over 10 phases, with 10 RS files.
- **README:** "Data for MATCH Part A.docx".

There is one physical phantom, so one subject.
verdicts.real_xray:
Yes, but it is a phantom, not a patient. The downloadable part is labelled "in silico", yet every image is a real acquisition on a Varian TrueBeam of a physical phantom moved on a HexaMotion stage at Aarhus. "In silico" only means the participants ran their trackers offline on these recorded images. I decoded a kV frame: DICOM RTIMAGE, Manufacturer Varian, model IPS, GantryAngle 91. I also decoded two XIM CBCT projections: TrueBeam acquisition system version 2.7.304.16, KVSourceRtn 90 and 179 degrees.

The intrafraction kV frames are masked in software, not collimated at acquisition. The files are named *_masked.dcm. In the frame I sampled, only a 324x324-pixel square of the 1024x768 image is non-zero, which matches the 7x7 cm field at isocentre. The unmasked originals are not in the release. The CBCT projections are full-field and not masked. In the one sampled kV frame I could not identify any vertebra. In the one CBCT projection I contrast-enhanced, ribs and lung are clearly visible. Whether the spine shows up over the whole rotation has not been checked.
verdicts.paired_ct:
Yes, for the same physical subject. There is a static planning 3DCT at 0.6 mm (Siemens SOMATOM go.Open Pro, 346 slices for each tumour plan) and a 4DCT at 1.5 mm with 10 phases. Both come with RT structure sets, plans and dose. There are also setup 3D and 4D CBCTs acquired under motion. The geometry per frame is in the headers:
- **kV DICOM:** GantryAngle, RTImageSID, RTImagePosition, XRayImageReceptorTranslation.
- **XIM:** KVSourceRtn, KVDetectorLat/Lng/Vrt, the collimator settings and the couch position.

Ground-truth target positions for all four deliveries are on GitHub. The phantom moves rigidly, as a whole, so there is no motion of the spine relative to the rest of the body.
verdicts.anatomy: A thorax only: the anthropomorphic phantom of Hazelaar et al. (Med Phys 2018, doi 10.1002/mp.12644), 3D-printed from one lung-cancer patient's CT. Its bones are printed in gypsum, its lung structures and three tumours in nylon, and the soft tissue is silicone. The released data covers two tumours in the right lung. The planning CT spans about 208 mm craniocaudally (346 slices x 0.6 mm). The paper's discussion names vertebrae and the diaphragm as high-contrast objects a tracker could latch onto. There is no lumbar spine, pelvis or sacrum.
corrections: The candidate has the parts backwards. It says the experimental phantom part is what is available and that 'Part A is in silico'. What is actually downloadable is Part A, the retrospective study. Its kV, MV and CBCT images are real TrueBeam acquisitions of the physical phantom at Aarhus University Hospital, per the AAPM page, the README docx and the paper. 'In silico' only means participants tracked offline on recorded images.

Part B, the prospective experiment done at each participant's own institution, is not released as a dataset. The only Part B-related link, the Dropbox folder of individual participant results, is commented out on the page and now returns a Dropbox error. The in-silico Dropbox link is dead too; the live source is the Google Drive zip.
The kV fields are not 'collimated'. A 7x7 cm field (5.5x7 cm for Plan 2) was emulated by masking pixels in software, and the files are *_masked.dcm. Only the masked versions are released.

The candidate says the kV frames were 'not counted'. There are 6,241 kV intrafraction frames over four deliveries, plus 7,197 MV cine frames and 3,466 CBCT projections (895 per 3D scan and 838 per 4D scan, times two plans).
The ground-truth motion is not in the Drive zip. It is in the GitHub repo MarcoMueller-MCT/AAPM_GrandChallenge_MATCH (GroundTruth.zip and Motion.zip), which has no licence.

The licence is informal. It is a sentence on the webpage with a request to cite. There is no licence file, and commercial use and redistribution are unaddressed. During the challenge, access went through a data usage agreement with Washington University in St. Louis.
Publication: Med Phys 2022;49(2):1161-1180, doi 10.1002/mp.15418, PMID 34913495, PMC8828678. The images were acquired on 2020-01-08, per the folder names.
The 3D CBCT reconstruction is described as '515 x 512' on the page and in the README. That is probably a typo for 512x512, but I did not check it.

The data comes from one gypsum-bone phantom of the upper thorax, moved as a single rigid body. I saw no spine in the one kV frame I sampled. I did not check whether the spine is visible in the full-field CBCT projections. For spine fluoroscopy it is at best a phantom geometry and CBCT-projection resource.

verdicts.real_xray: Yes, but they come from Part A, not the experimental part. The paper calls Part A the "in-silico study", yet the paper says "Four treatments were simulated in a phantom experiment… The imaging and planning data were generated at Aarhus University Hospital" on a TrueBeam with the phantom on a HexaMotion stage. I downloaded frames with range requests and read the DICOM headers. The kV frames are RTIMAGE, Manufacturer 'Varian Medical Systems', ImageType ORIGINAL/PRIMARY, KVP 120, exposure time 10 ms, SID about 1800 mm, SAD about 1000 mm. The gantry angle changes from frame to frame and quantum noise is visible. They were acquired on 2020-01-08. They are not DRRs. The CBCT projections are real Varian XIM files. I decoded three of them: full 1024x768, half-fan. The subject is a phantom, not a patient. The MV cine frames are EPID MV portal images and should be excluded.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, same phantom, same session set. 'Planning CT and treatment plans' holds a static 3DCT: Siemens SOMATOM go.Open Pro, 346 slices, 0.6 mm thickness and spacing, 512x512, 1.08 mm pixels, z from +98.4 to -108.6 mm. The Plan1 and Plan2 folders each have 346 slices; I did not check whether they are the same scan. There is also a 4DCT of 780 slices (10 phases x 78) at 3 mm thickness according to the header ('Respiratory Motion 4D Spiral 3.00'), although the readme says the GTV was drawn on a 1.5 mm 4DCT. Each plan has RT structure, plan and dose files. Setup CBCT reconstructions are included: 3D (88 slices) and 4D (11 phases x 117 = 1287 slices) for each plan. The plan isocentre is defined as the origin of the phantom motion.
verdicts.anatomy: Thorax only. I rendered axial planning-CT slices. They run from the clavicles and thoracic inlet (z +64) to the lung bases and diaphragm (z -90). The phantom is cut off below that, and the slice at z -106 is empty. Only thoracic vertebrae and ribs are present. There is no lumbar spine, sacrum or pelvis in any CT, CBCT or kV image. The kV frames are masked to a 7x7 cm field (324x324 px) for Plan 1, or 5.5x7 cm (255x324 px) for Plan 2, around the lung tumour. Thoracic vertebrae enter that field only at some gantry angles; I saw them at about 201 degrees. The full-field CBCT projections do show the thoracic spine and ribs.
verdicts.counts: One subject: a single anthropomorphic 3D-printed thorax phantom made from one patient (Hazelaar 2018). The zip has 21,173 entries in 12,284,104,646 bytes. From the listing: 6,241 intrafraction kV DICOM frames (1610 + 1610 + 1510 + 1511 over 4 VMAT deliveries, 11 Hz, pre-masked, files named *_masked.dcm). 3,466 CBCT projections in XIM format: 895 x 2 from the 3D scans (15 Hz, 360 degrees, 60 s) and 838 x 2 from the 4D scans (7 Hz, 120 s). 7,197 MV cine frames (12.7 Hz, MV portal, exclude). The CT and CBCT reconstruction counts are given under paired_ct.
verdicts.licence: There is no formal licence. The AAPM page says "Anyone is welcome to use the MATCH Challenge datasets for their research. Any study that makes use of the MATCH Challenge dataset should cite" Mueller et al., Med Phys 2022;49(2):1161-1180, doi 10.1002/mp.15418. The GitHub analysis repository reports license: null.
verdicts.access_now: The Google Drive link on the AAPM page ('MATCH upload.zip', 11G) downloads without a login. Checked 2026-09-21: range requests return HTTP 206 and I read the central directory and several files. The two Dropbox links on the same page, for the "in-silico dataset" and the participants' results, return Dropbox 'shared_link_disabled'. Ground-truth target positions for each Part A experiment are public on GitHub: MarcoMueller-MCT/AAPM_GrandChallenge_MATCH, GroundTruth.zip and Motion.zip. I found no public release of the Part B images; each participant acquired those at their own institution.
corrections: The claim is inverted. The real, downloadable X-ray data are Part A (named the 'in-silico study'). They are real TrueBeam acquisitions of the phantom at Aarhus: 'Four treatments were simulated in a phantom experiment'. The claim 'Only the experimental part is real; Part A is in silico' is refuted.

No public release of the experimental-part (Part B) images was found. Each participant ran Part B with a shipped phantom at their own institution. The page offers only participant results, through a Dropbox link that now returns shared_link_disabled. The 'experimental phantom part' in the candidate's name does not match what can be downloaded.

The kV field is not physically collimated. The data readme says the field size 'was emulated by masking out pixels outside this area'. Files are named *_masked.dcm and pixels outside the box are zero: 324x324 px (7x7 cm) for Plan 1 and 255x324 px (5.5x7 cm) for Plan 2, on a 1024x768 detector.

The CBCT projections (3,466 XIM files) are NOT masked. They are full 1024x768 half-fan frames that show ribs and thoracic spine, which is more spine than the intrafraction kV frames show. The candidate did not mention this.
Anatomy is thoracic only. The CT ends at the lung bases, where the phantom is cut flat. There is no lumbar spine, sacrum or pelvis in any image, so this dataset cannot serve lumbosacral level work.
The 4DCT included in the zip has 3 mm slice thickness per its DICOM header. The readme's 1.5 mm refers to the 4DCT the GTV was delineated on.

Counts, which the candidate left uncounted: 6,241 kV frames, 3,466 CBCT projections, 7,197 MV cine frames (MV portal, exclude), 346-slice 0.6 mm 3DCT, 780-slice 4DCT. All come from one phantom in one session on 2020-01-08.

Labels: each frame has a gantry angle plus SID and SAD in its DICOM header. Ground-truth 3D target positions for each image are on GitHub. The RT structure set has target and organ contours (BODY, Lung Total, Heart, Aorta, Trachea, Bronchi, Esophagus, Spinal Cord, GTV/PTV) but no vertebra labels. I saw no calibrated projection matrices stated.
The data were generated only at Aarhus University Hospital. Image X (Sydney) and Amsterdam UMC appear as organisers and collaborators, not as data sources.
The licence is a website permission statement ('Anyone is welcome to use… for their research', with citation required), not a formal licence. The GitHub repository has no licence.
Access through the AAPM page's Dropbox links is broken. Only the Google Drive zip, 12.28 GB, is live.

candidate.name: 4D cone-beam CT phantom data set (Madesta et al. 2020; Varian TrueBeam raw scans)

There is no planning CT, but the CBCT can be reconstructed from each scan. Useful only for detector and geometry calibration.
candidate.institution: University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf (Werner lab)
candidate.device: Varian TrueBeam
candidate.anatomy: Thorax phantom with simplified spine insert
candidate.subjects: 1 phantom, 6 scans with different insert motions
candidate.pose_or_labels: Scan.xml geometry; known motion

verdicts.access_now: Open. You can download it now with no login and no request. The Zenodo API returns access_right "open" and status "published". A HEAD request on the file content returns HTTP 200 with content-length 6322963396, and byte-range requests return 206. That let me read the zip's central directory and the inner files without downloading all 6.3 GB. The record shows 175 downloads.
verdicts.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (the API gives license id "cc-by-nc-sa-4.0"). It is non-commercial and share-alike.
verdicts.counts:
The record holds one file, 4d_cbct_boosting.zip, 6,322,963,396 bytes, md5 332e6b27884dc504d0078bf01afc7231. It contains metadata.yml (753 bytes) and six stored, uncompressed inner zips of 1.052 to 1.055 GB each (2018_08_09_session_1 to _6, raw_data/ptv_1/2018-08-09_HHMMSS.zip). Each inner zip is a Varian TrueBeam scan export with this content:
- ClinicalInfo.wox and Scan.xml
- Acquisitions/ScanPreview.h5
- one acquisition folder of 895 or 896 .xim projections (Scan.xml Count values are 894, 895, 895, 895, 894, 895, which sums to 5,368 projections)
- AIR flat-field .xim files (4 plus 2)
- Calibrations (AIR, ASC, CROISSANT, GEO, HU, SC, and the HU slice .h5 files)
- Reconstructions (Reconstruction.xml, ImgParameters.h5, CoreLib logs)

No reconstructed volume ships: Reconstruction.xml has an empty Volume UID and there are no image-volume files.

Acquisition settings from Scan.xml: KV4D mode "4D Thorax UKE", full arc from -180 to 180 degrees, half fan with the imager shifted laterally by -160 mm, SID 1500 mm, SAD 1000 mm, detector 1024x768 at 0.388 mm per pixel, 125 kV, 20 mA, 15 ms pulses, 15 fps, 6 deg/s, 10:1 scatter grid, titanium filter plus half-fan bowtie. The GEO calibration is the nominal factory file from 2006 with all offset coefficients zero, so no measured flexmap is included.

Motion (from metadata.yml): target insert moved ±10 mm superior-inferior with a ±5 mm surrogate, in sin or cos^4 patterns with periods of 5.0, 2.5 and 7.5 s.
verdicts.anatomy: CIRS Model 008A Dynamic Thorax Phantom, one physical phantom. According to the CIRS/Sun Nuclear datasheet (008A-PB-082521), the phantom body approximates the thorax "using simplified geometries" and "contains a 3D anthropomorphic spine with cortical and trabecular bone". The spine is a fixed part of the body and does not move. The moving part is an interchangeable lung-equivalent epoxy rod holding a soft-tissue spherical target. There are no vertebral labels, and the phantom has no lumbar spine, sacrum or pelvis. metadata.yml gives region_of_interest as "lungs". Because of the half-fan geometry, each projection covers only from about 25 mm on one side of isocentre to about 239 mm on the other, so the midline spine sits near the edge of the field.
verdicts.paired_ct: None supplied. There is no planning CT and no reconstructed CBCT volume. A CBCT, including 4D phase bins, can be reconstructed from each scan's projections using the Scan.xml geometry and nominal calibration. The projections are in Varian's compressed .xim format, which needs a XIM reader such as RTK's.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes. These are real kV projections from a Varian TrueBeam on-board imager (linac serial 2479; the imaging mode is called "DynamicGainFluoro"). They show a phantom, not a patient. They come from a radiotherapy CBCT arc, not an interventional C-arm fluoroscopy run.
corrections: The spine is not a 'simplified spine insert'. The manufacturer datasheet describes a static 3D anthropomorphic spine with cortical and trabecular bone built into the phantom body. The moving insert is a lung-equivalent rod with a soft-tissue spherical target, so only the lung target moves and the spine stays fixed.
Dates: the Zenodo deposit was created 2023-12-12. 'published 2020-08-09' is only the publication_date metadata field. Scan.xml shows the scans were acquired 2018-08-09.

Files: there is one 6.32 GB zip containing six stored inner zips of about 1.05 GB each, not six loose folders. Each scan has 894 or 895 projections (5,368 in total by Scan.xml Count) plus 6 AIR flat-field frames.
No CBCT or CT volume is included. Reconstruction.xml has an empty Volume UID. 'ct_or_cbct_same_subject' is true only in the sense that a CBCT can be reconstructed from the projections.
The geometry calibration is nominal. GEO/Factory/Calibration.xml from 2006 has all offset coefficients zero, so there is no measured flexmap. That limits the claimed use for geometry calibration.
Half-fan acquisition with a -160 mm imager offset means each frame covers only about half the phantom width, with the midline and spine near the field edge.

Not verified: I could not read the paper's data availability statement. Wiley returned 403, even with browser TLS impersonation, and Europe PMC lists the paper as not open access. The link between the paper and the data rests on the Zenodo relation 'isSupplementTo 10.1002/mp.14441' and the record description. The paper also used SPARE challenge and in-house patient 4D CBCT data, and none of that is in this record.

Institution: the Zenodo record gives no creator affiliations. UKE is inferred from the 'uke-ipmi' community and the scan mode name '4D Thorax UKE'. The creators are Madesta, Werner and Sentker; Gauer is an author of the paper but not of the record.

The CT/CBCT claim is overstated. None of the six scans ships a CT or CBCT volume. Each Reconstructions/ folder holds only Reconstruction.xml (a 3D FDK job, 512 matrix, 2 mm slices), ImgParameters.h5 and CoreLib logs. There is no planning CT either. ClinicalInfo.wox references an RT Plan instance (SOP class 1.2.840.10008.5.1.4.1.1.481.5) from a study dated 2017-11-12, but that plan and its CT are not in the deposit. A CBCT can be rebuilt only from these same projections, so it is not an independent 3D reference.

The spine is not a 'simplified spine insert'. The vendor datasheet says the phantom body 'contains a 3D anthropomorphic spine with cortical and trabecular bone'. It is fixed in the body, not an insert. The only moving part (the 'insert' in the Zenodo text) is the lung-equivalent rod with its spherical target. In the lateral projection I decoded (Proj_00447, gantry 180.3 deg), about six separate vertebral bodies with disc spaces and posterior elements are visible. So the spine is anthropomorphic, but it is a moulded phantom, not human bone.

Anatomy: this is a thorax phantom (metadata.yml says region_of_interest: lungs). No source states which vertebral levels the spine represents. The phantom has no lumbosacral junction, sacrum, pelvis or ribs, and the projections show none. The half-fan offset detector (ImagerLat -160 mm) leaves the spine at or past the image edge in some views: I could not see it in Proj_00000 (gantry 360 deg).

Image count: the 6 scan folders hold 5,374 raw kV projections in total (895, 896, 896, 896, 895, 896). Each is a Varian compressed .xim, 1024x768 pixels at 0.388 mm (header: 0.0388 cm). Scan.xml for scan 1 gives Count=894 but the folder has 895 files. There is one subject, a physical phantom; no human is imaged.

Acquisition parameters from Scan.xml and the per-frame headers: KV4D, full 360 deg trajectory (-180 to 180), half fan with bowtie, 125 kV, 20 mA, 15 ms pulses, 15 fps, 6 deg/s, SID 1500 mm, SAD 1000 mm, 10:1 grid, titanium filter. Frames come from the KVModule in DynamicGainFluoro mode with KVBeamOn=1 and MVBeamOn=0, so they are real kV acquisitions, not DRRs, simulations or MV portal images. The ClinicalInfo patient fields read 'Deidentified' and the StudyID is 'Phantom1'.

Pose: there is no registered pose, but every frame header carries nominal machine geometry: GantryRtn, KVSourceRtn, KVDetectorLat/Lng/Vrt/Pitch, KVSourceVrt, couch Lat/Lng/Vrt/Rtn and timestamps. Each scan also has Calibrations/GEO (factory), AIR, HU and scatter calibration files, a respiratory phase value (MMPhase0) and NDI marker-block surrogate traces. These are machine readouts, not a 2D/3D registration.

Labels: there are no anatomical labels, segmentations or vertebra names. The only ground truth is the programmed motion pattern (insert SI +-10 mm, surrogate +-5 mm; sin or cos**4 at a period of 2.5, 5.0 or 7.5 s).

Dates: the Zenodo publication_date field reads 2020-08-09, but the record was created on 2023-12-12. The scans were acquired on 2018-08-09 (Scan.xml CreationDate 2018-08-09T19:34:51). The paper appeared in Med Phys 47(11):5619-5631, Nov 2020 (PMID 33063329).

Institution: the Zenodo creators (Madesta, Werner, Sentker) list no affiliation. The record sits in the 'uke-ipmi' community, and the paper's affiliation is University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf. Machine ID in Scan.xml: Linac3_2479.

Packaging: the download is one 6,322,963,396-byte zip (6.32 GB, 5.89 GiB). It contains six uncompressed inner zips of about 1.05 GB each plus metadata.yml. Zenodo serves HTTP range requests, and I read everything above through them without a full download. The .xim files need a Varian XIM decoder, such as pylinac, RTK, or the delta-predictor decoding I used.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes, as real acquisitions of a phantom rather than a human. The frames are raw kV cone-beam projections from the TrueBeam on-board imager. Headers read ImageSourceId=KVModule, ImageModeId=DynamicGainFluoro, KVBeamOn=1, MVBeamOn=0, at 125 kV, 20 mA and 15 ms. They are not DRRs, simulations or MV portal images. The object imaged is a CIRS 008A thorax phantom.
verdicts.paired_ct: Not shipped. There is no planning CT and no reconstructed CBCT volume in any of the six scans; the Reconstructions folders hold only job xml, ImgParameters.h5 and logs. A 3D volume can be rebuilt with FDK from the same projections, using the Scan.xml geometry and the GEO calibration. That volume depends on the projections themselves, so it is not an independent reference. An RT plan from a 2017-11-12 study is referenced but not included.
verdicts.anatomy: CIRS 008A Dynamic Thorax Phantom. Its epoxy body approximates a thorax (30 x 20 cm cross-section) and contains a '3D anthropomorphic spine with cortical and trabecular bone' (vendor datasheet), plus lung lobes and a moving lung-equivalent rod with a spherical target. The lateral projection shows about six vertebral bodies with posterior elements. No source names the levels. The phantom has no lumbar-sacral junction, sacrum, pelvis or ribs.
verdicts.counts: One physical phantom and six 4D-CBCT scans, all acquired on 2018-08-09. The scans contain 5,374 raw .xim projections in total (895, 896, 896, 896, 895, 896), each 1024x768 at 0.388 mm/px over a 360 deg half-fan arc.
verdicts.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (Zenodo license id cc-by-nc-sa-4.0).
verdicts.access_now: Open, no login. Direct download from Zenodo of one 6.32 GB zip that holds nested inner zips. HTTP range requests work, so individual projections can be pulled without the full download.

candidate.name: Lungman chest phantom: two CTs + one real digital radiograph + segmentations (Bangor)
candidate.why_relevant: Weak NEED A: a real radiograph and CT of the same anthropomorphic torso phantom (Kyoto Kagaku Lungman), with the spine, sternum and clavicles segmented. It is chest only, has a single projection with no recorded pose, and was used for gVirtualXRay validation.
candidate.institution: Bangor University / Betsi Cadwaladr UHB (Vidal, Tugwell-Allsup)
candidate.device: GE Thunder Platform DR (90 kVp, 0.1946 mm); Siemens SOMATOM Definition Edge CT
candidate.anatomy: Chest phantom incl. thoracic spine
candidate.pose_or_labels: No pose; 3D segmentations

corrections: Existence, open access and licence are confirmed from the primary record. Zenodo record 10782644 (concept 10782643, one version only) is status 'published' with access_right 'open' and licence cc-by-4.0. DataCite shows the DOI as 'findable' under CC BY 4.0. On 2026-09-21 the file URL returned HTTP 200 without a login and honoured range requests. I read the zip's central directory and pulled members straight from Zenodo.

Files: there is a single file, lungman_data.zip, 504,476,442 bytes (about 504 MB), md5 ff482cecc1917839fa4302fd98ef4b58, holding 1,437 entries. Contents: CD1 has one 426-slice CT and one black image. CD2 has two CT topograms, one empty series, a second 426-slice CT and a 110-slice CT. CD3 has one DX radiograph. SEGMENTATION has 426 label TIFFs (512x512 int32) plus labels.dat. MESHES has 19 STL files. There are also a README.md and 2 PNGs.

The claim of 'two CTs' undercounts. The archive holds three separate axial CT series from 2017-06-02: CD1/SE000000 (426 slices, I50f kernel, 128 mA), CD2/SE000003 (426 slices, I70f, 142 mA, a different SeriesInstanceUID) and CD2/SE000004 (110 slices, I31f, 53 mA). All three are 100 kVp at 0.625 mm pixels. The record's '512x512x426 and 320x320x298 mm3' is one volume given in voxels and then in mm, not two volumes of different sizes. The README says 'one of the CT scans has been fully segmented' but does not say which of the two 426-slice series it is.

The 'one radiograph' claim leaves out two more projections. CD2/SE000000 and SE000001 are Siemens topograms (scouts) of the same phantom: 120 kVp, 512x512, 1 mm pixels, ImageType LOCALIZER, with ImagePositionPatient and ImageOrientationPatient in the CT scanner frame. They are CT-scanner projections, not radiographs, and both have the same frontal orientation.

'No pose' is too strong. The DX header records ViewPosition PA, DistanceSourceToDetector 1800 mm, DistanceSourceToPatient 1751 mm, a fixed focused grid, 90 kVp and 298 mA. What is missing is any registration of the radiograph to the CT frame, and it was taken on a different date (2017-05-23 against 2017-06-02 for the CT), so the phantom was repositioned. The paper recovered alignment by optimisation.

Radiograph details checked from the header: GE 'Thunder Platform', 1881 rows x 1871 columns. The 0.194556 mm spacing is ImagerPixelSpacing, measured at the detector, not at the object. The image is 14-bit with PixelIntensityRelationship LOG and processing tag 'postero-anterior^Custom1', so it is a processed clinical-style image, not raw. Pixel values are non-trivial (488 to 7817). Identifying fields are 'REMOVED'.

The spine is one merged structure, not per-level labels. labels.dat lists spine-hard-650 (16) and spine-soft-650 (17), with separate labels for scapulae (18/19), sternum (20/21) and clavicles (22/23). No vertebra is individually labelled or named, so it gives no level-identity ground truth. Anatomy is chest only (the Kyoto Kagaku Lungman), and the phantom's thoracic spine is synthetic.

Minor points. The candidate's affiliations are approximately right: the Zenodo record gives Vidal as Science and Technology Facilities Council, DataCite gives Bangor University and STFC, and Tugwell-Allsup is Betsi Cadwaladr UHB. The record's publication_date is 2024-03-05, created 2024-03-06. The linked paper (CMPB 234:107500, June 2023) carries a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence; the dataset itself is CC BY 4.0.
One subject (a single phantom): no patients, no fluoroscopy, no lumbar or pelvic anatomy.
verdicts.access_now: Open, direct download with no login or request (HTTP 200 checked 2026-09-21): one 504 MB zip on Zenodo record 10782644.
verdicts.licence: CC BY 4.0 (Zenodo metadata and DataCite rightsList). The linked CMPB paper is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.
verdicts.counts: 1 phantom. 1 real DX PA radiograph (1871x1881). 2 CT topograms (512x512). 3 axial CT series (426, 426 and 110 slices at 0.625x0.625 mm, 100 kVp). 426 segmentation TIFF slices with 19 labels. 19 STL meshes. 1,437 zip entries, 504,476,442 bytes.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes. One real diagnostic chest radiograph (GE Thunder Platform, PA, 90 kVp, grid, SID 1800 mm, processed LOG image) plus two real CT topograms from the Siemens scanner. None of it is fluoroscopy.
verdicts.paired_ct: Same phantom, not co-registered. The radiograph (2017-05-23) predates the CT (2017-06-02), so the phantom was repositioned between them. The topograms sit in the CT scanner frame, with IPP/IOP recorded. The README does not say which of the two 426-slice series was segmented.
verdicts.anatomy: Kyoto Kagaku Lungman anthropomorphic chest phantom. The synthetic thoracic spine is segmented as one merged structure (spine-hard-650 and spine-soft-650), with no per-vertebra labels. Scapulae, sternum, clavicles, airways, heart, diaphragm, tumours, skin, sheets and couch are also segmented. No lumbar spine or pelvis.

verdicts.real_xray: Yes, but it is a phantom, not a patient. I downloaded CD3/DICOM/ST000000/SE000000/DX000000 from the zip and read its header: Modality DX, SOP class Digital X-Ray For Presentation, ImageType ORIGINAL/PRIMARY, GE Healthcare Thunder Platform, 90 kVp, 298 mA, 5 ms, fixed focused grid, scintillator detector, PA view, BodyPartExamined CHEST, StudyDate 2017-05-23. It is a real diagnostic acquisition, not a DRR. The zip also holds two real CT topograms (CD2 SE000000 and SE000001: Modality CT, ImageType ORIGINAL/PRIMARY/LOCALIZER, 120 kVp, both frontal). The candidate does not count these. The only simulated image is Pictures/lungman_model.png, a gVirtualXray render.
verdicts.paired_ct: The same Kyoto Kagaku Lungman phantom was scanned on a Siemens SOMATOM Definition Edge (StudyDate 2017-06-02, supine feet-first). That was 10 days after the radiograph, on a different device and in a different position, so the radiograph shares no frame of reference with the CT. The claim of "two CTs" is wrong. All three axial series (CD1 SE000000 with 426 slices and kernel I50f; CD2 SE000003 with 426 slices and kernel I70f; CD2 SE000004 with 110 slices and kernel I31f) have AcquisitionNumber 3, the same StudyInstanceUID and the same FrameOfReferenceUID. That makes them one helical scan (100 kVp, pitch 0.6, 0.625 x 0.625 x 0.7 mm) reconstructed three times. The two topograms share that FrameOfReferenceUID, so their geometry relative to the CT could in principle be recovered from DICOM (source-to-detector 1085.6 mm, source-to-patient 595 mm, 1 mm pixels). No source says this, and nobody has checked it.
verdicts.anatomy: Chest only. The radiograph is a PA chest running from the lower cervical spine and shoulders to the upper abdomen. The topograms show the phantom's spine ending near the thoracolumbar junction, above a solid abdominal block with no bone in it. There is no lumbar spine below roughly the T12/L1 region, and no sacrum or pelvis. The segmentation covers the thorax only, 296 mm craniocaudally, cut off at the lower ribs. It is useless for lumbosacral or pelvic work.
verdicts.counts: One subject, a physical phantom. Real X-ray projections: 1 DX radiograph (1871 x 1881 px, 0.194556 mm) plus 2 frontal CT topograms (512 x 512, 1 mm). CT: one acquisition in three reconstructions (426 + 426 + 110 slices). Segmentation: 426 TIFF label slices for one reconstruction, plus 20 STL meshes.
verdicts.licence: CC BY 4.0, per the Zenodo record license id cc-by-4.0 and the DataCite rightsList. The linked CMPB paper is a separate item under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Crossref).
verdicts.access_now: Open. lungman_data.zip (504,476,442 bytes, md5 ff482cecc1917839fa4302fd98ef4b58) downloads without login from https://zenodo.org/api/records/10782644/files/lungman_data.zip/content. On 2026-09-21 I listed its members and extracted the files I needed over HTTP range requests.
corrections: 'Two CTs' is wrong. The DICOM shows ONE helical acquisition (AcquisitionNumber 3, one StudyInstanceUID and FrameOfReferenceUID) reconstructed with three kernels: I50f (426 slices), I70f (426 slices) and I31f (110 slices). The README's '512x512x426 and 320x320x298 mm3' is one volume given in voxels and in mm, not two scans.
'1 radiograph' undercounts the real projections. The zip also has two real CT topograms (LOCALIZER, 120 kVp, both frontal) in CD2 SE000000 and SE000001, and they share the CT's FrameOfReferenceUID.

The radiograph and the CT come from different sessions: DX on 2017-05-23 (GE Thunder, PA chest, SID 1800 mm, SOD 1751 mm) and CT on 2017-06-02 (Siemens, supine FFS). No pose links the DX to the CT. The paper aligned them by image registration (README abstract: 'the simulations are used in an image registration framework'), and the registration parameters are not in the archive.

The 'spine' segmentation (labels 16 spine-hard-650 and 17 spine-soft-650) is one class that also contains the whole rib cage (visible in my coronal and sagittal MIP of the labels). It has no per-vertebra or per-level labels and no landmarks. There are also labels for the scapulae (18/19), sternum (20/21) and clavicles (22/23), 19 structure labels in all.

Anatomy: thoracic only. The phantom's spine ends near the thoracolumbar junction, so there is no lumbar spine, sacrum or pelvis in the radiograph, topograms or CT. It offers nothing for lumbosacral work.
The subject is an anthropomorphic phantom (Kyoto Kagaku Lungman) with synthetic bone, not a human.
Publication date: Zenodo metadata publication_date is 2024-03-05. The record was created and the DOI registered on 2024-03-06, and the README is dated 2024-02-20.

Affiliation: Zenodo gives Vidal as Science and Technology Facilities Council. DataCite gives Bangor University plus STFC. Tugwell-Allsup is Betsi Cadwaladr UHB. The DICOM InstitutionName is REMOVED, so no file names the hospital where the images were taken.
Pixel spacing is confirmed as 0.194556 mm (DICOM ImagerPixelSpacing). The README rounds it to 0.1946.

candidate.name: Robarts endoleak phantom fluoro-CT pairs (Xing et al., TBME 2025 / IPCAI 2025; Canon Alphenix)
candidate.why_relevant: A new device (Canon Alphenix C-arm). There are 156 fluoroscopy frames at systematically varied LAO-RAO and CRA-CAU angles and SIDs, against a CT of the same torso phantom. The phantom contains spinal elements and an aortic stent graft in PVA cryogel, and aluminium fiducials give the C-arm pose. That makes it useful for rendering-physics calibration. Availability is not stated.
candidate.institution: Robarts Research Institute, Western University; Northern Digital
candidate.device: Canon Alphenix C-arm
candidate.anatomy: Torso phantom with spinal elements, aorta/stent
candidate.pose_or_labels: Aluminium fiducials for C-arm pose; annotated target points

verdicts.access_now: Not downloadable, and there is no request route. Neither paper has a data availability statement. That covers both arXiv versions (only v1 of each exists) and the published IJCARS version, whose Ethics declarations list only conflict of interest, ethical approval and informed consent. The papers never say "available on request". Searches of Zenodo, Borealis (Western University's Dataverse), figshare and Hugging Face turned up no deposit by Shuwei Xing and nothing on an endoleak phantom. The first author's GitHub (Xingorno, Robarts) has three related repositories, and none holds data. Xingorno/FLUX-NAV (MIT, created 2025-10-16, last push 2026-04-10) has 14 files: README.md, LICENSE and 12 figures in Figs/ (PNGs and one GIF, about 23 MB), linking to YouTube videos. It has no images, CT or code. Xingorno/Seamleass-integration-of-magnetic-tracking-into-Fluoroscopy-guided-Interventions holds a 140-byte README that points to the arXiv preprint. Xingorno/Magnetic_Tracking_Integration is an empty repository. The only route is to email the corresponding author, Shuwei Xing ([e-mail withheld], per the PubMed affiliation), with no stated terms.
verdicts.licence: No data licence, because nothing has been released. The paper licences are: arXiv 2411.07495 CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; arXiv 2505.14854 CC BY 4.0; IEEE TBME version under the standard IEEE licence (paywalled, not open access per Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar); IJCARS version copyright 2025 CARS (paywalled). The MIT licence on the FLUX-NAV repository covers only its README and figures.
verdicts.counts: These counts are described in the papers and not released. TBME / arXiv 2411.07495 has 156 fluoro-CT pairs: 54 LAO-RAO (-30 to 30 deg), 64 CRA-CAU (-30 to 30 deg) and 38 SID (90-125 cm). Table III adds 31 phantom-movement pairs, which are not part of the 156. The IPCAI / IJCARS paper (arXiv 2505.14854) says the 54/64/38 frames were randomly selected from three fluoroscopic videos of 133 (RAO-LAO), 107 (CRA-CAU) and 61 (SID) frames. It also has 90 fluoroscopic images from RAO 90 to LAO 90 in 2-deg steps with Canon Alphenix joint-encoder readings, and a YOLOv8 set of 133 fluoroscopic images with manually annotated fiducial centroids. Fluoroscopy frames are 1017x1017 px at 0.29 mm. The CT is 365x280x791 voxels (797 in TBME) at 0.71x0.71x0.30 mm. There is one phantom, with a post-insertion CT for the needle experiment.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes, real fluoroscopy of a physical phantom. But the frames are screen captures, not detector or DICOM data. An Epiphan DVI2USB 3.0 frame grabber recorded the C-arm monitor at 30 fps, and SID was read from the on-screen display by OCR. That means display-processed images with on-screen overlays. The radiolucent field generator and two layers of aluminium fiducials are in the beam, and the authors run a deep adversarial decomposition to remove them. For calibrating rendering physics these are post-processed display images, not raw intensities.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, per the papers: a CT of the same endoleak phantom, plus a post-insertion CT. Neither is released.
verdicts.anatomy: An endoleak-repair training phantom (TBME reference 30). It contains "spinal elements", an aortic stent graft, a simulated aneurysm and feeding vessels, embedded in PVA cryogel. Neither paper describes the spinal elements: how many levels, what material, or whether they look like real bone. The spine is not the target. There are no vertebra labels. The annotated targets are 20-23 stent intersection points per image, plus the fiducial centroids.
corrections: Access is not 'unknown'. It is 'not released', with no data availability statement in either arXiv version or in the published IJCARS version, and no 'on request' clause. The author's related GitHub repositories hold only a README and figures, a pointer to the preprint, and nothing at all (one is empty).
The TBME paper is in print as IEEE Trans Biomed Eng 73(3):978-990, March 2026 (IEEE document 11119446, PMID 40773402). 2025-08-07 is the Crossref record date (early access), not the issue date.
The IPCAI paper was published as IJCARS 20(7):1391-1399 on 2025-05-16, DOI 10.1007/s11548-025-03395-0, PMID 40380074. The candidate gives only the arXiv id.

The 156 pairs are frames sampled at random from three fluoroscopic videos (133 + 107 + 61 = 301 frames). TBME Table III lists 31 more phantom-movement pairs outside the 156. The IPCAI paper adds 90 RAO90-LAO90 images with encoder angles. So '156' undercounts what was acquired, and it is only a count in a paper.
The images were grabbed from the C-arm's display monitor, not exported as DICOM or raw detector frames. That weakens the claimed value for calibrating rendering physics.

The aluminium fiducials (nineteen 4 mm spheres per layer, on two layers) are fixed to the field-generator mounting frame under the phantom, not to the phantom. They give the C-arm pose relative to that frame. The pose relative to the phantom or CT comes from the authors' fluoro-CT registration (mean projection distance about 0.5-0.6 mm), so it is estimated, not independent ground truth.

Canon Alphenix is named explicitly for the phantom-targeting experiment (TBME) and the 90-image virtual-fluoroscopy set (IPCAI). I found no sentence in the TBME text naming the C-arm for the 156-pair registration set. That it is the same Alphenix is a likely inference, not a stated fact.
The phantom's 'spinal elements' are never characterised, and the phantom is built for endoleak repair. Its spine realism and any use for vertebra naming are unverified.
The co-authors from Northern Digital Inc. are Pardasani, Jayarathne and Illsley. Canon Medical Systems is listed as a funder.

This is not a released dataset. It is internal experimental data from two method papers. Neither arXiv version has a data-availability statement: 2411.07495 lists no declarations, and 2505.14854 lists only Funding, Competing interests, Ethics and Consent. The first author's GitHub repos do not hold the data. FLUX-NAV is MIT-licensed but contains only a README and figures, and Seamleass-integration-... is a single README linking to arXiv. Access is 'none public / ask the authors', not 'unknown'.
Licence: no data licence exists. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (2411.07495) and CC BY 4.0 (2505.14854) are the arXiv licences for the papers. MIT covers only the FLUX-NAV repo's README and figures.

'Torso phantom' is a conflation. In 2411.07495, Fig. 2 ('X-ray image of a torso phantom and FG') is a chest phantom with ribs, lungs and heart, taken from the earlier decomposition work (ref 13, Xia 2023). The endoleak phantom is a different object. It is described only as 'spinal elements, an aortic stent, a simulated aneurysm and feeding vessels, embedded in PVA-C'. In the setup photo it is a box on the FG frame, not an anthropomorphic torso.

The spine content is limited and levels are not stated. The published endoleak frames (2411.07495 Fig. 8; 2505.14854 Fig. 6) show a short segment of about 4-5 vertebral bodies. Their interiors show a cross-hatch infill pattern, which suggests 3D-printed vertebrae rather than bone; this is my observation and the papers do not say it. No sacrum, pelvis, ribs or femora are visible, and no vertebral level is named anywhere.

'Systematically varied angles' overstates it. The 156 are frames RANDOMLY selected from three continuous fluoroscopic videos: 54 of 133 RAO-LAO frames, 64 of 107 CRA-CAU frames and 38 of 61 SID frames (2505.14854 Sec. 3.1). All are within about ±30° LAO-RAO / CRA-CAU, at SID 90-125 cm (2411.07495 Table III). 'Pairs' means each frame is paired with the same single phantom CT.

Canon Alphenix is named only for the needle-targeting experiment (2411.07495 Sec. III-D) and for a separate 90-image RAO-LAO -90° to +90° sweep in 2° steps with joint-encoder readings (2505.14854 Sec. 3.2). Neither paper explicitly says the 156 registration frames came from the Alphenix. It is likely (same lab, same phantom) but not stated.

The images are real C-arm acquisitions of a physical phantom, but they appear to be processed monitor-display captures, not raw detector images. The stated acquisition path is a frame grabber (Epiphan DVI2USB 3.0) capturing the C-arm monitor, with the image 'cropped from the captured monitor display' and SID read by OCR (2411.07495 Sec. II-D). A published endoleak frame (Fig. 8 A-1) carries display overlay text 'B 0 / C 4095 / SF H15'. This limits use for rendering-physics calibration, and kVp, filtration and dose are not reported.

Every frame has the radiolucent NDI field generator, an acrylic plate and 19 aluminium 4 mm spheres in the beam. The phantom CT and the FG-mounting-frame CT are separate and 'not co-registered' (2505.14854 Sec. 2.3). A DRR from the phantom CT alone therefore leaves out attenuators that are in the real frames.

Pose is estimated, not measured ground truth. The C-arm pose comes from PnP on the fiducials, refined by intensity registration. Intrinsics come from the SID shown on the monitor, not from calibration, and the authors attribute their 0.7 mm vs 0.25 mm gap to gantry flex and an uncalibrated SID. Neither paper says how the 'ground-truth' extrinsics for the phantom mPD were obtained.

'Annotated target points' are 20-23 stent-strut intersection points chosen in CT, not anatomical labels. The only manual 2-D annotations are fiducial centroids on 133 YOLO training images and needle tip/shaft points in the needle videos. There are no vertebra, level, segmentation or landmark labels on the spine.

The CT scanner and modality detail are not stated. The papers call it a phantom 'CT', 'pre-operative CT' or 'contrast-enhanced CT volume': 365x280x797 voxels (TBME arXiv) or 365x280x791 voxels at 0.71x0.71x0.30 mm (IPCAI arXiv). It is not stated whether it is diagnostic CT or CBCT from the Alphenix. A separate post-insertion non-contrast CT and an FG-frame CT also exist.

Additional unreleased image sets beyond the 156: 31 phantom-movement frames, the 90-image ±90° encoder-tagged sweep, 133 YOLO training images, and needle videos (39/31/40 frames). Subjects: one phantom, no humans or cadavers.

Missing ID and dates: the IPCAI paper was published as IJCARS 20(7):1391-1399, DOI 10.1007/s11548-025-03395-0, online 2025-05-16. The TBME article is vol 73(3):978-990, March 2026 issue; Crossref shows the DOI created 2025-08-07.
verdicts.access_now: None public. No data-availability statement in either arXiv version, and the IJCARS HTML is paywalled with none visible. The first author's (Shuwei Xing, GitHub Xingorno, Robarts) repos hold only a README and figures (FLUX-NAV, MIT) or a README linking arXiv. Getting the data would require a request to the authors (Xing / E.C.S. Chen, Robarts Research Institute).
verdicts.anatomy: A box-type endoleak phantom in PVA-C holding an aortic stent graft, a simulated aneurysm and feeding vessels, plus 'spinal elements'. The published frames show a short segment of about 4-5 vertebral bodies with a cross-hatch infill look, apparently 3D-printed. Levels are not named. No sacrum, pelvis, ribs or femora are visible. The 'torso phantom' figure in the TBME paper is a different chest phantom.
verdicts.counts: One phantom and no human subjects. The 156 registration frames (54 RAO-LAO, 64 CRA-CAU, 38 SID) were randomly chosen from videos of 133, 107 and 61 frames, all within ±30° and at SID 90-125 cm. Also: 31 phantom-motion frames, a 90-image RAO-LAO ±90° sweep with Canon Alphenix encoder readings, 133 YOLO training images, and needle videos of 39/31/40 frames. Frames are 1017x1017 px at 0.29 mm. None of it is released.
verdicts.licence: No data licence. The papers are arXiv CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (2411.07495) and CC BY 4.0 (2505.14854). The FLUX-NAV repo is MIT but contains no data. TBME and IJCARS are publisher copyright.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, for the same physical phantom: one phantom CT (365x280x791-797 voxels, 0.71x0.71x0.30 mm, described as contrast-enhanced), plus a post-insertion non-contrast CT and a separate CT of the FG mounting frame that is not co-registered to it. The scanner is not stated, and so is whether it is diagnostic CT or C-arm CBCT.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes: real C-arm fluoroscopy of a physical phantom, not DRRs; DRRs appear only as the registration's simulated images. They appear to be monitor-display captures via a frame grabber, with display overlay text visible. The FG and aluminium fiducials are in every frame, and the C-arm is Canon Alphenix, named explicitly only for the needle and ±90° sweep sets. kVp and filtration are not reported.

candidate.name: Balgrist Femur multi-view C-arm X-ray + photon-counting CT (Flepp et al., IJCARS/IPCAI 2025) [kept: open extremity CT + real C-arm]
candidate.why_relevant: This is femur only, so it fails NEED A on anatomy. It is kept under the extremity exception because it is open and pairs a real calibrated C-arm with a same-specimen CT. There are 5 cadaveric specimens with 10 views each about 9 degrees apart, poses calibrated from a 16-sphere fiducial, and a photon-counting CT. It is a new Siemens device (Fluorospot Compact S1) for rendering-physics calibration. It comes from the same Balgrist group as the Jecklin lumbar request and is now also shipped in xvr-data.
candidate.institution: Balgrist University Hospital / University Children's Hospital Zurich / ETH Zurich
candidate.device: Siemens XA Fluorospot Compact S1 (976x976); CT Siemens NAEOTOM Alpha photon-counting (0.2 mm)
candidate.anatomy: Distal femur (extremity)
candidate.pose_or_labels: Calibrated per-image poses; fiducials
candidate.licence: None stated on Zenodo; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 in the xvr-data remix

verdicts.access_now: It is open and downloadable now with no login. On 2026-09-21 an unauthenticated HEAD request to https://zenodo.org/api/records/15753063/files/dataset_ipcai.zip/content returned HTTP 200 with content-length 6,670,978,774. A ranged GET returned a valid ZIP (PK) header, and I read the whole central directory over HTTP range requests. The Zenodo record is published, access_right is open, and there is no access-request gate (allow_user_requests and allow_guest_requests are both false). The record shows 307 downloads. There is one file, dataset_ipcai.zip (md5 cc8bf3e445495d2deb6d50dd058dc977, 6.67 GB zipped, 6.86 GB unzipped). The registration code is NOT open: the GitHub README says it is available only 'upon reasonable request' under a licence agreement, and it cites pending patent EP25168706.7. A second open copy is the remix at huggingface.co/datasets/eigenvivek/xvr-data under femur/. It is ungated, 404.6 MB, with 49 X-ray DICOMs, 5 NIfTI volumes, masks and fiducials.pt.
verdicts.licence: The candidate's 'None stated on Zenodo' is wrong. The record's rights field carries a custom 'Research-Only Dataset License'. The legacy API 'license' key is absent, which probably explains the earlier miss. Its terms: royalty-free use, derivatives and redistribution 'solely for Academic Research', defined as non-commercial research or teaching at a non-profit educational or governmental institution. Commercial use is prohibited without written permission from the licensor (3.1). Redistribution outside academic research or under a different licence is not allowed (3.2). Citing the paper is required. The licence is governed by Swiss law and terminates automatically on breach. The xvr-data remix is labelled CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and says it is 'hosted with permission from original authors'. Neither licence permits commercial or product work.
verdicts.counts: From the ZIP central directory: 6,663 entries. Five specimens (folders 1-5), each with CT_clean/, meshes/{hq,mid,lq}/ and x-ray images/{registration_views,control_views}. Specimen 1's folder is named 'x-ray images' with a space; the others use 'x-ray_images'. X-ray views per specimen are 10, 11, 10, 9 and 9, which is 49 in total, not 50. That is 34 registration views plus 15 control views, and each view has a pose .txt (49 .txt files). The xvr-data remix also has 49 (10/11/10/9/9). CT: 6,447 DICOM slices (1,466 / 1,227 / 1,141 / 1,156 / 1,457), 6.71 GB. Meshes: 60 STL files (femur, shaft, condyle_A, condyle_B at 3 resolutions per specimen). Images: 40 JPG plus 21 PNG. Specimen 4's X-rays are PNG, not JPG. The 12 remaining PNGs are control-view annotation masks for specimens 1, 2, 3 and 5; specimen 4 has none.
verdicts.anatomy: The anatomy is distal femur and knee only; no spine and no pelvis. The paper says 'five cadaveric distal femur specimens (three female, two male)', four right and one left, BMI 19-28. A sampled X-ray (specimen 1, view 11) shows the distal femur, condyles and proximal tibia, two K-wires, and the radiolucent fiducial cage with metal beads. The CT DICOM header has BodyPartExamined = EXTREMITY. Specimen 1's CT covers about 440 mm craniocaudally (1,466 slices at a 0.3 mm step). For a spine fluoroscopy project it serves neither need; at best it could calibrate rendering physics for this one device.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, each specimen has its own CT. Sampled header (specimen 1): Siemens Healthineers NAEOTOM Alpha (photon-counting, ImageType includes COUNT), Rows/Columns 1024x1024, PixelSpacing 0.439 mm, SliceThickness 0.4 mm, slice step 0.3 mm (ImagePositionPatient z 1836.369 to 1836.069), kernel Br84u, StudyDate 20240828. Patient name and ID read ANONYMIZED, but InstitutionName 'SCMI Balgrist Campus' is still in the header. This does not match the paper, which says 512x512 and 0.2 mm slice thickness; I checked only specimen 1. Segmentations ship as STL meshes, not voxel label maps. xvr-data adds mask.nii.gz and volume.nii.gz for each subject.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes, these are real C-arm images, 976x976; I viewed one. Per the paper the device is a Siemens XA Fluorospot Compact S1, but the release has no X-ray DICOM, so I could not confirm the device or exposure settings (kVp, mAs) from the files. The images are 8-bit greyscale stored as 3 identical RGB channels, already display-processed with a dark border frame. Specimens 1, 2, 3 and 5 are lossy JPEG; specimen 4 is PNG. The xvr-data .dcm files are 953,142 bytes (976x976 at 1 byte per pixel plus a header), so they are converted from the same 8-bit images, not raw detector data. Each view's pose .txt holds a rotation matrix R, a translation t in mm, a single focal length in px (for example 3745.67 and 3968.79) and principal point (488, 488). The paper says the poses come from the 16-bead (2 mm) fiducial and that the C-arm moved about 9 degrees between views. Lossy 8-bit post-processed stills limit rendering-physics calibration: there are no raw intensities and no acquisition metadata.
corrections: The licence IS stated on Zenodo. It is a custom 'Research-Only Dataset License' in the record's rights field: academic non-profit research only, no commercial use, no relicensing, Swiss law. It is not 'none stated'. The xvr-data remix is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 with author permission.
There are 49 X-ray images, not 50. Per specimen: 10/11/10/9/9 (34 registration views plus 15 control views). The paper's '10 perspectives per specimen' does not hold for specimens 2, 4 and 5.
The '6.7 GB' is the zipped size of the single file (6,670,978,774 bytes). Unzipped it is 6.86 GB, of which DICOM CT is 6.71 GB.
CT resolution: the released DICOM (specimen 1) is 1024x1024, 0.44 mm pixels, 0.4 mm thickness, 0.3 mm step. The paper and the candidate say 512x512 and 0.2 mm. Only specimen 1 was checked.

The X-rays are not DICOM and not raw. They are 8-bit greyscale JPEG (lossy), or PNG for specimen 4, already display-processed, with no acquisition metadata. The Fluorospot Compact S1 attribution rests only on the paper text.

Dates: the Zenodo metadata publication_date 2025-05-20 is the article's online date (Crossref published-online 2025-05-20). The record itself was created and published 2025-06-27. There is one version (1.0).
Zenodo minted no DOI for the dataset. The record's DOI field is the article DOI 10.1007/s11548-025-03391-4 (provider external), so the only unique dataset identifier is the record id 15753063.

The code is not open. The GitHub repo holds only a README: code 'upon reasonable request' under a licence agreement, pending patent EP25168706.7. The paper's claim that 'source code and the dataset are publicly available' is true only for the dataset.
The IJCARS article (vol 20, issue 7, pp 1401-1408, PMID 40394451) is not open access per Europe PMC. The arXiv preprint 2506.13292 is open.
Anatomy is distal femur plus knee (the proximal tibia is visible in the X-ray), with no spine or pelvis, so serves='neither' stands.

Not checked: the claimed link to a 'Jecklin lumbar request' from the same Balgrist group. The Zenodo creators are Balgrist and University Children's Hospital Zurich; the University of Zurich also appears as an affiliation, but ETH Zurich does not appear in the Zenodo creator list.

verdicts.real_xray: Yes. These are real C-arm acquisitions, not DRRs, not simulated and not MV portal images. I read the Zenodo zip remotely through HTTP range requests and pulled out sample files. The images show the 3D-printed fiducial frame with its metal beads, two metal pins in the bone, soft tissue, noise and detector edge vignetting. The paper says the images came from a Siemens XA 'Fluorospot Compact S1' at 976x976 with a 296.7 mm sensor, taken from about 10 perspectives roughly 9 degrees apart. That is a limited arc, not a full orbit. DRRs were used only to train the contour network. Caveat: the released X-rays are 8-bit display images, not raw detector data. Subjects 1, 2, 3 and 5 are lossy JPEGs of 65-90 KB each. Subject 4 is 8-bit PNG with inverted polarity, so bone is bright. All are 976x976 RGB with three identical channels. There are no X-ray DICOM tags (kVp, mAs, dose), so the device string cannot be checked against the files. The xvr-data .dcm files are 953,142 bytes each, which is 976x976 at 8 bits plus a header. They are rewraps of those 8-bit images, not original DICOMs.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, each X-ray set has a CT of the same specimen. There are 5 CT series in the CT_clean folders, one per specimen. The DICOM headers read Manufacturer 'Siemens Healthineers', Model 'NAEOTOM Alpha' (photon-counting), BodyPartExamined EXTREMITY, JPEG-lossless encoding, kernel Br84u. The headers contradict the stated spec. The files are 1024x1024 with 0.34-0.44 mm pixels and SliceThickness 0.4 mm at a 0.3 mm increment, with 1141-1466 slices per specimen covering about 340-440 mm. The paper's '512x512, 0.2 mm slice thickness' does not match. I also checked the pairing myself. I projected specimen 1's CT-frame femur mesh (meshes/lq/femur.stl) through the released R, t, focal length and principal point for 3 views (registration 4 and 19, control 12). It landed on the femur in all 3, but only after flipping image rows (v -> 2*cy - v). So the poses appear to be in the CT frame and usable as CT-to-X-ray ground truth, but the paper does not say so and does not document the row convention. I tested specimen 1 only.
verdicts.anatomy: Distal femur and knee only. Both the X-rays and the CT show the distal femoral shaft, condyles, patella and proximal tibia. The femur meshes are 164-207 mm long. There is no lumbar spine, sacrum or pelvis in any image or CT. It fails NEED A on anatomy.
verdicts.counts: 5 cadaveric distal-femur specimens (paper Table 1: 3 female and 2 male, 4 right and 1 left, age 65-76, BMI 19-28). There are 49 X-rays, not 50. Per specimen that is 10, 11, 10, 9 and 9. They split into 34 registration views (7/8/7/6/6) and 15 control views (3 per specimen). The HF xvr-data remix has the same 49 (10/11/10/9/9). There are 5 CT series, 1141-1466 slices each. The Zenodo file is one zip, dataset_ipcai.zip, of 6,670,978,774 bytes with 6,663 entries.
verdicts.licence: Zenodo does state a licence. The record page's rights field carries a custom 'Research-Only Dataset License'. It bans commercial use. It limits use to academic research at non-profit educational or governmental institutions. Redistribution is allowed only for academic research and must keep the licence. It forbids re-identification, ends automatically on breach, and falls under Swiss law. Only the legacy API 'license' field is empty, which probably misled the earlier pass. The HF xvr-data README labels the Femur set CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and says it is hosted with the authors' permission. That matches the arXiv paper's licence, not the Zenodo dataset licence. The code is not open: it is available on request under a licence agreement, and a patent application is pending (EP25168706.7).
verdicts.access_now: Open download with no login: one 6.67 GB zip from zenodo.org/records/15753063, under the research-only licence above. A remix with NIfTI volume and mask, 8-bit DICOM-wrapped X-rays, .pt poses, fiducials.pt and an undocumented warp.txt per specimen is public at huggingface.co/datasets/eigenvivek/xvr-data under femur/. The project page rflepp.github.io/BoneSubstructureContours2D3DRegistration/ returns 404.
corrections: The X-ray count is 49, not 50. Per specimen it is 10/11/10/9/9 (34 registration views and 15 control views). This contradicts the paper's '10 perspectives per specimen'. xvr-data also has 49.

The CT spec in the candidate and the paper (512x512, 0.2 mm) is contradicted by the released DICOM headers: 1024x1024, 0.34-0.44 mm pixels, 0.4 mm SliceThickness at a 0.3 mm increment, 1141-1466 slices, JPEG-lossless. Photon-counting NAEOTOM Alpha is confirmed.

Licence: Zenodo does state one, a custom 'Research-Only Dataset License' (non-commercial, academic research at non-profit institutions only, Swiss law). 'None stated on Zenodo' is wrong. xvr-data's CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 label matches the arXiv paper's licence, not the dataset's.

The released X-rays are 8-bit display exports: lossy JPEG for specimens 1, 2, 3 and 5, and polarity-inverted PNG for specimen 4. There are no raw detector values and no acquisition DICOM tags. That makes them weak for rendering-physics or intensity calibration. The xvr-data .dcm files are 8-bit rewraps, not original DICOMs.

The X-ray device 'Siemens XA - Fluorospot Compact S1' appears only in the paper. The release carries no X-ray metadata to confirm it, and the string may name Siemens imaging software rather than a specific C-arm model.

Labels: each image has a pose .txt with R, t, focal length about 3759 px and principal point (488, 488). There are CT femur meshes (femur, shaft and condyle_A/B at hq/mid/lq) and control-view contour masks (red diaphysis, green and yellow condyles). The contour masks exist for specimens 1, 2, 3 and 5 only; specimen 4's control views have no annotation file. The fiducial's 3D bead geometry is not in the Zenodo zip. xvr-data adds fiducials.pt and warp.txt without documenting them.

Pose frame: the paper says only that poses were estimated from the 16-bead fiducial (PnP, 0.8 px inlier threshold). It does not say they are in CT coordinates. My own projection test on specimen 1 (3 views) matched the femur only with a row flip, so the poses look CT-registered, but the convention is undocumented and I did not check the other specimens.

Dates: Zenodo publication_date 2025-05-20 equals the IJCARS e-publication date (Europe PMC, PMID 40394451; IJCARS 20(7):1401-1408, print July 2025). The record was created 2025-06-27. Both dates are correct for different events.
The 16-sphere fiducial is confirmed: 16 metal spheres of 2 mm in a radiolucent 3D-printed frame mounted on a K-wire. The released images also show two metal pins through the femur.
The Zenodo creator list leaves out Leon Nissen, who is a paper author. This is minor.
Not checked: the claimed tie to 'the Jecklin lumbar request'. Fürnstahl (Balgrist) is an author, but I found no primary source linking this record to a lumbar dataset.
Anatomy is distal femur and knee only in both X-ray and CT, with no lumbar spine, sacrum or pelvis. It serves neither need, and keeping it rests only on the extremity exception.

candidate.name: Goswami IOERT pig data on IEEE DataPort: 7 calibrated C-arm projections + CT [kept: open extremity CT + real C-arm]
candidate.why_relevant: A correction to the known entry, which lists this as Elekta kV. The DataCite record describes 7 C-arm projections at different poses of a pig lower-limb specimen, geometrically calibrated with fiducials on the applicator, plus its CT. It is limb anatomy, kept under the extremity exception for device calibration only.
candidate.institution: Universidad Carlos III de Madrid / Hospital Gregorio Marañón (Goswami, Pascau)
candidate.device: C-arm (model not stated in record)
candidate.anatomy: Pig lower limb
candidate.pose_or_labels: Fiducial-based geometric calibration; registration GT

corrections: The candidate's main 'correction' is wrong. The known entry was right to call these Elekta kV images. The source paper (Goswami et al., IEEE Access 8:137501, 2020, doi 10.1109/ACCESS.2020.3011915, section IV.A.1.d) says the '2D C-arm radiographs ... were acquired with the same Elekta Synergy LINAC' at 120 kVp and 5 mA, one every 15 degrees from -45 to +45. That is the on-board kV imager of a radiotherapy linear accelerator (PerkinElmer amorphous-silicon flat panel, 410x410 mm, 1024x1024 pixels, source-to-detector distance 1536 mm). The paper uses 'C-arm' generically. No surgical or mobile C-arm was used.

The claim of a fiducial-based geometric calibration is overstated. Section IV.A.4 says the Elekta Synergy 'was confirmed to be regularly geometrically calibrated, providing accurate intrinsic parameter values. Thus, no additional calibration was necessary.' The applicator fiducials were used only to estimate each projection's pose. The ground truth comes from a 3D-3D registration of the intraoperative CBCT to the preoperative CT, combined with a point-based registration of the applicator CT. It is not a fiducial calibration.

Institution: the submitter and first author (Goswami) are at the Biomedical Image Technologies Lab, ETSI Telecomunicacion, Universidad Politecnica de Madrid (UPM). The dataset is not primarily UC3M/Gregorio Maranon. Pascau (UC3M/IiSGM) is one of six authors. The paper does not name the site where the pig was imaged.

Access is 'open' only after a login. The DataPort page says 'Open Access dataset files are accessible to all logged in users ... free IEEE account ... IEEE Membership is not required'. Every file link is an href='#' pop-up, and the pop-up shown to anonymous users says 'This dataset requires an IEEE DataPort Subscription' (template text that contradicts the page). Guessed anonymous S3 paths returned 403. I did not complete an actual download.

The release has two imaging conditions, not one: PlanarImagesSofttissue.zip and PlanarImagesNoSoftTissue.zip, plus CBCT_SoftTissue.zip and CBCT_NOSoftTissue.zip. The paper describes only one intraoperative state (after about 3 cm of soft tissue was removed). The release may therefore hold more than 7 projections, perhaps 2 x 7. The figure of '7 projections' comes from the paper; I could not open any file to count. Transform matrices are provided only for the SoftTissue condition.

Documentation is minimal. The only instructions are 'These are the raw data and some preliminary data retrieved from them.' DataCite gives no sizes or formats, and neither source states the file formats (DICOM, MHA, etc.).

The paper does not cite the DataPort DOI. It only says 'With this paper, we also make the data available as a new resource.' The DataPort record (created 2021-04-20, about 9 months after publication) links back to the paper at ieeexplore 9149621.

The paired CT is not the same state as the projections. The preoperative CT (Siemens CT simulator) was taken before the soft-tissue removal and before the specimen moved to the LINAC room. Only the intraoperative CBCT (Elekta, 1 mm isotropic, 70 kVp) matches the projection setup.
The human feasibility data in the paper used simulated DRR projections, not real X-ray, and is not part of this release (title: 'Pig data ...'). The anatomy is a pig lower limb only, with no spine.
verdicts.access_now: The record is live and 'Open Access' on IEEE DataPort (DataCite state 'findable', resourceType 'Open Access Dataset'). Files are behind a login: the page says a free IEEE account is enough and membership is not needed, but the pop-up shown to anonymous users says a DataPort subscription is required. Anonymous S3 access returned 403. I have not verified a download.
verdicts.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DataCite rightsList cc-by-4.0). The paper itself is also CC BY 4.0.
verdicts.counts: 7 files, about 195.5 MB in total: CTscan_Pig.zip 46.1 MB; CBCT_SoftTissue.zip 41.61 MB; CTscan_Applicator.zip 40.57 MB; PlanarImagesSofttissue.zip 11.75 MB; CBCT_NOSoftTissue.zip 43.66 MB; PlanarImagesNoSoftTissue.zip 11.82 MB; MatricesSoftTissue.zip 4.73 KB. One specimen (an 11 kg pig lower limb). The paper reports 7 projections at -45..+45 in 15-degree steps; the two planar zips (about 11.8 MB each, consistent with 7 x 1024x1024 16-bit each) suggest two sets. Not verified by opening them.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes, these are real kV projection radiographs. They come from the Elekta Synergy LINAC's on-board kV imager (PerkinElmer a-Si flat panel 410x410 mm, 1024x1024 pixels, source-to-detector distance 1536 mm, 120 kVp, 5 mA), not from a surgical or mobile C-arm fluoroscope.
verdicts.paired_ct: Three volumes: (1) preoperative CT of the pig limb (Siemens CT simulator; 0.98x0.98x1 mm; 512x512x480; 130 kVp), taken before the ~3 cm soft-tissue removal; (2) intraoperative CBCT (Elekta Synergy; 1x1x1 mm; 410x410x264; 70 kVp), taken at the same setup as the projections, supplied as a SoftTissue and a NoSoftTissue version; (3) CT of the applicator (0.25x0.25x1 mm; 512x512x248). The ground truth is a CBCT-to-CT registration.
verdicts.anatomy: Pig lower limb (11 kg ex vivo specimen in a tray) with a methacrylate IOERT applicator carrying 10 Suremark fiducials and 4 mm skin markers. No spine.

corrections: The device claim is wrong, and so is the 'correction to the known entry'. The IEEE Access paper (Sec. IV-A-1-d) and the Goswami thesis (Sec. 5.2) both say the '2D C-arm radiographs' were taken with the SAME Elekta Synergy LINAC used for the CBCT: its gantry-mounted kV imager, PerkinElmer a-Si flat panel, 410x410 mm active area, 1024x1024 pixels, source-to-panel distance 1536 mm, 120 kVp, 5 mA. The authors call the LINAC gantry a 'C-arm'. No surgical C-arm or fluoroscope was used. The known entry ('Elekta kV') was right; 'C-arm (model not stated)' should be reverted to Elekta Synergy kV imager.

The images are real kV projections of a physical specimen, not DRRs and not MV portal images: 120 kVp on the kV panel. But they come from a radiotherapy LINAC imager, not an intraoperative fluoroscope, so their geometry and image formation are not C-arm fluoroscopy.

The poses are gantry angles -45, -30, -15, 0, +15, +30 and +45 degrees about the radial axis. The candidate says the C-arm was 'geometrically calibrated with fiducials on the applicator'. That is only the workflow's pose estimate. The ground truth uses the Elekta's routine geometric calibration for the intrinsics ('no additional calibration was necessary'), plus a transform built from applicator-marker registration to the CBCT and a CBCT-to-CT 3D-3D registration.

The file list is incomplete. The DataPort page lists CTscan_Pig.zip (46.1 MB), CTscan_Applicator.zip (40.6 MB), CBCT_SoftTissue.zip (41.6 MB), CBCT_NOSoftTissue.zip (43.7 MB), PlanarImagesSofttissue.zip (11.75 MB), PlanarImagesNoSoftTissue.zip (11.82 MB) and MatricesSoftTissue.zip (4.7 KB). So there are two intraoperative CBCTs and two planar-image sets, not just '7 projections + CT'. Neither the paper nor the thesis says what the SoftTissue/NoSoftTissue split means, or how many images each zip holds. I could not see inside the files because downloading needs a login. Only 7 projections are described in the text.

The paper's human sarcoma case is NOT real X-ray: its C-arm images were simulated as DRRs from the intraoperative CT. Going by the title ('Pig data') and the file list, the human data are not in the release.

Institution: the lead lab is Universidad Politecnica de Madrid (Goswami, Ledesma-Carbayo). The animal data were collected at Clinica Universidad de Navarra, Madrid: the acknowledgment thanks A. Perales Molina 'for his assistance with the collection of animal data', and the LINAC in Fig. 4d carries CUN branding. Gregorio Maranon is where the (simulated) human data came from. UC3M enters only through Pascau.

Anatomy: one 11-kg pig lower limb (the paper says 'lower limb' and does not say fore or hind). About 3 cm of soft tissue was removed to mimic a surgical cavity, and a PMMA applicator carrying fiducials was placed on it. No source says lumbar spine, sacrum or pelvis is present. The example radiograph (Fig. 5a) shows limb bone, applicator and skin markers only. It gives no lumbosacral anatomy and is at most a geometry or registration test.

Access: the page is labelled Open Access, but downloading requires logging in with a free IEEE account. The licence is CC BY 4.0 according to the DataCite rightsList. The DataPort page text I extracted does not show a licence statement.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes, real acquisitions, but not from a C-arm. The images are kV planar projections (120 kVp, 5 mA) of a physical pig-limb specimen, taken with the Elekta Synergy LINAC's gantry-mounted kV imager: PerkinElmer a-Si panel, 1024x1024 pixels, 410 mm field, source-to-panel distance 1536 mm. They are not DRRs and not MV portal images. The paper's human-data radiographs were DRRs and, going by the title and file list, are not in the release.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, same specimen. There is a preoperative CT of the pig limb (Siemens CT simulator, 0.98x0.98x1 mm, 512x512x480, 130 kVp), taken before tissue removal. There are intraoperative CBCTs from the same Elekta Synergy (1 mm isotropic, 410x410x264), taken in the same setup as the planar images; the file list has two, SoftTissue and NOSoftTissue. There is also a separate CT of the applicator. The ground-truth pose comes from a CBCT-to-CT registration and a point registration of the applicator markers.
verdicts.anatomy: One 11-kg pig lower limb (not stated whether fore or hind), with about 3 cm of soft tissue removed and a PMMA IOERT applicator carrying fiducials, plus 4 mm skin markers. No source says lumbar spine, sacrum or pelvis is present. The example radiograph shows limb bone only.
verdicts.counts: One animal specimen. The paper and thesis describe 7 kV projections at gantry angles from -45 to +45 degrees in 15-degree steps. The release has two planar-image zips (SoftTissue and NoSoftTissue, about 11.8 MB each), two CBCT zips, a pig CT, an applicator CT and a matrices zip (4.7 KB). The number of images per zip is not stated anywhere I could read, and the files need a login.
verdicts.licence: CC BY 4.0 according to the DataCite rightsList. The associated IEEE Access paper is also CC BY 4.0.
verdicts.access_now: IEEE DataPort Open Access. The page loads without an account, but downloading the files requires a free IEEE account login. The DOI resolves and the record is active.

candidate.name: Science Data Bank 10-case CT + native-DICOM fluoroscopy set for 2D-3D registration (HeadPhantom_2D3D_TrainingDataset) [kept marked: off-target anatomy]
candidate.why_relevant: Ten cases, each with one CT and several fluoroscopy frames in native DICOM, in one 5.37 GB zip. The file name and keywords ('head', '2d-3d registration', 'style transfer') point to a head phantom, so it fails both needs on anatomy. It is kept, by analogy with the extremity exception, because it is open real fluoroscopy plus CT of bone. The native fluoroscopy DICOM headers (device and geometry tags) could help device calibration. Only DataCite surfaces it. Access conflict: one pass read shareStatus PUBLIC with no embargo; another got 'PERMISSION NO ACCESS' from the SciDB API, so a login may be needed. The anatomy is unverified.
candidate.institution: Northeastern University, Shenyang, China (Zixuan Qin)
candidate.device: not stated (native DICOM)
candidate.anatomy: Head phantom (per file name and keywords; not verified)
candidate.n_images: Multiple fluoroscopy frames per case (count not listed)
candidate.pose_or_labels: unknown

corrections: Access is open with no login. The download endpoint returned HTTP 200 anonymously, with Content-Length 5,370,184,583 and Accept-Ranges: bytes. Using only range reads, I read the zip's central directory (4,619 entries, ZIP64) and decoded real DICOM from inside it. The 'PERMISSION NO ACCESS' / login report is explained by the SciDB file-tree browsing API (getFileTree), which returns code 20001 'User Not Login'. The getAllUrl and download endpoints do not need a login. The versionList API reports shareStatus PUBLIC, protectMonth 0 and status 3 (published).

Rate limiting: after a few hundred anonymous range requests the download host returned HTTP 429, and it was still returning 429 more than 10 minutes later. A single full download should be unaffected, but a scripted per-file census from one IP gets throttled.

The 'CT' is not a diagnostic CT. In each case it is a C-arm cone-beam CT reconstructed on the angiography system itself. The tags are Modality XA, SOP class CT Image Storage, SeriesDescription 'GCT_20sGCT' and DerivationDescription 'CONTRAST-3D Recon From 2D XRay Angiography'. Slices are 512x512 at 0.493 mm: 376 slices per case on the 8 NeuAngio 43C cases and 512 per case on the 2 NeuAngio 33F cases. It is a paired CBCT from the same subject and the same device, not a CT.

The device IS stated in the DICOM headers. It is Neusoft Medical Systems NeuAngio 43C (8 studies, serial 325867020671, acquired 2024-10-10) and NeuAngio 33F (2 studies, serial 3258670209151, acquired 2024-10-12). Both are angiography C-arms. The UID root 1.2.156.14702 is consistent with Neusoft.

The candidate omits the most useful part.
