For a spine fluoroscopy project: pelvic AP/inlet views only, no vertebral content, at most 5 to 8 real image pairs, and none of it is downloadable.

The image count is wrong. The paper does not give '8 real intraoperative X-rays + CT per patient'. The Dataset section says 'we utilize 8 real intraoperative X-ray images' in total. The figures show one AP view and one inlet view per patient for 8 patients: 5 in Fig. 5 and Table 4, and 3 'additional patients' in Supplementary Fig. 4. That points to 8 AP/inlet pairs (about 16 images), which conflicts with the stated 8 images. The exact number of real images is not clear from the paper.

The pose/labels claim is overstated. The real X-rays have no ground-truth labels of any kind. The paper says 'Since real X-ray data lack ground truth labels' and 'only SSIM and NCC are used as metrics due to the lack of real labels'. The 'tracked POIs on X-rays' and 'registration results' are model predictions, not annotations. The only human labels are 3D POIs placed in 3D Slicer on CT with clinical partners: pelvic landmarks such as ASIS, AIIS and the pubic symphysis, with three POIs drawn per view.

There is no ground-truth pose for the real images. The method assumes a known relative C-arm geometry (Limitations). The supplement models AP and inlet as DeepDRR alpha = 0 and 45 degrees, with nominal parameters: SDD 1160 mm, source-to-isocenter 1000 mm, pixel 0.194, fx/fy 5979.38. These are DRR simulation settings, not measured intrinsics or poses of the real C-arm shots.

'Pelvic-fracture' patients is not stated for this cohort. 'Pelvic fracture' appears only in the keywords and the introduction. The Dataset section says only 'CT scan data and X-ray images from 8 patients' from the Fourth Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital. The study was retrospective under an ethics waiver (No. S2022-781-01).

The anatomy description needs refining. The real AP images (Fig. 5 column b, Supp. Fig. 1 and 4) show the whole pelvis, both hips, the sacrum and the lower lumbar vertebrae, roughly L4-L5, in most cases. Case 4 AP is dominated by bowel gas with little spine visible. The inlet views show the sacral promontory and pelvic ring. The sacrum and lumbar spine are visible but never labelled or named in the text; all POIs are on the pelvis.

'Intraoperative' is stated only once, and the paper also calls its data an 'ideal dataset' free of instruments or screws (Limitations). A thin wire or line is visible in Cases 3 and 5. The paper gives no device, vendor, kVp or detector for the real images; the candidate's 'device: not stated' is correct.

The paper contradicts itself on DRR counts. The abstract says '300 pairs of simulated DRRs from two views for each patient'. Methods and supplement say 3000 per patient (2700 train / 300 test), with DeepDRR poses sampled U(-8,8) degrees and U(-15,15) mm.

The CT is preoperative. The supplement says 'DRRs are generated by casting simulated X-rays through the preoperative CT volume', and registration is done per patient, so the CT is the same subject. It is not CBCT. No CT scanner or slice parameters are given.

The licence claim needs splitting. The article is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. The data have no licence and no repository; the Data availability statement says only 'requests for data and materials should be addressed to Jingxin Zhao' ([e-mail withheld]). The GitHub repo has no licence and holds just 4 files (Requirements.txt, unet_cbam.py, Unet_cbam_train.py, Unet_CBAM_test.py) with 'your path' placeholders, no data and no weights.
The possible overlap with a 'MetaPose private set' is not mentioned anywhere in this paper or its supplement and could not be verified from these sources.
Publication date 2025-07-18 is confirmed (received 21 Jul 2024, accepted 7 Jul 2025). DOI 10.1038/s41598-025-10884-4, PMC12274519, PMID 40681637.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes. The paper calls them 'clinical real X-ray images', 'real intraoperative X-ray images' and 'real X-ray images, directly collected from hospitals'. They are not DRRs or MV portal images. The figures show real radiographs with bowel gas, and some have a thin wire. The model is trained only on DeepDRR renders, and the real images are passed through CycleGAN into DRR style before inference. No device, vendor, kVp or C-arm model is stated.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, a same-subject preoperative CT for each of the 8 patients (the supplement says 'preoperative CT volume'). It is diagnostic CT, not CBCT. No scanner or slice parameters are given. Not released.
verdicts.anatomy: Pelvis in AP and inlet views. The real AP images show the whole pelvis and both hips, with the sacrum and lower lumbar spine (about L4-L5) visible in most cases; Case 4 AP shows little spine because of bowel gas. The inlet views show the sacral promontory and pelvic ring. The labelled landmarks are all pelvic (ASIS, AIIS, pubic symphysis). The sacrum and lumbar spine are visible but never labelled.
verdicts.counts: 8 patients. The text says '8 real intraoperative X-ray images' in total. The figures show an AP and an inlet view for all 8 patients (5 in Fig. 5 / Table 4 plus 3 in Supp. Fig. 4), so there are probably 8 two-view pairs, about 16 images; the paper is internally inconsistent here. DeepDRR renders: 3000 pairs per patient according to Methods and supplement, 300 according to the abstract.
verdicts.licence: The article is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. The data have no licence and no repository and are available only on request to the corresponding author, Jingxin Zhao ([e-mail withheld]). The code repo (TUYaYa1/Points-of-Interest-tracking-network) has no licence, only 4 files, no data and no weights.
verdicts.access_now: Nothing can be downloaded. The images and CT would have to be requested from Jingxin Zhao at the Fourth Medical Center, PLA General Hospital. The only public material is the figure panels in the article and supplement, plus a code stub.

candidate.name: MetaPose private pelvic-fracture X-ray + CT set (Wang et al. 2026)
candidate.why_relevant: The abstract reports evaluation 'on public and private pelvic fracture datasets'; the private one is a real pelvic X-ray + CT set with registration GT. The Elsevier full text needs an API key, so the data statement, size and device were not read. It may overlap Ju et al. (same hospital).
candidate.institution: Chinese PLA General Hospital; Zhejiang University of Technology; China Jiliang University
candidate.device: not retrieved
candidate.anatomy: Pelvis (fractures)
candidate.pose_or_labels: Registration ground truth (mTRE)

verdicts.access_now: Not downloadable. There is no dataset record anywhere. The abstract itself calls the set "private". Crossref lists no relations, OpenAlex lists no datasets, there is no arXiv preprint, and a GitHub search for MetaPose registration returns 0 repositories. Whether the data can even be requested is unknown, because the data availability statement could not be read. ScienceDirect returned a captcha (HTTP 403) from the home IP, from WSL, and from a WSU grid compute node (141.217.136.19). The Elsevier full-text API redirected every request, with or without an API key, to https://lapsus.bz (HTTP 302). The Wayback Machine has no snapshot. CORE, Europe PMC and DOAJ hold no copy. Treat it as not available.
verdicts.licence: No data licence. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 covers only the article (Crossref, version of record, from 2026-06-01). The Elsevier TDM user licence covers text-mining of the article. Nothing licenses any data.
verdicts.real_xray: Unverified. The abstract never says the private set contains real intraoperative X-rays. The method trains on rendered X-rays ("differentiable X-ray rendering optimization"), and related work often evaluates on DRRs simulated from patient CT. Ju et al. 2025 did this: 8 patients, 300 simulated DRR pairs per patient. So the private set could be CT-only with simulated projections. The candidate's real_xray=true has no primary source.
verdicts.paired_ct: Unverified. A 2D/3D registration evaluation implies a CT for each case, but whether real X-rays of the same subject exist, and how registration ground truth for mTRE was obtained, is in the unread full text.
verdicts.anatomy: Pelvis (pelvic fracture reduction surgery), per the abstract. Spine is not mentioned.
verdicts.counts: Not retrievable. Subjects, CT volumes, X-ray images and device are all unknown, because only the abstract was readable. The abstract says evaluation was on "public and private pelvic fracture datasets" and meta-training was on "an open-source pelvic dataset". The reference list includes Grupp 2020 (DeepFluoro, 10.1007/s11548-020-02162-7) and Liu 2021 (CTPelvic1K, 10.1007/s11548-021-02363-8), so these are the likely public sets. That is inferred from citations only; which one was used is not confirmed.
corrections: The article exists. MetaPose: A meta-learned framework with dual-branch frequency-aware network for fast and accurate 2D/3D image registration, Biomimetic Intelligence and Robotics, article 100349, PII S266737972600077X. Published 2026-06 (Crossref record created 2026-06-03). Funded by NSFC U23A20345.

Authors and affiliations: Qianxin Wang and Pengyun Liu (School of Mechanical Engineering, Zhejiang University of Technology); Shibo Cai (China Jiliang University, corresponding); Lihai Zhang (Department of Orthopedics, Chinese PLA General Hospital, Beijing, corresponding). OpenAlex also wrongly tags Zhejiang University of Science and Technology.
access 'unknown' should be 'none'. The abstract calls the dataset private. No repository, DOI, Zenodo record, GitHub code or preprint exists.

The data availability statement was NOT read, and I found no primary source for whether data are offered on request. Blocked on every route: ScienceDirect captcha (403) from three IPs, including a WSU compute node; Elsevier API 302 to lapsus.bz even with an API key; no Wayback snapshot; not in CORE, Europe PMC or DOAJ.
real_xray=true has no primary source. The abstract does not say the private set contains real intraoperative X-ray or fluoroscopy. It may be CT with simulated DRRs.

'Registration ground truth (mTRE)': the abstract names mTRE and success rate as metrics, but how ground truth was obtained (fiducials, manual registration, or simulated poses) is not stated in anything readable.
Device, subject count and image count are unknown. Not 'not retrieved' by chance: the full text was unreachable.
The candidate's licence note mixes article and data. CC BY-NC-ND applies to the article text only. No data licence exists.

The suggested overlap with Ju et al. is unsupported. Ju et al. 2025 (Sci Rep, 10.1038/s41598-025-10884-4, PMC12274519) comes from a different group: Beijing University of Technology plus the Fourth Medical Center of PLA General Hospital, corresponding author Jingxin Zhao. No author is shared with MetaPose. Ju used clinical X-ray and CT from 8 patients plus 300 simulated DRR pairs per patient, under ethics approval S2022-781-01. Its data statement reads 'requests for data and materials should be addressed to Jingxin Zhao', meaning on request only, not released. The only link to MetaPose is the same hospital system.

Possibly related prior work, not verified: Jiang et al., ROBIO 2024 (10.1109/robio64047.2024.10907299), which has an author named Zhang, on 2D X-ray/3D CT registration for robot-assisted pelvic fracture reduction. Whether it shares the private data is unknown.
Not relevant to spine: the anatomy is pelvis only, and nothing in the abstract suggests lumbar or sacral labels.

ACCESS IS WRONG: the article's Data availability statement (ScienceDirect page, read directly) names the private set 'PelvisFracture' and says 'The PelvisFracture dataset is confidential.' Access is 'not available', not 'unknown'. It does not say the data can be requested.

real_xray=true HAS NO PRIMARY SOURCE. The abstract says only 'A systematic evaluation was conducted on public and private pelvic fracture datasets'. The article is a Journal Pre-proof whose body is only in a PDF. The PDF could not be retrieved: Cloudflare and Elsevier bot checks blocked it from the home IP, from headless and visible Chrome, and from a Wayne State grid compute node (job 40411165, 403 on every browser fingerprint). Unpaywall, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar and the Wayback Machine have no other copy. Nothing seen says whether PelvisFracture holds real intraoperative X-rays or DRRs rendered from its CTs. It should be treated as unverified, and it may well be DRRs.

Why DRRs are plausible: a sister pelvic-fracture registration paper from Chinese PLA General Hospital (Ju et al. 2025, Sci Rep 15:26183) says 'We collected clinical X-ray and CT data from 8 patients and generated 300 pairs of simulated DRRs from two views for each patient'. Only '8 real intraoperative X-ray images' were used for real-image checks. Private 'pelvic fracture datasets' in this literature are mostly simulated.

ct_or_cbct_same_subject=true is inferred, not stated. 2D/3D registration needs a CT, so the private set almost certainly has CTs. No accessible text says it also holds real X-rays of the same patients.

pose_or_labels: the abstract reports mTRE and success rate, which implies a ground-truth pose. How that pose was obtained (known DRR pose, fiducials, or a reference registration) is not stated. If the images are DRRs, the 'registration GT' is just the render pose.

The public sets are CTPelvic1K and DeepFluoro (links in the Data availability statement). CTPelvic1K is CT only; the abstract's 'open-source pelvic dataset' used for meta-training is presumably this one. DeepFluoro is real cadaver fluoroscopy with CT but has no fractures, so the abstract's 'public ... pelvic fracture datasets' is loose wording.

The overlap with Ju et al. is speculation. Ju et al. 2025 is a different author group (Beijing University of Technology plus the Fourth Medical Center of PLA General Hospital, corresponding author Jingxin Zhao, ethics approval S2022-781-01). MetaPose's clinical author is Lihai Zhang (Dept. of Orthopedics, PLA General Hospital, Beijing 100853), who also co-authored Jiang et al. ROBIO 2024 (doi 10.1109/ROBIO64047.2024.10907505 was not resolved; found by a Crossref title search). No source says the datasets are shared.

Institutions confirmed from Crossref and OpenAlex raw affiliations. Wang Qianxin and Liu Pengyun: School of Mechanical Engineering, Zhejiang University of Technology. Cai Shibo (corresponding): China Jiliang University. Zhang Lihai (corresponding): Chinese PLA General Hospital. OpenAlex also adds 'Zhejiang University of Science and Technology', which is a mis-disambiguation.
Date: available online 3 June 2026 as a Journal Pre-proof, article 100349, issue dated June 2026, Biomimetic Intelligence and Robotics (KeAi/Elsevier).
Licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 covers the article text only. The PelvisFracture data has no licence and is confidential.
Anatomy: the abstract says pelvis with fractures. No accessible text says whether the lumbar spine or sacrum is in the X-ray field. Their presence is unverified.
Subjects, image count and device: no primary source was reachable, so all three are unknown.

Side note on the search itself: api.elsevier.com, fetched from the grid compute node, returned an unrelated HTML page titled 'LAPSUS$' instead of Elsevier content. It was treated as untrusted and ignored.
verdicts.real_xray: Unverified. No accessible primary source says whether the private PelvisFracture images are real intraoperative X-rays or DRRs. The abstract says only 'private pelvic fracture datasets'. The full-text PDF was blocked. A sister PLA General Hospital paper (Ju et al. 2025) used mostly simulated DRRs plus 8 real X-rays.

verdicts.anatomy: Pelvis with fractures (from the abstract). The source does not say whether the lumbar spine or sacrum is in the X-ray field.
verdicts.counts: Not available from any reachable source. Patients, images and device are unknown.

candidate.name: CT2X-IRA private clinical CT/X-ray set (Geng et al., PMB 2023)
candidate.why_relevant: Low priority. The abstract reports evaluation on 'public and private clinical datasets' (TRE 2.33 mm on the private one) for minimally invasive surgery. The full text is paywalled, so the anatomy (likely spine or pelvis), size and access are unverified.
candidate.institution: Beijing Institute of Technology; Chinese PLA General Hospital
candidate.device: not retrieved
candidate.anatomy: not verified (likely spine or pelvis)
candidate.pose_or_labels: TRE ground truth

corrections: Wrong anatomy. The private clinical set is a CHEST dataset, not spine or pelvis. Section 4.1 reads: 'Chest dataset. We retrospectively collect 110 clinical CT/x-ray image pairs of 45 patients and 30 CT scans of another 30 patients.' Only the PUBLIC set is pelvis: Regi2D3D from Grupp et al 2020, which is the DeepFluoro cadaver set (6 specimens, which the paper calls 'patients'). That set is already known and is not new.

Access is request-only, not 'unknown'. The Data availability statement says: 'The data cannot be made publicly available upon publication because they contain sensitive personal information. The data that support the findings of this study are available upon reasonable request from the authors.' No repository, accession number or download link exists.
No code release. GitHub search for 'CT2X-IRA' returns 0 repositories, and the paper gives no code link.

The 2.33 mm TRE (chest) and 2.13 mm TRE (pelvis) are MEDIANS (50th percentile), not means. Table 1 for the proposed method: chest TRE mean 4.53 ± 5.01 mm, 90th percentile 8.83 mm, gross failure rate (TRE >10 mm) 6.3%. Pelvis: mean 3.51 ± 3.96 mm, 90th percentile 8.25 mm, gross failure rate 5.7%.

Ground truth is a rigid pose, not landmark TRE ground truth. Tgt is 'obtained from an experienced radiologist by manually refining the initial registration results generated by CMA-ES' and 'confirmed by another two experienced radiologists'. TRE is then computed over n = 50 points placed at random in the CT volume, not over anatomical landmarks. There are no vertebra or level labels.

The paper never calls the x-rays intraoperative. It calls them 'clinical CT/x-ray image pairs'. Only the Introduction mentions intraoperative fluoroscopy, and only as motivation. Figure 9 shows lower-chest frames with ribs and some thoracic spine, and the registration contours are mainly ribs. Imaging device and C-arm model are not stated.

Split: 78 pairs from 30 patients for training and 32 pairs from 15 patients for testing. The 30 CT-only scans were used for DRR augmentation. CT voxel spacing is 0.68 x 0.68 x 0.65 mm or 0.79 x 0.79 x 2.5 mm. X-ray pixel spacing is 0.37 to 0.51 mm, and image size is 512x512 to 1024x790.
Dates: received 14 Mar 2023, accepted 7 Aug 2023, published online 22 Aug 2023, in print Phys. Med. Biol. 68(17) 175024 on 7 Sep 2023. The candidate's '2023-08-07' is the acceptance date.

Institution corrected: Beijing Institute of Technology plus the Department of Interventional Radiology, The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital. Corresponding authors: [e-mail withheld], [e-mail withheld], [e-mail withheld].

The paper is not simply paywalled. From home and WSL IPs, iopscience returns a Radware bot captcha. The version-of-record PDF (18 pages, 3.1 MB) downloaded normally through a Wayne State grid batch job (job 40411145, WSU IP). OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar list the paper as hybrid OA under CC BY-NC-ND, but the VoR itself says '(c) 2023 Institute of Physics and Engineering in Medicine. All rights, including for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies, are reserved.' Europe PMC: not in PMC. Local copy: laptop-scratchpad:ct2x.pdf, with extracted text in ct2x_fulltext.txt in the same folder.
verdicts.access_now: Cannot be downloaded. The private set is available only 'upon reasonable request from the authors' (Data availability statement), and there is no repository, record, or code. The only public data the paper uses is Regi2D3D/DeepFluoro (Grupp et al 2020), which is already known.
verdicts.licence: No licence for the data, which is unreleased and request-only. The article's version of record reads '(c) 2023 IPEM, all rights including text and data mining and AI training reserved'. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar tag a hybrid OA copy as CC BY-NC-ND, and that tag covers the article text only.
verdicts.anatomy: Private set: CHEST, meaning lower-chest frames with ribs and part of the thoracic spine visible, registered mainly on rib contours (Figure 9). Not spine and not pelvis. Public comparison set: pelvis (Regi2D3D/DeepFluoro cadavers). There are no vertebral level labels.
verdicts.counts: Private chest set: 110 CT/x-ray pairs from 45 patients (78 pairs from 30 patients for training, 32 pairs from 15 for testing), plus 30 CT-only scans from another 30 patients. Public pelvis set as used: 232 pairs from 6 specimens (172 pairs from 4 for training, 60 pairs from 2 for testing). File sizes: none published.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes, real clinical x-ray images paired with CT (pixel spacing 0.37 to 0.51 mm, size 512x512 to 1024x790). The paper does not say they were intraoperative or fluoroscopic, and it does not name the device.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, the same patient's CT for each of the 110 pairs, with a rigid 6-DoF pose (Tgt) that a radiologist refined by hand from a CMA-ES registration and two more radiologists confirmed. It is not released.

corrections: The full text is not paywalled. Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list it as hybrid open access (CC BY-NC-ND) at the IOP PDF URL. IOP's Radware bot manager blocks automated fetches from the local IP, but the full PDF (18 pages, 3.1 MB) downloaded normally from a Wayne State grid compute node, and every point below comes from that PDF.

Anatomy: the private dataset is a CHEST dataset (section 4.1, 'Chest dataset'), not spine or pelvis. The pelvis results come from the PUBLIC Regi2D3D / DeepFluoro set (Grupp et al 2020, 6 patients, 172 training and 60 test pairs), which is already known and is not this candidate.

I rendered the chest cases in Figures 1 and 9. They are AP frames of the lower thorax and upper abdomen showing ribs, the lower thoracic spine, catheters and guidewires, and bowel gas. The bottom edge may reach the thoracolumbar junction. No lower lumbar spine, sacrum or pelvis is visible, and the text never names vertebral levels.

TRE 2.33 mm is the MEDIAN (50th percentile), not the mean. Table 1 on the chest set gives mean TRE 4.53 +/- 5.01 mm, 90th percentile 8.83 mm and gross failure rate (TRE > 10 mm) 6.3%. The public pelvis set's 2.13 mm is also a median (mean 3.51 +/- 3.96 mm).

'TRE ground truth' overstates it. The ground truth is a manually refined rigid 6-DoF pose (Tgt): an experienced radiologist refined a CMA-ES registration and two more radiologists confirmed it. TRE is then computed on n = 50 points placed at random in the CT, not on independent fiducials or annotated landmarks. The paper's limitations section concedes that the manual ground truth carries about 1 mm of error.

The paper never names an imaging device, a procedure or 'intraoperative' for the chest set. It says only 'retrospectively collect 110 clinical CT/x-ray image pairs'. The C-arm geometry (primary and secondary angle) is read from the x-ray DICOM header, the last author sits in a Department of Interventional Radiology, and the figures show catheters. Together these suggest interventional angiographic fluoroscopy, but that is my inference.

Access is not 'unknown'. The data availability statement reads: 'The data cannot be made publicly available upon publication because they contain sensitive personal information. The data ... are available upon reasonable request from the authors.' No data licence is given.
Dates: Crossref records the accepted manuscript online on 2023-08-07, the version of record on 2023-08-22 and the issue (vol 68, no 17, 175024) on 2023-09-07.
The dataset has no name. 'CT2X-IRA' is the name of the registration method, not of a dataset.
verdicts.access_now: Private. Available only 'upon reasonable request from the authors' (data availability statement); nothing is downloadable. The contacts are the Beijing Institute of Technology group (Jian Yang, Danni Ai) and the Department of Interventional Radiology, First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital.
verdicts.anatomy: Chest / upper abdomen: ribs, the lower thoracic spine, the diaphragm region and bowel gas, with catheters and guidewires in the field (from rendered Figures 1 and 9; the text says only 'Chest dataset'). There is no stated or visible lower lumbar spine, sacrum or pelvis. The pelvis images in the paper belong to the public DeepFluoro/Regi2D3D set.
verdicts.counts: Private chest set: 110 real CT/x-ray pairs from 45 patients (78 pairs from 30 patients for training, 32 pairs from 15 patients for testing), plus 30 CT scans from another 30 patients used as CT/DRR augmentation with no x-ray. X-rays range from 512x512 to 1024x790 at 0.37 to 0.51 mm pixel spacing. CT spacing is 0.68x0.68x0.65 or 0.79x0.79x2.5 mm, 200 to 270 slices. Test poses are augmented by perturbation (32 x 80 = 2560 test cases), but the number of distinct real test images is 32.
verdicts.licence: No data licence; the data are private and shared only on reasonable request. The article itself is open access under CC BY-NC-ND per Unpaywall; that licence does not cover the data.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, same patient. Each of the 110 x-rays is paired with that patient's CT (45 patients), and each pair has a radiologist-refined rigid 6-DoF pose (Tgt), with the projection geometry P taken from the x-ray DICOM header. The 30 extra CT scans have no paired x-ray.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes. The 'clinical' x-rays are real, retrospectively collected, and separate from the DRRs the method renders from CT. The paper names no device, and 'intraoperative' appears only in the general motivation, never for this dataset. The figures show AP interventional-style frames with catheters, consistent with angiographic C-arm fluoroscopy (my inference, not stated). They are not MV portal images.

candidate.name: UC Davis cadaveric AR 2D-3D registration screw study: 6 cadavers, CT + intraoperative X-rays, 151 screws C-spine to SI (Global Spine J 2025)
candidate.why_relevant: Six human cadavers each had a preoperative CT (Siemens Somatom Perspective, 1 mm) registered 2D-3D to intraoperative X-rays by the xvision-Spine (Augmedics) AR system. Five surgeons placed 151 screws: cervical 36, thoracic 54, lumbar 41, sacroiliac 20, graded by Gertzbein-Robbins and Heary. So there is cadaver X-ray with CT (A) and screws in the images (B), and registration poses probably exist in the navigation logs. The data statement says available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. The C-arm model is not stated.
candidate.institution: University of California, Davis, Department of Neurological Surgery
candidate.device: C-arm with xvision-Spine AR (C-arm model not stated); CT Siemens Somatom Perspective
candidate.anatomy: Cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine; sacroiliac
candidate.pose_or_labels: Navigation registration poses (implied); screw grades

corrections: The paper exists, but there is no dataset release. The only data statement (PMC12528066 full text) reads: 'The data supporting the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.' There is no repository, no accession number and no supplementary-material file in the JATS XML. That phrase most plausibly covers the screw error and grade tables, not the images.

Europe PMC tags this record 'supporting_data', but the tag is a text-mining false positive. Its datalinks API resolves it to DOI 10.14444/8142, which is reference 7 (Sommer et al., Int J Spine Surg 2021, a review paper), not a dataset.

The study was not run at UC Davis. The Methods say it 'was conducted ... at Augmedics headquarters (Chicago, Illinois)', under 'Augmedics internal anatomical-research protocols DHF-VAR-000018 and DHF-VAR-000020'. Only the donor bodies came from the UC Davis Willed Body Program. Augmedics supported it in kind, supplying 'the augmented reality navigation system, imaging equipment, and technical assistance', and 'The 2D3D registration was completed by an experienced imaging technician'. The images and navigation logs therefore probably sit with a commercial vendor, and a request to the UC Davis corresponding author may not be able to release them.

The X-ray count is tiny and is now stated, not 'not stated'. Methods: 'A C-arm ring adapter was utilized for acquiring two intra-operative X-ray images.' Discussion: 'Each cadaveric spine required two low-dose fluoroscopic images for 2D-3D registration (mean 1.8 ± 0.2 exposures per specimen)'. That is roughly 11–12 real X-ray frames across all 6 specimens. The two figures (two images, and a mean of 1.8) do not agree with each other.

Serves B is refuted for the X-rays. The registration X-rays were taken before any screw went in ('Following registration, instrumentation was performed'). The screws appear only in the '3D post-op scan' taken at the end of each cadaver. No post-screw fluoroscopy is described, so the real X-rays show no hardware.

Registration poses are not stated to have been recorded or exported. What the paper says was recorded is 'virtual screw trajectories recorded during navigation', which were compared against the post-op CT in 3D Slicer. Treat the poses as unconfirmed.

The C-arm is an image-intensifier unit. The ring adapter is 'Fixated to 12″ or 9″ Round C-Arm's X-Ray Image Intensifier', and a double-plate adapter sits in the beam. Expect calibration-plate fiducials and intensifier distortion in the frames. The C-arm make and model are not stated anywhere, and neither is the post-op 3D scanner.
Specimens were 'six complete human cadaveric torsos' (5 male, 1 female; ages 64–89; BMI 16.4–36.0). Trajectories ran from C3 to S1, with C1–C2 excluded. Cadaver 2 was shared by surgeons 1 and 2.

Confirmed as claimed: 151 screws (cervical 36, thoracic 54, lumbar 41, sacroiliac 20), five surgeons (4 orthopaedic, 1 neurosurgeon), a pre-op Siemens Somatom Perspective CT at 1 mm (spelled 'Persepctive' in the paper), and Gertzbein-Robbins and Heary grading by two radiologists. Accuracy: 147/151 (97.4%) in the safe zone.
Dates: published online 2025-10-15, then in print as Global Spine J 2026 May;16(4):1804–1813 (PMID 41093539). The article is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; no licence covers any data.

The DOI redirects to journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/21925682251387550, which returned HTTP 403 to scripted fetches, including curl_cffi with Chrome impersonation. The publisher page was not checked for extra supplements; the PMC JATS copy lists none.
verdicts.access_now: Not downloadable. The only route is the 'upon reasonable request' line, addressed to the corresponding author (Richard L. Price, UC Davis Neurological Surgery, [e-mail withheld]). There is no repository, accession or supplementary file. The imaging was done at Augmedics HQ under Augmedics internal protocols with vendor equipment, so the vendor may control the images.
verdicts.licence: No data licence (nothing is released). The article itself is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.
verdicts.counts: 6 cadaveric torsos (5M/1F). About 2 intraoperative X-ray frames per specimen (the paper says 'two', and elsewhere 'mean 1.8 ± 0.2 exposures'), so about 11–12 real X-rays in total. 6 pre-op CTs at 1 mm and 6 post-op 3D scans. 151 screws (C 36, T 54, L 41, SI 20) placed by 5 surgeons. No file sizes: there are no files.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes. The same specimen has a pre-op CT (Siemens Somatom Perspective, bone kernel, 1 mm) and a post-op '3D scan' with the screws in place (scanner not stated). None of it is released.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes, real cadaver C-arm fluoroscopy through a 9 or 12 inch image intensifier, with Augmedics' double-plate ring adapter in the beam and a patient marker on the specimen. There are only about 2 frames per specimen, all taken before the screws went in, so no hardware is visible. The C-arm model is not stated.
verdicts.anatomy: Complete torsos. Instrumented trajectories run from C3 to S1 plus sacroiliac screws; C1–C2 were excluded. Which vertebral levels each registration X-ray covered is not stated.

verdicts.real_xray: Yes, according to the text, but no X-ray is published. Real intraoperative X-rays were taken on cadavers with a C-arm. The text says the ring adapter mounts on a "12″ or 9″ Round C-Arm's X-Ray Image Intensifier", so it is an image-intensifier C-arm, not a flat panel, and the images are not DRRs. The C-arm make and model are not stated. None of the three figures shows a fluoroscopic frame. Fig 1 is the setup photo and the ring adapter. Figs 2 and 3 are XVS navigation views, which are CT reformats with virtual trajectories, and post-op CT. So the realism of the images rests on the text alone.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, the same subject. Each cadaver was scanned supine before surgery on a Siemens "Somatom Persepctive" (sic) with a bone setting and 1 mm slicing and spacing. There is also a post-op 3D scan of every cadaver at the end of instrumentation ("a 3D post-op scan was performed"; it is later called "postoperative CT"; the scanner is not stated). This scan contains the screws. So each specimen has a pre-op CT, about 2 registration X-rays, and a post-op CT with hardware.
verdicts.anatomy: Specimens: "Six complete human cadaveric torsos (5 males, 1 female)". Trajectories ran from C3 to S1, and C1–C2 were excluded. Screws: cervical 36, thoracic 54, lumbar 41, "sacroiliac (SI)" 20. The patient marker was a spinous process clamp and/or a percutaneous iliac pin. So the lumbar spine, sacrum and pelvis were physically present and would be in the CT. The paper never says which region the registration X-rays covered, or their projection (AP/lateral). It is unexplained how about 2 image-intensifier shots per specimen could register C3 to S1. Either more X-rays were taken than reported, or the registration covered only part of the spine. Unknown.
verdicts.counts: 6 cadavers: S240219, S240263, S240204, S241162, S241330, S241348. Five surgeons; cadaver 2 was shared by surgeons 1 and 2. 151 screws, and the Table 3 sums check out (36/54/41/20). X-ray images: the text says "two intra-operative X-ray images" and "two low-dose fluoroscopic images for 2D-3D registration (mean 1.8 ± 0.2 exposures per specimen)". That is about 11–12 real X-ray frames in the whole study. A mean of 1.8 with SD 0.2 over 6 whole-number counts is not arithmetically possible, so even that count is unreliable. Nowhere is an image count per region or per registration given.
verdicts.access_now: None public. The only statement is: "The data supporting the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request" (Richard L. Price, [e-mail withheld]). The "findings" are screw-error measurements and radiologist grades, and the statement does not say the X-rays, CTs or registration logs are included. The work ran under Augmedics internal protocols DHF-VAR-000018/000020, at Augmedics HQ, with Augmedics supplying the imaging equipment in kind. The raw navigation data are therefore likely held by the company. Europe PMC's "supporting_data" tag is a text-mined DOI of reference 7 (10.14444/8142, Sommer et al. review), not a dataset.
verdicts.licence: The article is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. The data have no stated licence and are not deposited.
corrections: Study site is wrong: the text says the study "was conducted in compliance with the ethical guidelines for human cadaver studies at Augmedics headquarters (Chicago, Illinois)" in a simulated OR. UC Davis is the authors' affiliation and the donor source (UC Davis Willed Body Program), not where the images were taken. Augmedics supported the study in kind, including the imaging equipment.

Claim B (screws in the X-rays) is refuted. The only X-rays described are the about 2 registration shots taken BEFORE instrumentation ('Following registration, instrumentation was performed'). No X-ray after placement is described. The screws appear only in the post-op 3D scan/CT. The images may show a spinous-process clamp or iliac-pin marker, but the paper does not say.

'Navigation registration poses (implied)' is not supported. The paper does not say the CT-to-X-ray registration transform was saved or can be released. What it says was recorded is the 'virtual screw trajectories recorded during navigation', used against post-op CT for the angular/translational error. The labels that do exist are per-screw Gertzbein-Robbins/Heary grades from 2 radiologists (plus a third to break ties) and per-screw errors measured in 3D Slicer on CT, not on X-ray.

n_images is stated, not missing: about 2 per specimen ('mean 1.8 ± 0.2'), so about 11–12 X-rays in total. This is internally inconsistent: 1.8 ± 0.2 is not possible for 6 whole-number counts, and 2 image-intensifier frames cannot cover C3–S1.

The anatomy shown in the X-rays is not stated. The lumbar spine, S1 and pelvis are present in the specimens and the CT, and lumbar (41) and SI (20) screws were placed. But no primary source says which levels or projections the registration X-rays show, and no X-ray is published.
The detector is an image intensifier (9″ or 12″ round, per the Fig 1B caption), so the images carry intensifier distortion. The C-arm make and model are not stated.
A second CT of the same subject exists: a post-op 3D scan of every cadaver with the screws in place. The candidate lists only the pre-op CT.
Dates: published online 2025-10-15. Issue: Global Spine J 2026 May;16(4):1804-1813. PMID 41093539, PMC12528066.

Quality flags from outside the headline numbers. The Discussion says '98.7 % Grade A/B' and '98.1 % compared to 97.4%', which contradicts the 97.4% in the Results. It calls the means 1.47/1.47 '99% upper bound limits'. Cadaver 1's BMI of 17.72 does not follow from 59 in / 120 lb (that gives 24.2).

candidate.name: Spine-DART (JHU): Loop-X cadaver CT + 35 fluoroscopic images for vertebroplasty path planning (Íñigo, Killeen, Unberath et al., Front Robot AI 2026)
candidate.why_relevant: One cadaver was imaged on a Loop-X: a CT and 35 fluoroscopic images at varied orientations (biplane pairs), with 'accurate projection matrices' from the device. Sixteen vertebrae were collected and 12 reconstructed; ground truth came from TotalSegmentator with manual refinement, and a clinician graded 32 real X-ray paths. The data statement says the raw data 'will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation', which is an explicit request route. It may be the same specimen as the known FluoroSAM Loop-X torso; confirm when requesting.
candidate.institution: Johns Hopkins University (ARCADE / LCSR: Unberath, Killeen, Uneri, Khan)
candidate.device: Loop-X (medPhoton; distributed by Brainlab)
candidate.anatomy: Thoracolumbar spine (16 vertebrae)
candidate.pose_or_labels: Loop-X projection matrices; vertebra segmentations; graded paths
candidate.licence: CC BY (article); data licence not stated
candidate.is_update_of_known: FluoroSAM Loop-X full-torso cadaver (JHU, MICCAI 2025): possibly the same specimen, unconfirmed; adds an explicit data-availability statement

verdicts.access_now: You cannot download it now. The data is available only on request. I found no data deposit anywhere. The only public file is the journal supplement, Video 1: one 3.2 MB MP4 (3,205,822 bytes, md5 7c6da8d1120ecdfdb8cbb5dda93056f4) on Frontiers figshare, article 31801096, under CC BY 4.0. It is a demo video and holds no CT, X-ray or projection data. The data availability statement, the same on Frontiers and PMC, says only: "The raw data supporting the conclusions of this article will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation." This is the standard Frontiers wording, and it is a promise, not a release. The arXiv version (2512.05803, submitted 5 Dec 2025) has no data availability statement at all. Searches of GitHub (the arcadelab org's 20 repos plus a keyword search), Zenodo and HuggingFace turned up no Spine-DART code or dataset. The request route is the corresponding author, Blanca Inigo ([e-mail withheld]).
verdicts.licence: The article is CC BY 4.0 (PMC, OpenAlex and figshare agree), and so is the supplementary video on figshare. The paper states no licence for the cadaver CT or X-ray data. It also has no ethics or consent statement for the cadaver. Frontiers' "author contributions" and "conflict of interest" sections are present, but no ethics section. Missing donor or ethics terms could limit what the authors are able to share.
verdicts.counts: The paper's Table 1 (identical in PMC, Frontiers and arXiv) lists the test specimen as: CT = 1, vertebrae = 16, DRR/X-ray = 35. The text says "we used a LoopX device to collect a CT scan and 35 fluoroscopic images from varying orientations." 12 of the 16 vertebrae were reconstructed and planned by Spine-DART; the 2D-GeoPlan baseline got both paths on 5 of 16. On real X-rays the reconstruction scored DICE 0.7280, NSD 0.5231 and HD-95 7.1910. Figure 9 reports 32 graded real-X-ray paths. The paper does not say how many view pairs were drawn from the 35 images, and gives no file sizes, formats or image dimensions for the cadaver data.
verdicts.anatomy: The paper says only "16 vertebrae." It never names the cadaver's spinal levels or says whether they are thoracic, lumbar or both. The T6/T12/L3 and L3/T5 examples in Figures 7 and 8 come from VerSe19 DRRs, not from the cadaver. "Thoracolumbar spine" is an inference with no primary source.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes. The images are real projections from a Loop-X on one cadaver, and the paper states "accurate projection matrices were available" from the Loop-X (Brainlab) system. The Table 3 caption calls them "real clinical X-rays." That wording is inconsistent with the cadaver study, but these are cadaver images, not patient images.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, according to the paper. The same Loop-X session produced a CT of the same specimen. Ground-truth vertebra segmentations came from TotalSegmentator with manual refinement. None of this is released.
corrections: Access: 'on request' is correct, but this is the standard Frontiers sentence ('will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation'), not a specific data-sharing arrangement. There is no repository, accession number or DOI for the data. The arXiv version has no data statement at all.
Public files: the only file published with the paper is Video 1.mp4 (3,205,822 bytes, CC BY 4.0, figshare 31801096). It is not CT, X-ray or projection data.
Data licence: none is stated, and the paper has no ethics or consent statement for the cadaver. The candidate's 'data licence not stated' is correct.

'Biplane pairs' is imprecise. The paper describes 35 images 'from varying orientations', and the method takes N=2 views per vertebra. It never says how many pairs were formed or used, or that the images were acquired as dedicated biplane pairs.
Anatomy: 'Thoracolumbar spine' is not in the paper. It only says 16 vertebrae, with no levels. The level-labelled examples in Figures 7 and 8 are VerSe19 DRRs, not the cadaver.
Device: the paper names only 'LoopX (Brainlab)'. medPhoton, the manufacturer, is not mentioned in the article; that attribution comes from outside the paper.

FluoroSAM link: no primary source supports it. The Spine-DART paper does not cite FluoroSAM (zero hits in the PMC XML, the Frontiers HTML and the arXiv HTML), and the FluoroSAM README says nothing about Loop-X or a shared specimen. Treat 'possibly the same specimen' as speculation.
Dates: PMC gives e-publication on 26 Feb 2026, and the figshare supplement was created 18 Mar 2026. arXiv 2512.05803 v1 was submitted 5 Dec 2025. Both are consistent with the candidate.

Confirmed as stated: one cadaver; Loop-X CT plus 35 X-rays; projection matrices from the device; TotalSegmentator with manual refinement; 12 of 16 vertebrae reconstructed; 32 real-X-ray paths graded by an interventional radiology resident; authors Inigo, Killeen, Choi, Song, Uneri, Khan, Bailey, Krieger, Unberath (JHU); funded by NIH R01 EB036341.

verdicts.real_xray: Yes. The paper says it "tested our model on real X-ray data acquired from a cadaver study... used a LoopX device to collect a CT scan and 35 fluoroscopic images from varying orientations". Figure 3's 'X-rays' row and Figure 3/4 panels show real kV radiographs of the cadaver: lung fields and soft tissue, with no DRR look. These are not DRRs and not MV portal images. The Table 3 caption calls them 'real clinical X-rays', but they are cadaver images.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, the same subject. The same Loop-X device acquired both the 'CT scan' and the 35 images, so the volume is in practice a Loop-X cone-beam reconstruction; the paper calls it CT and never says CBCT. The paper states 'accurate projection matrices were available'. It does not say explicitly that the CT and the projections share one frame, and it does not say the matrices would be released.
verdicts.anatomy: The paper never names the cadaver's levels. It says only '16 vertebrae' (12/16 reconstructed; 5/16 for the baseline). Figure 3 shows the only real full frame: an AP chest/thoracolumbar view with GT colours running from about T4 to L2. The T1–L5 list is just the legend. No sacrum or pelvis appears in any real-image figure. The method's SSMs cover only T1–T4, T5–T8, T9–T12 and L1–L5, with no sacral model. Whether lower lumbar, sacrum or pelvis is present is NOT confirmed and looks unlikely from the figure shown.
verdicts.counts: 1 cadaver specimen; 1 CT (Loop-X); 35 fluoroscopic images; 16 vertebrae (Table 1: Specimen CT 1, Vertebrae 16, DRR/X-ray 35); 12 of 16 reconstructed; 32 real paths graded (Fig. 9 caption: '200 synthetic paths and 32 real X-ray paths', i.e. 16 vertebrae x 2 pedicles).
verdicts.licence: The article is CC BY (Europe PMC license 'cc by'). No data licence is stated. No repository, DOI or accession for the data exists. Figshare 31801096 holds only the 25-second supplementary 'Video 1' mp4 (crops and optimisation curves), not the data.
verdicts.access_now: None public. The data availability statement is the Frontiers boilerplate: 'The raw data supporting the conclusions of this article will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation.' That is a route to ask the authors, not a release. It does not say that images, the CT or the projection matrices would be shared. There is no code or data link in the article.
corrections: 'Biplane pairs' is wrong as a description of acquisition. The Loop-X has one source and one detector. The 35 images were acquired one after another 'from varying orientations', and pairs were formed afterwards: 'two views were randomly selected per sample'. They are not simultaneous biplane.

The clinician grading was not done on real X-rays. 'we simulated orthogonal DRRs with the reconstructed cannulas rendered as metallic objects', and one 'medical resident in Interventional Radiology' graded the paths on a 3-point scale.

Anatomy 'Thoracolumbar spine (16 vertebrae)' has no primary source for the levels. The paper gives only the count 16. The one real frame shown (Fig. 3) runs from about T4 to L2, with no sacrum or pelvis visible. For lumbosacral use this does not confirm that L5, S1 or the pelvis is present.

Ground truth: TotalSegmentator plus manual refinement is confirmed, but it is 3-D CT vertebra segmentation. Figures 3 and 4 also show 2-D GT masks and 10 landmarks on the real frames; how those were made, presumably by projection, is not stated.
Pose: projection matrices 'were available' from the Loop-X. Nothing says they are part of any shareable dataset.
The figshare record (api.figshare.com/v2/articles/31801096) is the supplementary video only, not data.

Abstract '75% with cadaver data' matches 12/16 reconstructed. Figure 9's real-data Spine-DART planning bar reads about 69%, and the text reports full bipedicular reconstruction for the baseline at 5/16. The numbers are slightly inconsistent within the paper.
The article has no ethics or donor statement for the cadaver.
The paper does not cite FluoroSAM. The suggested identity with the FluoroSAM Loop-X torso has no support in this source.

Dates: arXiv 2512.05803v1 posted 2025-12-05; received 2025-12-02, accepted 2026-02-09, published 2026-02-26 (Front Robot AI 13:1759366; PMID 41836345; PMC12980022). The 2026-03-18 date is the figshare video record, not a second publication.
The 'CT' was acquired with the Loop-X itself, so it is a cone-beam volume, not a diagnostic MDCT; the paper does not say CBCT explicitly.

candidate.name: BG Klinik Ludwigshafen (MINTOS) cadaver lumbar fluoroscopy on three Siemens Cios detectors + 2D/3D pedicle-screw cadaver study
candidate.why_relevant: J Imaging 2026 (Beisemann et al., with Siemens Healthineers): four fresh-frozen whole-body cadavers were imaged AP and lateral at the lumbar spine (also ankle, radius and knee). Each was shot on three Cios systems on the same mechanical platform and SID: Cios Fusion (a-Si, the DeepFluoro detector), Cios Flow (CMOS) and Cios Flow.neo (IGZO), at 1/s and 10/s and at low and high dose. Identical anatomy across three detector technologies isolates detector terms in the physics model. The same group's Eur Spine J 2025 study placed 80 pedicle screws (T8-L5) in 4 cadavers under 2D/3D registration guidance, which used preoperative CT with intraoperative X-rays. The detector study states no CT. Both are available only on reasonable request (J Imaging: 'not publicly available due to ethical and institutional restrictions'). Ask for both.
candidate.institution: BG Klinik Ludwigshafen / Heidelberg University (MINTOS group) with Siemens Healthineers
candidate.device: Siemens Cios Fusion (a-Si), Cios Flow (CMOS), Cios Flow.neo (IGZO)
candidate.anatomy: Lumbar spine (plus ankle, radius, knee); T8-L5 in the screw study
candidate.subjects: 4 whole-body cadavers (J Imaging); 4 cadavers, 80 screws (Eur Spine J)
candidate.pose_or_labels: Image-quality ratings; the screw study registered preoperative CT to intraoperative X-rays (CT not stated for the detector study)

corrections: Authorship: the J Imaging paper is Brunken F, Bullert B, Brauweiler R (Siemens Healthineers employee), Grützner PA, Vetter SY, Beisemann N. Brunken is first author; Beisemann is last and corresponding author ([e-mail withheld]). 'Beisemann et al.' is wrong. PMID 42645936, PMC13514627, epub 2026-07-24, J Imaging 12(8):337.

Access claim REFUTED for the Eur Spine J study. Its Data availability statement on the Springer page reads 'No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study.' It does not say 'available on reasonable request', so nothing is offered. Only the J Imaging study offers data on request.

The Eur Spine J study (Bullert B, Gierse J, Mandelka E, Freischmidt H, Poelstra K, Gruetzner PA, Vetter SY; published 2025-10-13, Eur Spine J 35:2815-2825) used ONE C-arm, a Siemens Cios Spin at dose 'Low', running VUZE 2D/3D guidance software (Vuze Medical, Israel). It did not use the Cios Fusion, Flow or Flow.neo. Preoperative CT was a GE Revolution at 0.625 mm slices, and a CBCT was acquired after instrumentation to assess accuracy. Beisemann is not an author of it.

'Same four cadavers' is not supported. The two studies have different ethics application numbers (J Imaging 2024-17893; Eur Spine J 2024-17616), and neither paper says the specimens are shared. Treat them as separate cohorts.

J Imaging image count, from the primary text: 384 images were rated in total, with 384 forced-choice pairs. That is 4 specimens x 4 sites (ankle, distal radius, knee, lumbar spine) x AP/LAT x 2 pulse rates (1/s, 10/s) x 2 dose levels (0.015 and 0.026 uGy/pulse at the detector) x 3 systems. By arithmetic the lumbar subset is about 96 images, or 32 per detector. The paper does not break the count down by site.

Each acquisition kept only ONE frame, taken 1 s after the start, with temporal filtering k=8 and default vendor processing. What is described is single processed frames, not fluoroscopy sequences, and raw or unprocessed frames are not mentioned.

Detector facts stated in the paper: a-Si (Cios Fusion) 0.194 mm native pixels, 1536^2; CMOS (Cios Flow) 0.152 mm, 1952^2; IGZO (Cios Flow.neo) 0.109 mm, 2776^2. All ran in 2x2 binning (768^2 / 976^2 / 1388^2), 16-bit, 30x30 cm field, filtration 3 mm Al + 0.1 mm Cu, automatic exposure control on, same platform and SID. The paper does not give the SID value.

The J Imaging study states no CT or CBCT. It says only 'no radiographic evidence of pre-existing fractures or implants', and 'This study only evaluated 2D imaging.' ct_or_cbct_same_subject=false is correct for it.
Neither PMC JATS record has a supplementary-material element, so no image files come with the article. Zenodo and DataCite searches found no deposit.
Not checked here: the claim that the Cios Fusion is 'the DeepFluoro detector' comes from outside these records and was not verified against the DeepFluoro source in this pass.
The article texts are CC BY 4.0 (MDPI; Springer open access). That licence covers only the papers and their figures, not any underlying images.
verdicts.access_now: J Imaging detector study: not downloadable. The Data Availability Statement says, verbatim: 'The data presented in this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. The data are not publicly available due to ethical and institutional restrictions regarding data obtained from human specimens.' The contact is N. Beisemann. Eur Spine J screw study: nothing is available, not even on request. Its statement is 'No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study.' No repository record exists for either study.
verdicts.licence: Data: none, not public, request-only for J Imaging and not offered for Eur Spine J. Article texts: CC BY 4.0, covering the papers only.
verdicts.counts: J Imaging: 4 fresh-frozen whole-body specimens (mean BMI 23.04, range 20.66-29.26), 384 single processed frames across 4 sites, of which about 96 are lumbar AP/LAT (32 per detector). One frame per acquisition. Eur Spine J: 4 cadavers, 80 K-wires and 80 pedicle screws T8-L5 placed by 8 surgeons on one Cios Spin. The number of X-ray frames is not stated, and no dataset is offered.
verdicts.paired_ct: J Imaging: none stated. Eur Spine J: preoperative GE Revolution CT (0.625 mm) and postoperative Cios Spin CBCT per cadaver, but the paper declares that no datasets were generated or analysed, so the CT is not offered.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes. Real mobile C-arm frames of cadavers. In J Imaging: lumbar AP and LAT on Cios Fusion (a-Si), Cios Flow (CMOS) and Cios Flow.neo (IGZO). In Eur Spine J: intraoperative Cios Spin frames.
verdicts.anatomy: J Imaging: lumbar spine AP/LAT, plus upper ankle, distal radius and knee. No fractures or implants. Eur Spine J: thoracolumbar T8-L5 with K-wires, Jamshidi needles and pedicle screws.

corrections: Authorship: the J Imaging paper's first author is Fenna Brunken. Nils Beisemann is the last and corresponding author, so 'Beisemann et al.' is wrong. The Eur Spine J paper is Bullert B, Gierse J, Mandelka E, Freischmidt H, Poelstra K, Gruetzner PA, Vetter SY; Beisemann is not on it. 'Same group' holds: both papers come from MINTOS / BG Klinik Ludwigshafen, and Bullert and Vetter are on both.

Image count is stated, not 'not tabulated'. J Imaging Results: 'A total of 384 individual images were evaluated', plus 384 forced-choice pairwise comparisons. That equals 4 specimens x 4 regions x AP/LAT x 2 pulse rates x 2 doses x 3 systems. So there are about 96 lumbar-spine images (4x2x2x2x3), but this is my arithmetic; the paper does not give the number.

Only one frame per acquisition was analysed: 'a single fluoroscopic frame obtained one second after acquisition start'. The paper does not say whether full 1/s or 10/s sequences were kept. Images are processed display output (default system processing, temporal noise filter k-factor 8, automatic exposure control changing kV and mAs), read as DICOM in Horos. They are not raw or flat-field frames.

The claim that identical anatomy on three detectors 'isolates detector terms' is contradicted by the paper itself. It says automatic exposure control and post-processing were proprietary and not standardised, and 'the findings should be interpreted as a comparison of complete C-arm systems rather than an isolated comparison of detector technologies'. Specimens were repositioned for each C-arm with 3D-printed guides and checked by eye. No geometric registration or pose between systems is reported.

The Cios Fusion to DeepFluoro link is not stated in J Imaging, but it is supported from outside. Grupp et al. (arXiv 1911.07042) state DeepFluoro used a 'Siemens CIOS Fusion mobile C-arm with 30 x 30 cm2 detector', 1536x1536 at 0.194 mm. This matches J Imaging's a-Si native specs. J Imaging, however, ran all systems in 2x2 binning (768x768 at 0.388 mm for the a-Si).
The Eur Spine J C-arm is a Siemens Cios Spin, not the Cios Fusion, Flow or Flow.neo. It does not add a fourth view of the detector-comparison specimens.

Eur Spine J CT: stated. Guidance used 'preoperative CT datasets generated using a GE Revolution CT scanner', 0.625 mm slices. A CBCT was also acquired after instrumentation to grade accuracy. Registration was done inside commercial VUZE software (Vuze Medical). No pose, calibration or registration output is reported as saved, and the number of X-ray images is not stated (only fluoroscopy time 201.0 +/- 45.8 s and DAP 396.7 +/- 98.1 cGy*cm2 per procedure).

Access claim refuted for Eur Spine J. Its Data availability statement reads 'No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study', with no offer on request. Only J Imaging states 'available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request... not publicly available due to ethical and institutional restrictions'. So 'both are available only on reasonable request' is false.

No primary source says the two studies share cadavers. They have different ethics approvals (Eur Spine J 2024-17616; J Imaging 2024-17893), different C-arms, and neither cites the other. Assume the four J Imaging specimens have no CT.

J Imaging mentions CT/CBCT only in the Discussion as literature background ('This study only evaluated 2D imaging'). No CT or CBCT of the specimens is stated, which supports ct_or_cbct_same_subject=false for the detector study.

Anatomy: the lumbar images are AP and LAT. The Figure 3 AP example crops (checked visually) show lumbar vertebrae down to about the lumbosacral junction, with both iliac crests in the lower corners. How much sacrum or pelvis is in the full 30x30 cm frames is not stated, and no lateral lumbar example is shown. Eur Spine J instrumented T8-L5; sacrum or pelvis coverage is not stated.

Labels in J Imaging are subjective only: 5-point Likert ratings (overall quality, clinical assessability, noise, edge enhancement) from two residents, plus pairwise preferences. There are no landmarks, segmentations, poses or geometric calibration.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes, for both studies. J Imaging: real fluoroscopy of four fresh-frozen whole-body human specimens on three mobile C-arms (Cios Fusion a-Si, Cios Flow CMOS, Cios Flow.neo IGZO). They share one mechanical platform, source-to-image distance and 30x30 cm field, and all ran 2x2 binning (768², 976² and 1388² pixels, 16-bit). The frames are processed output with automatic exposure control and temporal filtering, one frame per acquisition. Eur Spine J: real intraoperative X-rays of cadavers on a Cios Spin at 'Low' dose. None of it is DRR, simulated or MV portal imaging.
verdicts.paired_ct: J Imaging (detector study): no CT or CBCT of the specimens is stated. Eur Spine J (screw study): a preoperative CT of the same cadavers (GE Revolution, 0.625 mm) and a CBCT after instrumentation are stated. That study's data availability says no datasets were generated. Nothing shows the two studies used the same specimens (different ethics numbers).
verdicts.anatomy: J Imaging: lumbar spine AP and lateral, plus upper ankle, distal radius and knee. The Fig. 3 AP examples reach about the lumbosacral junction, with the iliac crests visible at the lower corners. Full-frame sacrum or pelvis coverage is not stated. Eur Spine J: screws placed T8 to L5; sacrum or pelvis not stated.
verdicts.counts: J Imaging: 4 specimens (2 male, 2 female, age 79 to 93, BMI 20.66 to 29.26). 384 images evaluated in total, plus 384 pairwise comparisons. About 96 are lumbar (my arithmetic, not stated). Eur Spine J: 4 cadavers, 80 pedicle screws and 80 K-wires, 8 surgeons. X-ray image count not stated (fluoroscopy time about 201 s per procedure).
verdicts.access_now: J Imaging: 'available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request; not publicly available due to ethical and institutional restrictions' (corresponding author [e-mail withheld]). Eur Spine J: 'No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study'; no on-request offer (corresponding author [e-mail withheld]). Neither has a public download.
verdicts.licence: Both articles are CC BY 4.0 (text and figures). No data licence exists; the imaging data are not public.

candidate.why_relevant: A 'large human cadaver study' of real mobile C-arm spine frames acquired toward standard projections, with k-wires and screws, C-arm pose updates and landmarks. It is not in the known list. Whether a CT/CBCT exists and whether the data can be shared are unverified.
candidate.institution: DKFZ Heidelberg / Siemens Healthineers
candidate.device: Siemens mobile C-arm (model not retrieved)
candidate.anatomy: Spine
candidate.pose_or_labels: C-arm pose updates; landmarks

verdicts.access_now: Not downloadable. I found no public release of the cadaver X-rays, the reconstructions or the code. The MICCAI 2021 conference version, which describes the same cadaver study with the same group, device and ethics approval (Rheinland-Pfalz No. 2020-15423), lists "Link to the dataset(s): N/A" and "Link to the code repository: N/A". Reviewer 1 there wrote "authors did not share code or data". Zenodo has no data record by Kausch; her two Zenodo records are a body-part-regression model. GitHub has no matching repository. I could not read the MedIA 2022 full text, so I cannot quote its own data availability statement. ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403 from both the Windows/WSL machine and a grid compute node. The Elsevier TDM API returned only coredata, and HTTP 401 for view=FULL. The 2022 Wayback snapshot holds only the abstract. The 80 MB Heidelberg dissertation (heiDOK 31972, DOI 10.11588/heidok.00031972) sits behind an Anubis anti-bot challenge, which I did not get around. So whether the MedIA paper says "available on request" or "not available" is unverified. Nothing I read offers the data. Siemens Healthineers funded the authors (per the COI statement), and the data would have to be requested from DKFZ, [e-mail withheld].
verdicts.licence: No data licence, because no data was released. The article is open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Unpaywall, Crossref and the Elsevier API all say openaccessArticle=true), funded through the Germany LE Tracking agreement. That licence covers the article text, not any images.
verdicts.counts: From the MICCAI 2021 chapter (LNCS 12904, pp. 352-362), sect. 2.6 and 3.2-3.3: 16 acquisition datasets on lumbar torso specimens. 7 datasets had no metal (specimens S0-S6), 5 had k-wires and 4 had screws. The metal figures label specimens S0 and S7-S10, so roughly 11 distinct specimens over 16 datasets; S0 was reused. There were 1364 projections per dataset ("For each specimen 1364 X-rays"; "9·1364 real X-rays containing k-wires ... and screws"), about 21,824 real projections in total. The projections were sampled with α in [-30°, 30°] from orbital sequences at β in [-15°, 15°]. Training was on DRRs only, from 47 full-body CTs (60/20/20 split), plus VerSe for segmentation and 10 CTs with landmarks for L2-L5. The MedIA 2022 extension may have changed these counts; I could not check its full text.
verdicts.anatomy: Lumbar spine in torso cadaver specimens. The C-arm isocentre was on L4, with the AP standard projection of L4 as the target. Screw trajectories were planned for L2-S1, and k-wires and screws were placed in selected pedicles. There is no thoracic or cervical data and no lateral target view in the MICCAI version. The related IJCARS 2020 cadaver study (4 cadavers) was hips only, not spine.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, on paper: each dataset has "orbital projection sequences ... and corresponding 3D reconstructions" from the Siemens Cios Spin, which is intraoperative CBCT of the same specimen. The reference standard plane was set in those reconstructed volumes. None of it has been released.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes. Real X-ray projections from a Siemens Cios Spin mobile 3D C-arm on human cadaver torsos, with and without k-wires and pedicle screws. The ground-truth poses are the α/β angulations the Cios Spin writes into each acquisition's metadata; translation is not tracked. Artefacts from the body bag and from air pockets of decay are reported.
corrections: Access is 'not released / no public data found', not 'unknown'. The MICCAI 2021 version of the same cadaver study lists dataset N/A and code N/A.

ct_or_cbct_same_subject should be true, not false. Each cadaver dataset includes a Cios Spin 3D reconstruction (CBCT) of the same specimen, and the reference standard plane was defined in it. It is unreleased.
Device: the model is known. It is the Siemens Cios Spin mobile C-arm (MICCAI 2021 sect. 2.6; IJCARS 2020).
Subjects: 16 acquisition datasets from about 11 distinct lumbar torso specimens (S0-S10). 7 had no metal, 5 had k-wires and 4 had screws, and S0 was reused.
n_images: 1364 projections per dataset, about 21,824 total. A MICCAI reviewer read this as 1364 in total, but the chapter text says 1364 per specimen.
Anatomy is narrower than 'Spine': it is lumbar only, centred on L4, with the AP standard view as the target.

pose_or_labels: the ground truth is C-arm α/β angles from device metadata, rotation only with no translation. Landmarks were defined on DRRs and CT for training; I found no evidence of landmark annotation on the real cadaver X-rays.

The candidate's Europe PMC evidence URL (query=EXT_ID:35933944 without SRC:MED) returns an empty response ({"version":"6.9"}). With 'AND SRC:MED' added it resolves: MED record, OA via publisher, cc by-nc-nd, hasData=N, hasSuppl=N.
Unverified: I could not read the MedIA 2022 data availability statement (ScienceDirect 403; Elsevier API 401 for FULL view). Its specimen or image counts may differ from the MICCAI 2021 version.
'Siemens' is funding and co-authorship (H. Kunze; COI statement), not a released Siemens dataset.

verdicts.real_xray: Yes, real acquisitions. The validation images were acquired on a physical Siemens Cios Spin mobile C-arm on human cadaver torso specimens, not DRRs. Only the training data are DRRs (DeepDRR renderings of 47 full-body CTs). One detail matters: most validation frames are projections sampled from orbital acquisitions on the Cios Spin, the sweeps it uses for 3D reconstruction (alpha in [-30°, 30°]), rather than freehand fluoroscopy shots. There are also manually acquired AP standard views. None of this is MV portal imaging. The paper also notes artefacts from body bags and decay air pockets. Source: MICCAI 2021 companion paper (DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-87202-1_34), Sec. 2.6 and Discussion. The MedIA 2022 abstract confirms only 'a large human cadaver study ... including k-wires and screws'.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, a CBCT of the same specimen exists, which contradicts the candidate's ct_or_cbct_same_subject=false. MICCAI 2021 Sec. 2.6 says 'A dataset consists of orbital projection sequences acquired at different angulations (beta in [-15°, 15°]) and corresponding 3D reconstructions.' The Discussion defines the reference AP plane 'in the reconstructed volumes'. So each dataset has a Cios Spin intraoperative CBCT reconstructed from the same orbital sweep as the projections. No diagnostic CT of the specimens is mentioned. The MedIA 2022 full text was not read, so this is not confirmed for the journal version.
verdicts.anatomy: Lumbar spine. The C-arm isocentre was aligned to L4 and the target is the L4 AP standard projection. K-wires and screws went into 'selected pedicles'. The real images in MICCAI Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 2 show AP views of about L2 to L5, with iliac crests or upper iliac wings at the lower corners in several specimens. The sacrum is not clearly shown in any published real frame, and no source states that the sacrum or pelvis is in the field. The screw-trajectory planning covering L2 to S1 applies to the CT/DRR simulation only. The authors' earlier IJCARS 2020 paper used a separate 4-cadaver hip study (proximal femur), which is not this spine study.
verdicts.counts: From MICCAI 2021 (not verified for MedIA 2022): 11 distinct specimens, S0 to S10, giving 16 datasets. Seven have no metal (S0 to S6), 5 have k-wires (S0, S7, S8, S9, S10) and 4 have screws (S0, S7, S8, S9). Each dataset has 1364 sampled projection images, so 16 x 1364 = 21,824 real projections. The paper's own phrase for the 9 metal datasets is '9·1364 real X-rays'. Training used 47 full-body CTs as DRR sources, 3969 test DRRs from 9 CTs. The MedIA 2022 journal version may differ in counts; its full text could not be opened.
verdicts.access_now: No public release was found. There is no dataset DOI, repository or download link in the MICCAI paper, its supplement, the BVM 2023 abstract, the MedIA abstract or highlights, or web and GitHub (MIC-DKFZ) searches. The MedIA data availability statement could not be read. Realistic route: request from the corresponding author ([e-mail withheld], DKFZ Medical Image Computing) or the MINTOS group at the Trauma Surgery Clinic Ludwigshafen. The study ran under Rheinland-Pfalz ethics approval No. 2020-15423, which may constrain sharing. Siemens Healthineers co-authored and funded the work.
verdicts.licence: Data: no licence stated anywhere I could access, so unknown and presumably not public. The MedIA 2022 article itself is hybrid open access under CC BY-NC-ND per Europe PMC, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar metadata; that licence covers the paper, not the data.
corrections: ct_or_cbct_same_subject should be TRUE, not false. MICCAI 2021 Sec. 2.6 says each dataset has orbital projection sequences 'and corresponding 3D reconstructions' (Cios Spin CBCT of the same specimen), and the reference AP plane was defined 'in the reconstructed volumes'. This rests on the MICCAI 2021 companion paper, not the MedIA text.

Device is a Siemens Cios Spin mobile C-arm (flat panel, 3D-capable), not 'model not retrieved'. The simulation parameters describe it with a 300 mm detector, 1952² pixels and a source-detector distance of 1164 mm.

Subjects: 11 cadaver torso specimens (S0 to S10) across 16 datasets (7 without metal, 5 with k-wires, 4 with screws). n_images: 1364 sampled projections per dataset, about 21,824 in total. These figures come from MICCAI 2021; the MedIA 2022 counts were not verified.

The pose ground truth is the gantry alpha/beta angles the Cios Spin stores in each acquisition's metadata. They are relative to a manual initial alignment of the isocentre to L4 with alpha=beta=0 as the AP standard, so this is not a full 6-DoF calibrated pose. With the CBCT from the same sweep, though, projection geometry relative to the volume is in principle available.

The 'landmarks' claim is wrong for the real data. Landmarks (process tips, pedicles, end plates) exist only on simulated DRRs, projected from 3D annotations on the training CTs. No source states that landmark or segmentation annotations exist on the real cadaver X-rays.
Anatomy should read 'lumbar spine centred on L4', not generic 'Spine'. The sacrum and pelvis are not shown to be in the field; published real frames show about L2 to L5 and iliac crests only.

Most real frames are projections sampled from orbital acquisitions (alpha in [-30°, 30°]), not freehand intraoperative fluoroscopy. That domain differs from clinical fluoro shots, and the specimens were imaged in body bags.
Institution should also list the MINTOS Research Group, Trauma Surgery Clinic Ludwigshafen, and University Hospital Marburg. Ethics: Rheinland-Pfalz No. 2020-15423.

Not verified: the MedIA 2022 full text, including its Methods, counts and Data availability statement. ScienceDirect returned 403 to every client. The heiDOK copy of Kausch's 2022 dissertation sits behind an anti-scraping proof-of-work gate (Anubis), which I did not bypass. The claim that MedIA uses the same cadaver cohort as MICCAI 2021 is inferred from identical authors, abstract wording and study design, not stated in anything I read.

Security note: api.elsevier.com, served through Cloudflare, answered with a 302 redirect to https://lapsus.bz even for a request with no credentials. The first request, which carried the ELSEVIER_API_KEY header, went only to api.elsevier.com. The redirected follow-up failed at the TLS handshake (curl exit 35), so the key was not sent to lapsus.bz. Worth checking before the FluoroCap harvester sends that key again with redirects enabled.

unique.name: Giessen/Jena canine biplanar fluoroscopy of the lumbosacral junction with CT of the same dogs (Front Vet Sci 2021, plus companion craniocervical studies); raw videos held in the Jena Collection of X-ray Movies
unique.why_relevant: Merged record: the Giessen paper and the Jena video archive are one dataset. The paper supplies the CT and the solved poses; the archive holds the raw video. Four living German Shepherds were filmed on a treadmill with biplanar C-arm fluoroscopy of the pelvis, sacrum, L6 and L7. Each bone was tracked by scientific rotoscoping, and the same dogs had helical CT of the whole spine and pelvis, so every tracked frame has a CT-to-frame pose. The Jena lab corrects distortion with a perforated-metal grid and calibrates 3-D space with a steel-sphere cuboid, so the projection geometry can be recovered. In the archive, subproject szeb_subproject_00000167 ('Dog vertebral column Giessen') holds films 606 and 612-615, each with 90-174 files (raw Roentgen_A/B_VisarioG2.avi biplanar videos plus per-day calibration films), recorded 2015-2018. The metadata can be read through an open Solr index behind a proof-of-work gate, but file downloads return HTTP 403 without login. The archive also has beagle and dachshund films and one canine cadaver lumbar/thoracic mobility film (024) with calibration-body films; the archive has no CT for these. Companion studies with the same setup cover the craniocervical junction in Chihuahuas and Labradors (10.3389/fvets.2021.709967) and in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels (PLOS ONE 2023); they have CT of the head, spine and pelvis. All three papers say raw data 'will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation'. The archive says to contact Prof. Martin S. Fischer ([e-mail withheld]). The subjects are dogs, which have 7 lumbar vertebrae.

unique.name: Utrecht ISI 'Standardized Evaluation Methodology for 2D-3D Registration' gold-standard database (van de Kraats et al., IEEE TMI 2005)
unique.why_relevant: This lead turns out to be lost. The set paired real AP and lateral fluoroscopy of two cadaveric lumbar spine segments (3 and 5 vertebrae) with 3DRX, CT and MR of the same specimens, with source, detector and volume poses in one world frame. That is exactly the NEED A kind. The database page was live from 2006 to about 2012-06; by 2013-08-08 it read 'This database is no longer available'. The download (a 51 MB zip, needing a one-day key and a no-redistribution agreement) was never captured in Wayback under any ISI, UMC Utrecht or Erasmus host. The last documented users were Birkfellner and Spoerk in Vienna (2009-2012). The documented formats are .raw/.sta volumes, .raw/.rad projections with 4x4 detector poses, and source .txt files. The only route is a private copy: van Walsum or Niessen (Erasmus MC), Penney (KCL), Tomazevic (Ljubljana), or the earlier Vienna licensees.

unique.name: FORCAST-EST data: Siemens Artis C-arm CBCT sinograms and arbitrary-trajectory projections of a lumbar spine phantom, with CBCT volume (Tönnes & Zöllner, Mannheim)
unique.why_relevant: Real flat-panel projections from a Siemens robotic C-arm of a lumbar spine phantom; the DICOM PatientName is 'CKM_LumbalSpine'. They are paired with a CBCT reconstruction of the same phantom, with and without an inserted metal object, under CC BY 4.0. The DynaCT sweeps have 496 frames of 1240x960 at 70 kV and SID 1198 mm, with per-frame primary and secondary angles in the DICOM tags. There are also arbitrary 'Arc' (1201 frames) and 'Sinusoidal' (161 frames) trajectories with no ground-truth poses. The CBCT volumes are 395 x 512x512 at 0.487 mm. It suits calibrating an Artis-type flat-panel projection model against a known 3D object, including metal. Limitations: the phantom type is not stated, there is no clinical CT, and the sweeps give vendor angles rather than 3x4 matrices.

unique.why_relevant: New facts about a known item. (1) Images are not on MrOS Online, which serves derived data only. Publication Guidelines v5.9 (2025-07-25) route image requests through a Publications Committee analysis plan and a DUA, possibly with an ancillary-study proposal. (2) The route works: a UW group received 10,351 annotated lateral spine radiographs (67,215 vertebral bodies) from the Coordinating Center under a DUA. (3) The NIA AgingResearchBiobank holds no MrOS images. (4) As of 2026-09-21 all MrOS Online accounts are disabled pending NIH identity-verified re-registration with an institutional email. (5) Protocol: films and QCT were taken at the same baseline visit, about 3,600-3,786 men have both, and film SID is fixed at 1016 mm. The CT is three limited slabs: T12/L1-L2 at 1 mm, mid-L3 to mid-L5 at 5 mm, and a hip slab at 3 mm. The sacrum, SI joints and L5-S1 junction are in no CT series. The CT is supine, so each vertebra must be registered separately against the films. The NIA terms say 'not available for commercial use', which matters for the product track.
