The five CT crops overlap in z (L1 70-104, L2 100-145, L3 131-174, L4 164-203, L5 195-228 mm) over a common in-plane window of about x 20-117, y 23-119 mm, so they can be stitched into one continuous 158 mm lumbar column at ~97x96 mm field, which is the nearest thing to a whole-specimen volume obtainable here.
verdicts.anatomy: One cadaveric lumbar spine, L1-L5, of an 80-year-old female, "with some soft tissue", tied with nylon strings into a plastic tube that was then FILLED WITH WATER to simulate soft tissue (MICCAI 2002, section 2). Six fiducial markers were screwed to the outside of the tube: 1.5 mm metal balls for CT and X-ray, 2 mm spherical cavities of Dotarem contrast solution for MR. n = 1 specimen. No sacrum, no pelvis, no femora, no ribs, no thoracic levels, and therefore nothing at the lumbosacral junction, which is the level-identity question this project is built around.
corrections: REFUTED, the candidate's main content claim: 'CT and MR come only as per-vertebra L1-L5 crops ... so there is no surrounding soft tissue for DRR calibration'. The crops are unmasked rectangular boxes, 0.0 per cent zero voxels, border median 64 equal to the water/soft-tissue bulk value, so surrounding medium IS present inside each box. The specimen itself was imaged 'with some soft tissue' inside a water-filled tube, per MICCAI 2002. The two real barriers are different and should be stated instead: (a) every CT and MR volume is DataType uint8, rescaled 8-bit with no Hounsfield units, so no attenuation calibration; (b) the ~97 mm transverse crop excludes the plastic tube wall and the six fiducial markers, which do attenuate in the 18 radiographs.

MISSED: the five CT crops OVERLAP in z (L1 70-104, L2 100-145, L3 131-174, L4 164-203, L5 195-228 mm) and share an in-plane window, so they stitch into one continuous 158 mm column at roughly 97x96 mm field. 'Not whole-specimen volumes' is true of the tube cross-section but understates what is reconstructible along the spine axis.

IMPRECISE, 'Radiographs at multiple known poses' and real_xray true are right, but these are NOT C-arm or fluoroscopic images. MICCAI 2002: source and detector were FIXED and the phantom was rotated on a turntable, explicitly to avoid C-arm gravitational sag and mechanical imperfection. The set therefore contains, by construction, none of the distortion, sag or circular-field geometry that the fluoro formation work has to model.

MISSED: the X-ray images are 3x3 median filtered and subsampled by a factor of two from the 0.143 mm native Trixell PIXIUM 4600 pitch. The 0.286 mm, 1560x1560 float32 images are a processed derivative, not detector-native output, so any resolution or noise-model experiment inherits that filtering.

The licence conflict is three-way, not two-way, and the candidate understates it. Beyond page-says-CC and guide-says-agreement, the 2017 archived site ALSO required a signed agreement with PDF and DOC forms, and MICCAI 2002 says 'available on request from the authors' in both abstract and conclusion. The CC claim is unversioned free text whose only link is to a Wikipedia article, with no deed URL and no licence file inside the zip. Note the clauses are substantively contradictory: BY-NC-ND permits verbatim redistribution, the guide forbids distribution outright. Do not treat the CC grant as settled without written confirmation from [e-mail withheld].

COULD NOT CHECK: whether the 2021-06-16 refresh changed the contents relative to the 2017 bundle. The Wayback CDX holds no capture of GSPublic.zip itself, only of the page linking it. The 2017 listing said 76.3 MB against today's 75.39 MiB (79,049,365 B), and the three top-level folder entries carry 2021-06-16 timestamps while every file carries 2002-2004 ones, which suggests a repack rather than new data, but I cannot prove it.

PARTLY CORRECT: 'The LIT resource list has no other spine 2D-3D set' holds, the only other gold standard is cerebral angiograms. But the list does carry two further spine sets that are CT-only, xVertSeg (fractured vertebrae) and a 'Lumbar vertebra segmentation CT image database', the latter historically also agreement-gated.

MISSED: the archive ships NO segmentation masks or vertebra labels. 'pose_or_labels' could be read as offering labels; what exists is 10 gold-standard 4x4 matrices, 8 target points plus 1 centre point per vertebra, 20 standard initial-displacement files and 20 precomputed registration results.

doi_or_id CONFIRMED via Crossref: 10.3109/10929080500097687 resolves to Tomazevic, Likar, Pernus, 'Gold standard data for evaluation and comparison of 3D/2D registration methods', Computer Aided Surgery 9(4):137-144, issued 2004. Crossref reports no licence field for it.

Stated accuracy, for the record, is expected TRE about 0.2 mm CT-to-X-ray and about 0.3 mm MR-to-X-ray. That is the authors' own figure from their fiducial reconstruction, not an independent evaluation.

verdicts.real_xray: Real acquisitions, confirmed from the bundled primary source and from the pixels. MICCAI 2002 paper shipped inside the zip (Documents/Miccai2002_paper.pdf, sec. 3): "X-ray images were captured by PIXIUM 4600 (Trixell) digital X-ray detector. The detector had a 429x429 mm active surface, with 0.143x0.143 mm pixel size and 14-bit dynamic range. To simulate C-arm acquisition X-ray source and sensor plane were fixed while the spine phantom was rotated on a turntable ... By rotating (step=20 deg) the spine phantom around its long axis, 18 X-ray images were acquired. The X-ray images were filtered by 3x3 median filter and then sub-sampled by the factor of two." I rendered im000.raw: single-energy flat-panel image of a specimen in a cylindrical tube, with dead-pixel speckle, the detector's circular active field (42.9% of pixels are exactly 0 outside it), metal-ball fiducial screws and the turntable mount in the frame. Not a DRR, not simulated, not MV portal. Two traps for reuse: (1) intensities are transmission-like float32 (open beam ~255-285, bone/water ~45-140, 0 outside the field), not log-attenuation, and ~15% of pixels sit exactly at 255, so the open beam is partly clipped; (2) the poses are not measured, they are a retrospective fiducial calibration (12 parameters fitted on 9 of the 18 images, RMS 0.31 mm, validated by 3D reconstruction from the other 9 at RMS <0.06 mm).
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, same specimen, but CT only (no CBCT, no MV/CBCT pair) and only as per-vertebra crops. Images/Ct/L1-L5: uint8 raw volumes, 0.273438 mm in-plane, 1 mm slices, 87-97 mm x 84-95 mm x 33-45 mm. Images/MR/L1-L5: uint8, 0.390625 mm, 1.9 mm slices (Philips Gyroscan NT Intera 1.5 T, T1). Two corrections to the candidate's reading. (a) CT is 8-bit, not HU, so no physical attenuation calibration is possible without re-mapping. (b) The crops are NOT bone-only: the specimen sat in a water-filled plastic tube "with some soft tissue", and the crops carry that water and residual tissue inside the circular reconstruction field; what is missing is everything outside that field - 40-46% of each CT crop is flat-filled at the water value 64 (verified: value is exactly 64 at every corner and over ~44% of voxels), and bone never touches the fill boundary (0 bone voxels adjacent to it in any of the five volumes), so no bone is truncated but the outer attenuation path (tube wall, turntable, air gap) is absent. The five CT crops share one axis-aligned frame (gold_ctLX.txt are pure translations equal to each volume's own TPosition) and their z ranges overlap (70-104, 100-145, 131-174, 164-203, 195-228 mm), so a composite L1-L5 volume spanning ~158 mm can be assembled for geometric DRR work; intensity-calibrated DRR is not supported. MR gold transforms carry small rotations (CT frame is the reference frame).
verdicts.anatomy: Cadaveric lumbar spine L1-L5 only, one 80-year-old female specimen ("A cadaveric lumbar spine, comprised of vertebra L1-L5 with some soft tissue, of an 80 year-old female was placed into a plastic tube and tied with thin nylon strings", MICCAI 2002 sec. 2). No sacrum, no pelvis, no hips, no femora, no ribs, no thoracic levels. Confirmed in the render: the radiograph shows only the lumbar column inside the tube, six fiducial markers and the turntable base. For a lumbosacral/level-identity or spinopelvic product this set contains no sacrum and no pelvis at all.
verdicts.counts: 1 subject (one cadaver specimen). 18 X-ray images (im000-im017), each 1560x1560 float32, 9,734,400 bytes, 0.286 mm pixel pitch, with a matching .rad header giving a 4x4 detector pose and the source position. Source-to-detector distance computed from all 18 .rad files is constant at 1009.6 mm, corroborating the fixed source/detector + rotating turntable account (a real C-arm orbit would not give a constant SDD to 0.1 mm). Poses cover 360 deg in 20 deg steps about the specimen's long axis. Plus 5 CT crops and 5 MR crops. 157 files, 210,162,660 bytes uncompressed.
verdicts.licence: Conflict confirmed. The live resource page states: "Authors Dejan Tomazevic / License Creative Commons (CC): BY-NC-ND". The user guide bundled with the download (2D-3D-GS_UG.pdf, p. 2, file Last-Modified 2003-07-14) states: "The all rights to gold standard data posses the Laboratory of Imaging Technologies. The non-authorized distribution of this data is strictly forbidden. This gold standard data can only be obtained and used after signing the agreement form between the user and Imaging Technologies Laboratory", and its introduction repeats "can be obtained on request from the authors". The 2017 archived tools page also said "The gold standard can only be accessed after signing the agreement with the Laboratory of Imaging Technologies" with PDF/DOC agreement forms linked. No agreement is enforced today. Either reading is non-commercial (BY-NC-ND, or a signed academic agreement), and BY-NC-ND additionally forbids derivatives - relevant if derived crops, DRRs or labels were to be redistributed.
verdicts.access_now: Open and direct, no login, no agreement gate. https://lit.fe.uni-lj.si/data/research/resources/2D-3D-GS/2D-3D-GS.zip returns HTTP 200, Content-Type application/zip, Content-Length 79,049,365, Last-Modified Wed, 16 Jun 2021 11:57:56 GMT (page prints it as 75.39M = MiB). The user guide at .../2D-3D-GS.pdf returns 200, 707,342 bytes, Last-Modified Mon, 14 Jul 2003 09:23:36 GMT. The 2017 route is dead: the snapshot at web.archive.org/web/20170503232346 links href="./contents/tools/GoldStandard/GSPublic/GSPublic.zip", and both http (301 to https) and https now return 404. Local copies in the working tree match byte-for-byte on size (2D-3D-GS.zip 79,049,365 bytes, 2D-3D-GS_UG.pdf 707,342 bytes).
corrections: REFUTED as worded: 'CT and MR come only as per-vertebra L1-L5 crops ... so there is no surrounding soft tissue for DRR calibration.' The crops DO contain surrounding water and residual soft tissue - the specimen was in a water-filled tube specifically 'to simulate soft tissue and, therefore, to obtain more realistic MR, CT, and X-ray images' (MICCAI 2002 sec. 2). What is actually missing is everything outside the ~93 mm circular CT reconstruction field, which is flat-filled at the water value 64 over 40-46% of each crop. Correct statement: the attenuation path is truncated at the recon circle, not that there is no soft tissue.

MISSING and material: the CT and MR volumes are 8-bit unsigned (DataType: uint8 in every .sta header), not HU and not 16-bit. Any intensity-based DRR or attenuation-model work needs an assumed HU mapping; the dataset cannot calibrate one.

xray_kind 'Radiographs at multiple known poses' understates the constraint. Source and detector were FIXED and the specimen was rotated on a turntable in 20 deg steps through 360 deg about one axis; SDD computed from all 18 .rad files is identical at 1009.6 mm. This is a single circular orbit of a bench setup, explicitly chosen to avoid C-arm gravitational sag - it is not C-arm and not fluoroscopy, and it carries none of the C-arm distortion, scatter or exposure variation a fluoro model needs.

MISSING: the 18 poses are not independently measured. Nine images (0,40,...,320 deg) were used to fit the 12-parameter geometry (RMS 0.31 mm) and the other nine to validate 3D fiducial reconstruction (RMS <0.06 mm). Pose error is therefore correlated with the fiducial localisation in CT, and the quoted 0.2 mm (CT) / 0.3 mm (MR) are expected target registration errors, not measured pose accuracy.

MISSING: images are 3x3 median-filtered and 2x down-sampled from the native 0.143 mm detector, so they are not raw detector output; and intensities are transmission-like float32 with 42.9% of pixels exactly 0 (outside the circular field) and ~15% exactly 255 (clipped open beam). The user guide only says 'the best range to observe the vertebra bone is 0-110'.

pose_or_labels is confirmed but should say what is NOT there: no segmentation masks, no landmarks beyond 8 pedicle-border target points and 1 centre point per vertebra, and no level annotation on the X-ray images. Level identity is recoverable only by projecting the named CT crops through their gold transforms. Also present: 450 standardised initial displacements per vertebra per modality (start_*.txt, 1800x4) with the index pair of X-ray images per trial (rad_*.txt, 450x2), and example registration results from Tomazevic's method.

DOI 10.3109/10929080500097687 verified on Crossref (Tomazevic, Likar, Pernus, '"Gold standard" data for evaluation and comparison of 3D/2D registration methods', Computer Aided Surgery 9(4):137-144, 2004; alias 10.1080/10929080500097687), but note the download itself never cites it - the bundled user guide references only MICCAI 2002 and the 2002 MSc thesis, and the resource page gives no DOI.

'published 2004 (current zip dated 2021-06-16)' is loose: every data file inside the zip is dated 2002-08-21, the Matlab analysis scripts 2004-03-24, the user guide 2003-07-14; 2021-06-16 is only the repackaging date of the three top-level folders.

'The LIT resource list has no other spine 2D-3D set' - confirmed against the live list, which holds one other gold standard (3D-2D cerebral angiograms, Mitrovic) and two 3-D-only spine sets (xVertSeg, lumbar vertebra segmentation CT database). No refutation found.

For the intended project, the binding limits are anatomical and statistical, not licensing: n=1 specimen, L1-L5, no sacrum or pelvis, 18 frames on one circular orbit, in a water tube rather than a torso. It can validate 2D-3D registration geometry; it cannot support any claim about naming levels on real fluoroscopy, and non-commercial terms bar the product track either way.

candidate.name: FORCAST-EST data: Siemens Artis C-arm CBCT sinograms and arbitrary-trajectory projections of a lumbar spine phantom, with CBCT volume (Tönnes & Zöllner, Mannheim)
candidate.why_relevant: Real flat-panel projections from a Siemens robotic C-arm of a lumbar spine phantom; the DICOM PatientName is 'CKM_LumbalSpine'. They are paired with a CBCT reconstruction of the same phantom, with and without an inserted metal object, under CC BY 4.0. The DynaCT sweeps have 496 frames of 1240x960 at 70 kV and SID 1198 mm, with per-frame primary and secondary angles in the DICOM tags. There are also arbitrary 'Arc' (1201 frames) and 'Sinusoidal' (161 frames) trajectories with no ground-truth poses. The CBCT volumes are 395 x 512x512 at 0.487 mm. It suits calibrating an Artis-type flat-panel projection model against a known 3D object, including metal. Limitations: the phantom type is not stated, there is no clinical CT, and the sweeps give vendor angles rather than 3x4 matrices.
candidate.institution: Medical Faculty Mannheim, Heidelberg University (Computer-assisted Clinical Medicine)
candidate.device: Siemens AXIOM-Artis robotic C-arm (PX4700 flat detector), DynaCT
candidate.xray_kind: CBCT sweep projections plus arbitrary-trajectory C-arm projections
candidate.anatomy: Lumbar spine phantom; metal object in one series
candidate.n_images: 2 x 496-frame sinograms; Arc 1201 frames; Sinusoidal 161 DICOMs; 2 CBCT volumes; about 4.6 GB
candidate.pose_or_labels: Per-frame primary and secondary angles plus SID for the DCT sweeps; no ground truth for Arc and Sinusoidal (estimated in Appl Sci 13:9179)

verdicts.access_now: Downloadable NOW, anonymously, no login, no request form. DOI resolves (https://doi.org/10.11588/data/GIWRQA -> dataset.xhtml, HTTP 200). Dataverse API shows one version, V1.0, versionState RELEASED, releaseTime 2023-10-18T09:13:49Z, six files, every one restricted=false, no termsOfAccess and no fileAccessRequest. I pulled bytes myself: HTTP 206 range reads on all six datafile ids (13580-13585) and complete anonymous downloads of the two CBCT volume zips (100,367,177 B and 99,465,329 B). Note HEAD on the three large files returns 503 (server quirk) while ranged/plain GET works — do not read that 503 as a dead file. Practical snag: Arc.zip (1.86 GB) inflates to a SINGLE 2.86 GB multiframe DICOM, so budget memory/streaming for it.
verdicts.anatomy: Lumbar spine phantom, one object, no humans. Verified by rendering, not by metadata alone: coronal MIPs of both downloaded CBCT volumes show five lumbar vertebrae with transverse processes, the sacrum below and lower thoracic/rib fragments at the top, inside a body-shaped shell with corner markers. DICOM PatientName is CKM_LumbalSpine on all six series. Paper text: "a CT scan of a lumbal spine phantom with an inserted metal object". Both volumes contain a thin needle/rod along the canal; the "with metal" volume additionally has a large L-shaped, hex-key-like dense object (p99.99 intensity 30,461 vs 6,559 in the without-metal volume). Phantom make/model is nowhere stated, in the record or the paper. No segmentations, no vertebra labels, no landmarks of any kind.
verdicts.counts: 6 zip files, 4,629,411,361 B total (4.63 GB / 4.31 GiB), inflating to roughly 7.6 GB. (1) CBCT Sinogram - 20sDCT Head 70kV.zip, 824,325,505 B -> one multiframe DICOM, NumberOfFrames=496, 1240x960, 16-bit, XA, 70 kV, 160 mA, SID 1198 mm, PositionerPrimaryAngleIncrement has exactly 496 values (98.92 deg to -99.06 deg) and PositionerSecondaryAngleIncrement 496 values. (2) CBCT Sinogram - Without Metal Object, 789,059,402 B, same geometry, 115 mA. (3) Arc.zip, 1,858,569,972 B -> ONE DICOM of 1201 frames at 1240x960 (2,859,358,720 B inflated). (4) Sinusoidal.zip, 957,623,976 B -> 161 single-frame DICOMs, each 9,536,512 B. (5)+(6) Prior CBCT Volume.zip / ...Without Metal Object.zip, ~100 MB each -> 395 slices each, 512x512, PixelSpacing 0.48679882 mm, SliceThickness 0.48679882, z span -339.13 to -147.34 mm.
verdicts.licence: CC BY 4.0, confirmed in the Dataverse API license object (name "CC BY 4.0", uri http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0). No termsOfUse, no termsOfAccess, no access-request gate. Publisher heiDATA (Heidelberg University). DataCite state "findable", but its rightsList is EMPTY, so the licence is asserted by heiDATA only, not by the DataCite record. Funder BMBF 13GW0388A. Contact [e-mail withheld].
verdicts.paired_ct: Same-object 3D prior exists but it is CBCT, not clinical CT: two DynaCT reconstructions (ImageType DERIVED\SECONDARY\AXIAL\3DANGIO\NAT_FILL, SeriesDescription "DCT Head Clear Nat Fill Full HU Normal [AX3D]"), 395 x 512 x 512 at 0.487 mm, one with and one without the inserted metal object, same PatientID/StudyDate as the projections (20201020), same phantom unmoved between acquisitions per the paper. So projections and volume are paired for the same physical object, but there is no diagnostic CT and no registration matrix shipped that maps volume to projections.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes, real flat-panel X-ray, not simulated. Modality XA, Manufacturer Siemens, ManufacturerModelName AXIOM-Artis, station ARTIS160969, detector string PX4700 present in the private header, ImagerPixelSpacing 0.154 mm, 70 kV, SID 1198 mm, SOD 785-821 mm, acquired 2020-10-20. Caveat for a fluoroscopy project: these are DR/CBCT acquisitions of a phantom, not live clinical fluoroscopy. The sweeps are DynaCT rotational runs; the 161 sinusoidal images are step-and-shoot single DR exposures at full 2480x1920 detector resolution (protocol P16_DR_L); only the Arc is a continuous 30 fps run (paper: 400 deg arc tilted 28 deg), and that one is the series with no positions.
corrections: Release date is 2023-10-18, not 2023-08-10. heiDATA publicationDate = 2023-10-18, version V1.0 releaseTime = 2023-10-18T09:13:49Z, DataCite registered = 2023-10-18. The 2023-08-10 in the candidate is DataCite 'created' (the draft), i.e. a timestamp on an unpublished record. One version only, no later revisions.

'No ground-truth poses' is right for Arc but wrong for Sinusoidal. Each of the 161 sinusoidal DICOMs carries its own nominal PositionerPrimaryAngle and PositionerSecondaryAngle plus SID 1198 and a per-image SOD (e.g. -75/10.7 SOD 785.0; -66/-17.3; 21/-26 SOD 814.8; 48/10.7 SOD 821.1). The paper matches this: it ran FORCASTER on the sinusoidal set 'using nearly accurate starting parameters', and says positional data were absent only for the arc ('Since there were no positional data reported by the Artis Zeego System' on the continuous arc). Arc.dcm indeed has PositionerMotion=STATIC with a single primary/secondary angle (-160/27.9) for all 1201 frames.

Sinusoidal frames are 2480x1920 at ImagerPixelSpacing 0.154 mm, not 1240x960. The DynaCT sweeps and the Arc are 1240x960 (2x2 binned, so ~0.308 mm). The candidate's '1240x960' applies to the sweeps and Arc only. Sinusoidal is also 161 separate single-frame files, while Arc and each sweep is ONE multiframe DICOM.

'The sweeps give vendor angles rather than 3x4 matrices' understates the file. Each sweep DICOM carries Siemens private block 'SIEMENS SMS-AX  ACQ 1.0' with (0021,1059) FL = 5952 floats = 496 x 12, and the first 12 parse as an orthonormal 3x4 rigid matrix in mm (rows [1,0,0.001,-1160.1], [0,-0.156,0.988,-0.7], [0,-0.988,-0.156,1100.2]), plus (0021,105A) FL = 496 x 6. I verified the layout and orthonormality myself; I could NOT find any primary documentation of what those private tags mean, so treat the per-frame 3x4 as present-but-undocumented, not as a published calibration.

The paper's Data Availability Statement does not release this data. It reads, in full: 'Source code is available at: https://github.com/ChristianToennes/FORCASTER accessed on 1 August 2023.' The link runs one way only - the heiDATA record cites the paper (10.3390/app13169179), the paper does not cite the heiDATA DOI. The data release is real regardless; but anyone auditing via the paper alone would not find it.

Device naming is inconsistent across sources and worth carrying as-is: DICOM says ManufacturerModelName 'AXIOM-Artis', detector 'PX4700', station ARTIS160969; the paper calls the same machine 'Artis Zeego'. The candidate's PX4700 claim checks out against the private header. SeriesDescription on the sweeps and volumes is '20sDCT Head 70kV' / 'DCT Head ...' - a HEAD protocol run on a lumbar phantom, so do not infer anatomy from SeriesDescription here.

Add for the fluoroscopy lens: n=1 phantom, zero human subjects (paper IRB statement 'Not applicable'), zero labels or segmentations, no clinical CT, and no 2D-3D registration ground truth shipped. The dataset calibrates an Artis-type projection model against a known object; it cannot supply vertebra-level naming labels or real-patient fluoro appearance.

Access-mechanics correction for anyone scripting this: HEAD on datafile ids 13580, 13581, 13582, 13585 returns HTTP 503 while GET (plain or ranged) returns 200/206. A HEAD-based liveness check would falsely report the three largest files as dead.

verdicts.real_xray: Real. Verified in the DICOM itself, not from the description: Modality XA, ImageType ORIGINAL/PRIMARY/SINGLE PLANE/SINGLE A, Manufacturer Siemens, ManufacturerModelName AXIOM-Artis, StationName ARTIS160969, DeviceSerialNumber 160969, DetectorDescription "5-PX4700 1.6 (I08)", DetectorID SN1443TU, InstitutionName "Universitaetsklinikum Mannheim", SoftwareVersions VD11C 200114, acquired 2020-10-20. Kilovoltage (KVP 70), so not MV portal. I decoded and rendered actual frames (Arc frame 0, Sinusoidal #80, without-metal sweep frame 0): they are transmission radiographs with flat-panel/heel-effect shading, the phantom's soft-tissue shell edges and its mounting screws visible — not DRRs and not simulated. Acquisition-side metadata is present and consistent (ExposureTime 1686, XRayTubeCurrent 160, AveragePulseWidth 3.4, RadiationMode PULSED, dose-area product, skin-dose accumulation), which a rendered dataset would not carry.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, and tighter than the candidate states, but it is CBCT only — there is no clinical CT. The two "Prior CBCT Volume" series are the vendor DynaCT reconstructions of the two 496-frame sweeps that ship in the same deposit: file 13584 carries RelatedSeriesSequence pointing at StudyInstanceUID ...0500000003 / SeriesInstanceUID ...0500000004 (exactly the 13581 sinogram) and AcquisitionDateTime 20201020093844 (exactly 13581's AcquisitionTime); file 13583 pairs the same way with 13582 via study ...0500000030 and AcquisitionDateTime 20201020152132. Both volumes: SOPClass 1.2.840.10008.5.1.4.1.1.2 (CT Image Storage) but Modality XA, ImageType DERIVED/SECONDARY/AXIAL/3DANGIO/NAT_FILL, 395 slices of 512x512, 0.48679882287979 mm isotropic, RescaleIntercept -1024 (true HU), ReconstructionDiameter 512, kernel HU/Normal. Same phantom throughout: PatientID "20.10.13-09:13:33-DST-1.3.12.2.1107.5.4.5.160969" and PatientName CKM_LumbalSpine are identical across all six files, one session on 2020-10-20. Volume extent measured from the data: z -339.13 to -147.34 mm (192.3 mm craniocaudal), 249.2 mm transverse.
verdicts.anatomy: Lumbar spine, sacrum AND pelvis (iliac wings) are all present — I confirmed this by rendering rather than trusting the PatientName string. The near-AP Sinusoidal projection (primary -1 deg) shows five lumbar vertebrae with transverse processes, radiolucent disc spaces, the sacrum with its promontory and median crest, and both iliac wings with visible sacroiliac joints. No femora, no acetabula in view. The CBCT coronal/sagittal MIPs and axial slices show the same column down to the sacrum; the ilia are partially truncated laterally by the 249 mm reconstruction FOV, matching the paper's remark that "the phantom is larger than the CT volume". The vertebrae are dry/hollow bone in a soft-tissue-equivalent torso shell (bright cortical rim, dark interior), so it is a physical phantom, not a cadaver or patient. Note the acquisition protocol is a HEAD protocol ("20sDCT Head 70kV", ProtocolName "20sDCT Head 70kV 480 0.40 01.20 DHLORST") applied to a lumbar phantom.
verdicts.counts: One phantom, one session (2020-10-20), zero human subjects. Projections total 2,354 frames: with-metal DynaCT sweep 496 frames (NumberOfFrames=496, 1240x960, 16-bit), without-metal DynaCT sweep 496 frames (1240x960), Arc 1,201 frames in a single multiframe file (1240x960), Sinusoidal 161 single-frame files at 2480x1920. Plus 2 CBCT volumes of 395 slices each = 790 slices. Six zips totalling 4,629,411,361 bytes (~4.63 GB / 4.31 GiB). All frame counts were derived from the DICOM tags and the uncompressed member sizes, not from the description.
verdicts.pose_or_labels: Geometry only — there are no anatomical labels of any kind (no segmentation, no vertebra-level labels, no landmarks, no README). Geometric content differs per series and the candidate gets it partly wrong. (a) Both 496-frame sweeps: per-frame PositionerPrimaryAngleIncrement (496 values, +98.92 to -99.06 deg, a 197.98 deg short scan) and PositionerSecondaryAngleIncrement (496 values, span only 0.57 deg), DistanceSourceToDetector 1198 mm, private "Source to Isocenter" 785 mm; AND private tag (0021,1059) holding 496 3x4 matrices. (b) Sinusoidal: each of the 161 files carries its own PositionerPrimaryAngle (-78 to +77 deg, 1 deg steps, 156 distinct values) and PositionerSecondaryAngle (-40.2 to +30.5 deg, oscillating), ImagerPixelSpacing 0.154 mm — but no (0021,1059). (c) Arc: nothing per-frame — PositionerMotion is STATIC with a single PositionerPrimaryAngle -160 / PositionerSecondaryAngle 27.9 for all 1,201 frames, and PositionerPrimaryAngleIncrement is absent; the paper confirms "there were no positional data reported by the Artis Zeego System". No pixel spacing tag on the 1240x960 series either (2x2 binned per DerivationDescription, implying ~0.308 mm).
verdicts.licence: CC BY 4.0, per the heiDATA dataset record (license.name "CC BY 4.0", uri http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0). Confirmed as claimed. Caveat: the DataCite record for the same DOI has an empty rightsList, so the licence is asserted by the repository record only, not by the DOI registration.
verdicts.access_now: Open, working, no credentials. I downloaded file 13584 in full over plain HTTPS with no token or login (100,367,177 bytes) and its MD5 was 4a1d46485f8895b0cdbde1f2e22e57e9, matching the checksum published in the dataset record. All six files are restricted:false and the /api/access/datafile/<id> endpoint honours HTTP Range requests, so individual members can be pulled without fetching whole multi-GB zips. The "fileAccessRequest: true" flag in the record is a repository setting and does not gate these files.
corrections: Publication date is wrong. The candidate says published 2023-08-10; that is the draft creation timestamp (Dataverse createTime 2023-08-10T13:35:30Z, DataCite created 2023-08-10T13:35:31Z). The dataset was actually released 2023-10-18 (Dataverse publicationDate/releaseTime 2023-10-18T09:13:49Z, DataCite registered 2023-10-18T09:15:29Z).

Image size is wrong for the Sinusoidal series. The candidate's '1240x960' is stated as if it covers the projections generally. The 161 Sinusoidal DICOMs are 2480x1920 single-frame images with ImagerPixelSpacing 0.154 mm. Only the two DynaCT sweeps and the Arc are 1240x960 (2x2 binned, per DerivationDescription 'DHLORST g_H_+00R_+00T_116L_200_-100_L_480_040_2x2'), and those files carry no ImagerPixelSpacing tag at all.

'No ground truth for Arc and Sinusoidal' is half wrong. Every one of the 161 Sinusoidal files carries its own PositionerPrimaryAngle (-78 to +77 deg in 1 deg steps, 156 distinct) and PositionerSecondaryAngle (-40.2 to +30.5 deg). It is only the Arc that has no per-frame pose: PositionerMotion STATIC, one angle pair (-160 / 27.9) for all 1201 frames, PositionerPrimaryAngleIncrement absent.

'The sweeps give vendor angles rather than 3x4 matrices' is wrong as stated. Each 496-frame sweep also carries private tag (0021,1059) with 5952 floats = 496 3x4 matrices. I verified they are rigid pose matrices, not pinhole projection matrices: det = 1.000000 and max|RR^T - I| = 1.8e-7, translation essentially constant across frames at (-1160.1, -0.7, 1100.2) mm (spread 0.9 mm), rotation reproducing the reported primary angle. To build a projection matrix you still need SID 1198, source-to-isocenter 785 and the detector pitch. I found no primary source documenting this private tag's meaning, so that interpretation is mine, not stated anywhere.

'With and without an inserted metal object' is imprecise, and there is no metal-free acquisition. The source paper for these data (Toennes et al., IJCARS 2022, doi 10.1007/s11548-022-02645-9) states: 'In the first scan a needle was inserted, the second scan had an additional large metal object and the needle position was changed slightly.' The 'Without Metal Object' sweep still contains the needle, which is visible in the frame I rendered. So the pair differs by the large metal object only.

Arc frame count conflicts with the paper. The file genuinely holds 1201 frames (NumberOfFrames=1201; uncompressed size 2,859,358,720 = 1201 x 1240 x 960 x 2), so the candidate's number matches the file. But the FORCAST-EST paper says the arc 'consists of 666 individual projections' over a 400 deg continuous arc. Nothing in the deposit documents which 666 were used or how the 1201 relate to them.

'The phantom type is not stated' is partly wrong. Both papers state it is a lumbar spine phantom imaged on an Artis Zeego. What is genuinely missing is the vendor/model of the phantom. Separately, no source states that the phantom includes the sacrum and iliac wings - that finding is mine, from rendering the projections, and should not be attributed to the authors.

Device naming mixes two sources. The DICOM ManufacturerModelName is 'AXIOM-Artis' (StationName ARTIS160969); both papers call it an Artis Zeego. The word 'robotic' comes from the papers, not from any DICOM tag.

The candidate omits that the sweeps are a ~200 deg short scan: the 496 per-frame primary angles run +98.92 to -99.06 deg (span 197.98 deg) with the secondary angle essentially flat (span 0.57 deg). It also omits that the DynaCT protocol is a HEAD protocol ('20sDCT Head 70kV') run on a lumbar phantom.

The deposit contains no documentation at all - six zips and nothing else. No README, no calibration file, no geometry file outside the DICOM tags, and no labels, segmentations or landmarks. Anyone using it must read the vendor tags directly.

'2 x 496-frame sinograms; Arc 1201 frames; Sinusoidal 161 DICOMs; 2 CBCT volumes; about 4.6 GB' is accurate as far as it goes, but the total projection count is not stated: 496 + 496 + 1201 + 161 = 2354 frames, plus 790 CBCT slices, over 4,629,411,361 bytes.

The claim 'there is no clinical CT' is correct and worth keeping prominent: both volumes are DynaCT reconstructions of the very sweeps in the deposit (ImageType DERIVED/SECONDARY/AXIAL/3DANGIO), so the 3D reference is not independent of the projections it would be used to calibrate. The 'CT scan' wording in the paper refers to these CBCT runs.

Unverifiable as stated: 'It suits calibrating an Artis-type flat-panel projection model against a known 3D object' is a judgement, not a claim in any primary source. Also note the object is NOT fully 'known' - there is no CAD model, no marker/BB phantom and no independent geometric ground truth; the only 3D reference is the CBCT reconstructed from the same data.

candidate.name: UMC Utrecht / Philips cadaver skin-marker 3D2D spine registration set (Bindels et al., IJCARS 2022)
candidate.why_relevant: Three fresh-frozen human cadaver torsos were imaged with Philips Zenition 70 mobile C-arm fluoroscopy at 40-90 degrees over thoracic and lumbar test cases. Each also had a baseline Brilliance 64 CT and AlluraClarity FD20 CBCTs before and after each case, for 780 vertebra registrations. The Zenition 70 is a device absent from our other sets. The article states the data are 'Not available'. The only route is the corresponding author ([e-mail withheld]) or the Philips co-authors.
candidate.institution: University Medical Center Utrecht with Philips Healthcare
candidate.device: Philips Zenition 70 mobile C-arm; Philips AlluraClarity FD20 CBCT; Philips Brilliance 64 CT
candidate.xray_kind: Mobile C-arm fluoroscopy, plus fixed C-arm CBCT
candidate.anatomy: Thoracic and lumbar spine, full torsos
candidate.pose_or_labels: Radiopaque skin-marker model; CBCT-based 3D-3D reference registration per vertebra

verdicts.access_now: Nothing is downloadable, now or on request. The article's own statement is the primary evidence: "Availability of data and material: Not available." (Europe PMC JATS, notes-type="data-availability", line 1675-1677 of the full-text XML). This is not "available upon reasonable request" — it is a flat refusal. The ONLY request route the paper offers is for analysis code: "Code availability: R-code available upon request with the corresponding author." That is R statistical code (R 4.0.3) for the TRE analysis, not imaging data. Searched and found NO dataset record: Zenodo (0 hits for "Bindels AND spine", 0 for "Zenition"), Crossref has no dataset relation on the DOI, Europe PMC core record shows no accession numbers, OpenAlex lists 23 works for this author with zero datasets, and the UMC Utrecht research-information portal record links no dataset. All 6 citing works (checked via OpenAlex) are other papers, none a data release. The paper states imaging files "were transferred to a secured portable computer" — a private, non-archival store. Structural obstacles to any future release: the work is a Philips Healthcare collaboration (grant "PROJECT UMC 55"), four co-authors are Philips employees, and a fifth is a co-founder/stockholder of SentryX BV; the algorithm is a commercial navigation product candidate. The DOI resolves (HTTP 200 to link.springer.com) and the article is not retracted or corrected.
verdicts.anatomy: Thoracic and lumbar spine in three fresh-frozen human cadaveric torsos, imaged prone on a surgical table. Coverage is NOT the contiguous thoracolumbar spine: only five centred vertebrae were used as test-case targets — T4, T7, T10 (thoracic) and L1, L4 (lumbar) — and each fluoroscopic image captured that vertebra plus two above and two below. So the imaged bands are roughly T2-T6, T5-T9, T8-T12, T11-L3 and L2-L5(+). No sacrum: "the algorithm did not register sacral vertebrae," so the L4-centred cases yielded four vertebrae instead of five. All three torsos carry spinal pathology on the baseline CT (sclerotic lesions possibly prostate-cancer metastases, lytic lesions at T9/T10, and compression fractures at T10/T11 and T12) — these are not normal spines. Subject demographics: male 88 y, male 78 y, female 51 y; waist circumference 121, 96 and 73 cm.
verdicts.counts: 780 vertebrae were successfully registered; 792 were attempted and 12 failed (two thoracic, ten lumbar) because they were not fully captured on both fluoroscopic images. 780 is a count of VERTEBRA registrations, not of images and not of image pairs. The number of fluoroscopic images is nowhere stated and is not safely derivable: each registration used one PAIR of opposed-angulation images covering 5 vertebrae (4 when L4 was centred), and the test-case grid was 3 subjects x 5 centred levels x 5 relative-angle differences (40/56/60/64/90 degrees) x 2 detector-skin distances (20 or 30 cm) x 7-9 skin markers, which does not multiply cleanly to 792. One CBCT was acquired before and one after each test case. Supplementary material is a single DOCX (287 kb) of figures on CT slice-thickness sensitivity — no imaging data.
verdicts.licence: No licence on the data, because no data are released. The ARTICLE is open access CC BY 4.0 (confirmed in the PMC permissions block and in Crossref, both content-versions tdm and vor, effective 2022-08-20); that licence covers the text and figures only and grants nothing over the fluoroscopic images, CT, CBCT or registration results. The candidate's "None (data not available)" is correct.
verdicts.paired_ct: Confirmed, and richer than the candidate states. Every torso had a baseline CT on a Philips Brilliance 64 (0.67 mm contiguous slices, 512x512 reconstruction matrix) acquired supine before thawing. A CBCT on a ceiling-mounted Philips AlluraClarity FD20 in the surgical suite was acquired immediately BEFORE the fluoroscopic images of each test case and a second CBCT from the exact same position immediately AFTER, so the same subject has CT + repeated CBCT + fluoroscopy. The reference standard is a 3D3D registration of each vertebra's baseline-CT volume to its CBCT position, which also corrects local vertebral deformation between CT and CBCT. A supplementary analysis additionally used post-processed baseline CT at slice thicknesses up to 5.0 mm.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes, genuinely real X-ray on real human tissue — not DRRs, not phantoms. 2D fluoroscopy on a Philips Zenition 70 mobile C-arm (Philips, Best, Netherlands), spine protocol, software version 5.1.7 (IQ NA HC R5.1.7), typical dose level 0.408 mGy at 20 cm PMMA, variable kV. Plus fixed-C-arm CBCT (AlluraClarity FD20) and fan-beam CT (Brilliance 64). All confirmed verbatim in the Methods. This is the one property of the candidate that is fully and unambiguously verified — and it is also the property that is unobtainable.
corrections: THE STATED ROUTE IS WRONG. The candidate says 'The only route is the corresponding author ([e-mail withheld]) or the Philips co-authors.' That is an inference, not a primary-source claim, and the primary source contradicts its spirit: the paper does not offer a data-request route at all. It says data are 'Not available' full stop, and reserves 'upon request with the corresponding author' exclusively for the R analysis code. Writing to the author is a cold ask against an explicit refusal, not a documented route. Treat access as 'unreleased, no route' rather than 'on request'.

THE ANGLES ARE MISDESCRIBED. The candidate says the torsos were 'imaged with Philips Zenition 70 mobile C-arm fluoroscopy at 40-90 degrees'. The C-arm was never positioned at 40-90 degrees. It stayed neutral craniocaudally and was rotated in the sagittal plane to individual angles of -45, -32, -30, -28, -20, +20, +28, +30, +32 or +45 degrees from AP. The 40-90 degree figure is the RELATIVE angle difference (RAD) between the two opposed images of a registration pair, taking only the five values 40, 56, 60, 64 and 90 degrees. Anyone budgeting for near-lateral views from this description would be wrong: the extreme single view is 45 degrees off AP.

780 IS NOT AN IMAGE COUNT. The candidate's n_images field ('Not stated; 780 vertebra registrations') is right that the image count is unstated, but 780 should not be carried forward as a proxy for dataset size. 780 is successfully registered vertebrae out of 792 attempted (12 failures: two thoracic, ten lumbar, not fully captured on both images). Because each image pair yields 5 vertebrae (4 for L4), the pair count is on the order of 160, i.e. roughly 320 fluoroscopic frames — but that is my arithmetic, not the paper's, and the test-case grid does not multiply cleanly to 792, so no image count should be quoted as sourced.

ANATOMY IS BANDED, NOT CONTINUOUS. 'Thoracic and lumbar spine, full torsos' overstates coverage. Only five centred levels were used (T4/T7/T10/L1/L4), each with two vertebrae above and below, and the sacrum is absent by design because the algorithm does not register sacral vertebrae. For a project whose thesis is naming vertebrae at the lumbosacral junction, note specifically that S1 and the L5-S1 junction are NOT in this set.

THE SPECIMENS ARE PATHOLOGICAL. Not stated in the candidate: all three torsos have spinal disease on baseline CT — sclerotic lesions throughout the vertebral column possibly representing prostate-cancer metastases, multiple lytic lesions at T9/T10, a T12 compression fracture and compression fractures at T10/T11. The table is flattened in the XML so I cannot assign each finding to a named subject with confidence, but the presence of metastatic and fracture pathology across the cohort is unambiguous. Useful for anomaly work, wrong for a normal-anatomy reference.

THE GROUND TRUTH IS 3-D POSE, NOT 2-D LABELS. The candidate's pose_or_labels field is accurate as far as it goes (radiopaque skin markers, CBCT-based 3D3D reference per vertebra), but nothing in the paper describes any 2-D annotation on the fluoroscopic images themselves — no vertebra-level names, boxes or landmarks drawn on the films. The measured points (vertebral body centre and left pedicle centre) came from a model-based segmentation of the spine in 3-D. Even if the data were obtained, per-image level labels would have to be derived by projecting the 3-D poses, not read off.

PHILIPS ENTANGLEMENT IS A HARD BLOCKER, not merely a co-author list. The work was funded under a UMC Utrecht-Philips collaboration agreement (grant id 'PROJECT UMC 55'); four of seven authors (van Mourik, Weijers, Homan, Rongen) are Philips Healthcare employees, and Verlaan is a co-founder and stockholder of SentryX BV. The imaging files live on 'a secured portable computer'. This is commercial pre-product validation data with a stated refusal to share — the prior on release should be near zero, and that is worth more than the corresponding author's email address.

UNVERIFIED PROJECT-INTERNAL CLAIM: 'The Zenition 70 is a device absent from our other sets' cannot be checked against any primary source and I did not attempt to verify it against the project's own inventory. It is asserted, not established, and it is the candidate's entire stated value proposition.

Springer's own article page could not be read directly (303 to idp.springer.com, cookie wall; the TDM PDF link returns 3 kB of HTML). The data-availability text quoted here comes from the publisher-deposited JATS XML in Europe PMC (PMC9468112), which is the version of record under CC BY, so the statement is primary — but I did not see it rendered on link.springer.com.

verdicts.real_xray: CONFIRMED real acquisitions, not DRRs and not MV portal. The 2D images were acquired on a Philips Zenition 70 mobile C-arm (kV fluoroscopy), spine protocol, "variable kV, typical dose-level 0.408 mGy 20 cm PMMA", software version IQ NA HC R5.1.7, written out as DICOM. Caveat that cuts both ways: DRRs are central to the method (the algorithm forward-projects the segmented CT into DRRs and matches gradients), so any file dump from this project would contain both real fluoro and synthetic DRRs and would have to be separated. Second caveat for content use: every fluoroscopic frame carries a randomly applied pattern of 7-9 radiopaque hemispherical skin markers laid over the spine within a 15x15 cm frame around the target vertebra (Fig. 1a shows nine markers on a frame). Subjects are fresh-frozen human cadaver torsos imaged prone, thawed 72 h, not living patients.
verdicts.paired_ct: CONFIRMED, and stronger than most candidates: each specimen has BOTH a baseline fan-beam CT and per-test-case CBCT. Baseline CT = Philips Brilliance 64, 0.67 mm contiguous slices, 512x512, acquired supine, FOV covering the whole subject (not spine-cropped; subject A has nearly twice the voxel size of subject C). CBCT = Philips AlluraClarity FD20 fixed ceiling-mounted C-arm in the surgical suite, one CBCT before and one after each test case (the second only to prove nothing moved; only the first was used as reference). So same-subject 3D exists in two modalities, with the CBCT in the same prone pose and with the same marker model as the fluoroscopy.
verdicts.anatomy: PARTLY REFUTED as stated. Thoracic and lumbar: confirmed (493 thoracic and 287 lumbar registrations). But the fluoroscopic fields are narrow, centered five-vertebra windows, not "full torsos": centered vertebrae were T4, T7, T10 (thoracic) and L1, L4 (lumbar), each image capturing the centered vertebra plus two above and two below. The pelvis is NEVER mentioned as imaged, targeted or registered, and no primary sentence places it in any fluoroscopic field. The sacrum appears only incidentally in the L4-centered window: "From the fluoroscopic images with L4 centered, only four vertebrae were registered because the algorithm did not register sacral vertebrae" - so S1 is inside that field of view but carries no reference registration. "Full torsos" describes the specimens (and the whole-subject baseline CT FOV), not the X-ray content. Anatomy is also not normal: subject A has multiple sclerotic lesions (possible prostate metastases) and a T12 compression fracture, subject B has lytic lesions at T9/T10 and compression fractures at T10/T11, subject C is clean.
verdicts.counts: Subjects CONFIRMED at 3 (male 88 y, waist 121 cm; male 78 y, 96 cm; female 51 y, 73 cm). 780 vertebra registrations CONFIRMED; the candidate omits that 792 were attempted and 12 (2 thoracic, 10 lumbar) failed because the vertebra was not fully captured in both images. Image count: the candidate is right that no image count is stated, but it is derivable and worth recording. Table 2 gives "Captured level: centered vertebra n = 165", i.e. about 165 registration image PAIRS. Pairs are opposed angulations drawn from acquisitions at -45/-32/-30/-28/-20/+20/+28/+30/+32/+45 degrees, giving relative angle differences of 40/56/60/64/90 degrees, so roughly 10 acquisitions per test-case setup yielding 5 pairs, i.e. about 33 setups and on the order of 330 real fluoroscopic images total. Treat ~330 as DERIVED, not as a stated figure. Registrations per angle difference: 40 deg n=143, 56 deg n=141, 60 deg n=283, 64 deg n=141, 90 deg n=72. Detector-skin distance 20 cm n=499, 30 cm n=281.
verdicts.pose_or_labels: No released labels of any kind. What exists internally: (a) a per-vertebra 3D3D reference registration of the baseline CT to the first CBCT, which is the ground-truth standard against which TRE was computed; (b) model-based automatic segmentation of every vertebra in the baseline CT, with vertebral-body-center and left-pedicle landmarks auto-derived; (c) a manual anatomical level indication of one vertebra on the CT and of one vertebra on one fluoroscopic image per case - a real 2D level annotation, though only one vertebra per image; (d) a 3D model of the radiopaque marker spheres and an Umeyama-based estimate of relative pose between the two images. Important refutation of any assumption of calibrated pose: the paper explicitly states the C-arm was NOT tracked and NOT calibrated, and its absolute angulation was not measured - the inter-image pose is itself an estimate from the skin markers. So there is no externally measured per-image projection matrix; ground truth is a registration, not a tracker reading.
verdicts.access_now: No route, confirmed verbatim by the primary source. The declarations read: "Availability of data and material: Not available. Code availability: R-code available upon request with the corresponding author." Note what that means precisely, and it is harsher than the candidate implies: the authors decline data availability outright and offer only the statistical R code on request. The candidate's assertion that "the only route is the corresponding author or the Philips co-authors" is an inference with no primary support - the paper documents no data route at all. Contextual friction against any request: four co-authors (van Mourik, Weijers, Homan, Rongen) are Philips Healthcare employees, the algorithm is a Philips prototype, the work was funded by Philips under UMC Utrecht collaboration agreement PROJECT UMC 55, and Verlaan declares SentryX BV interests. I found no follow-on release: only 6 works cite this paper (none from this group re-releasing the data), the UMC Utrecht institutional record links only the CC BY article with no dataset, and the supplementary file is a 287 kb DOCX of slice-thickness sensitivity figures, not data.
verdicts.licence: None for the data. The article itself is CC BY 4.0 (open access, hybrid, Springer), which covers the figures but not the underlying imaging. The candidate's "None (data not available)" is correct.
corrections: Anatomy overstated: 'full torsos' describes the cadaver specimens and the baseline CT field of view, not the X-ray content. Fluoroscopic fields are five-vertebra windows centered on T4, T7, T10, L1 or L4 with a 15x15 cm marker frame. Lumbar spine is genuinely present (287 lumbar registrations). Pelvis is never stated to be in any fluoroscopic image - refuted as unsupported. Sacrum appears only incidentally in L4-centered windows and was explicitly excluded from registration ('the algorithm did not register sacral vertebrae'), so there is no sacral reference pose.

Access claim is speculation: the paper states 'Availability of data and material: Not available' and offers only R code on request. There is no documented route to the data, not even via the corresponding author. The candidate's 'only route is the corresponding author or the Philips co-authors' has no primary support; the primary source affirmatively declines data availability.

Image count: correct that it is not stated, but it can be bounded from Table 2 ('centered vertebra n = 165' implies ~165 image pairs, ~330 real fluoroscopic acquisitions at 10 angles per setup). Record this as derived, not stated.
Omitted from the candidate: 792 registrations were attempted and 12 failed (2 thoracic, 10 lumbar) because the vertebra was not fully captured in both images.

Omitted domain caveat: every fluoroscopic frame contains 7-9 radiopaque skin markers superimposed over the spine, and the specimens are pathological (metastatic-appearing sclerotic and lytic lesions, three compression fractures across two of three subjects). Both matter for any content use as normal-anatomy X-ray.

Pose claim needs qualification: the C-arm was deliberately not tracked or calibrated, so no independently measured projection geometry exists. The relative pose between the two images is itself estimated from the marker model, and the only reference is a CT-to-CBCT 3D3D per-vertebra registration.
Cannot verify from any primary source that 'the Zenition 70 is a device absent from our other sets' - that is an internal claim about our corpus, not about this dataset.
Cadaver, prone, frozen-then-thawed, with the baseline CT acquired supine while the specimen was still frozen - not an in vivo or intraoperative acquisition.

candidate.name: Stanford CyberKnife clinical gold-standard spine 2D-3D data (Russakoff, Rohlfing, Maurer et al., 2003-2005)
candidate.why_relevant: 4-5 living spine radiosurgery patients, each with a planning CT and paired orthogonal kV X-rays from the CyberKnife in-room cameras. The gold standard comes from bone-implanted fiducials, and the camera geometry is known. No data page or data-sharing statement exists. The only route is the authors: C.R. Maurer (now at Accuray) and T. Rohlfing.
candidate.institution: Stanford University Image Guidance Laboratories
candidate.device: Accuray CyberKnife orthogonal amorphous-silicon kV cameras
candidate.anatomy: Cervical to lumbar spine
candidate.n_images: Stereo kV pairs per patient; counts not public
candidate.pose_or_labels: Known camera geometry; fiducial-based 6-DoF gold standard

verdicts.access_now: NOT DOWNLOADABLE, AND NOT EVEN "ON REQUEST" — there is no stated route of any kind. The primary URL in the candidate is not a data record; it is the authors' preprint PDF of the WBIR 2003 paper (archived 2005-03-27, HTTP 200, 294,262 bytes, 10 pages, full text extracted). I read all 10 pages and grepped the full 26,219-character text: "availab" appears once (in the copyright boilerplate about the PAPER), and "request" / "download" / "public" / "share" / "licen" / "http" / "ftp" / "contact" appear ZERO times. The Acad Radiol 2005 follow-up (13 pages, fetched from the same archive) likewise has no data-availability statement, no URL, no licence, no contact-for-data offer. So this is weaker than "available upon reasonable request" — nobody ever promised it. No repository record exists: TCIA's full collection list has only Spinal-Multiple-Myeloma-SEG and Spine-Mets-CT-SEG, nothing CyberKnife/2D-3D. A complete Wayback CDX crawl of stanford.edu/~rohlfing (148 distinct URLs, all snapshots) shows only paper PDFs and research blurbs — no data/, no downloads/ directory ever archived; the site's "Downloads" nav item is a link to paper PDFs. A domain-wide CDX of igl.stanford.edu surfaces only one relevant object, a second copy of this same paper PDF; igl.stanford.edu is now dead (curl returns 000, no connection). Live www.stanford.edu/~rohlfing returns 403. The only conceivable route is a private ask to the authors 21-23 years after acquisition: Maurer is Chief Scientific Officer at Accuray (corroborated), Rohlfing is now at Google (not SRI as the 2004 page states), Russakoff left medical registration entirely for ophthalmology AI (EuropePMC: his last spine paper is 2006, everything since 2016 is retinal OCT). Treat as unreleased with no route, not as a request-gated dataset.
verdicts.licence: None. Neither the WBIR 2003 preprint nor the Acad Radiol 2005 paper states any data licence or terms — the string "licen" does not occur in either full text. The only licence-like text is the preprint's own copyright notice restricting the PAPER ("One print or electronic copy may be made for personal use only. Systematic or multiple reproduction, distribution to multiple locations ... prohibited"), and Springer's TDM terms on the Crossref record for 10.1007/978-3-540-39701-4_16. Neither covers image data. Data were acquired under an FDA extended treatment protocol with patient informed consent for TREATMENT; no research-sharing consent is described.
verdicts.counts: Four patients, not "4-5". Per patient the authors state they obtained: (1) one pre-treatment contrast planning CT, 1.25 mm slice thickness, FOV covering the whole body cross-section; (2) "approximately 20-30 pairs of orthogonal projection x-ray images obtained at intervals of approximately 60 seconds for the duration of treatment", 512x512 pixels, 0.4 mm pixel size, 12-bit; (3) the camera calibration model and parameters for both cameras; (4) 3D positions of the four fiducials in CT; (5) 2D positions of the four fiducials in the x-rays. So roughly 80-120 real stereo kV pairs exist in the archive, but the paper states "Only one randomly chosen pair of projection x-ray images is used for the work reported in this paper" — i.e. 4 pairs were actually published on. Fiducials are 2x6 mm stainless-steel self-retaining tacks, four or more per patient, ~25 mm apart, non-coplanar, implanted in lamina or facet. No file sizes, no byte counts, no manifest are published anywhere, because nothing was released. The WBIR discussion adds that the group had "access to clinical gold-standard image data from at least twenty additional patients" spanning the column including lumbar, and "plan to analyze this data in the future" — I found no later paper that did: the Acad Radiol 2005, TMI 2005 and Med Phys 2005 follow-ups all re-use the same four patients.
verdicts.anatomy: Cervical and UPPER THORACIC only — the candidate's "cervical to lumbar spine" is wrong for the actual cohort. Primary text (WBIR 2003 §2, corroborated verbatim in ICCV 2003): "Two of these patients have cervical vertebrae lesions (C3 and C5) and two have thoracic vertebrae lesions (T1 and T8)." The sentence about lumbar patients ("Thoracic and lumbar spine patients rest in a conformal alpha cradle") describes the CyberKnife spine programme in general, not the four cases obtained. Lumbar appears only in the unfulfilled future-work sentence about ~20 additional unanalysed patients.
verdicts.paired_ct: Yes, confirmed from primary text, and it is a CT (not CBCT): a contrast-enhanced planning CT at 1.25 mm slice thickness acquired before treatment on the same patient, with the four fiducial markers localised in 3D in the CT and in 2D in the x-rays. The two-camera orthogonal imaging system is calibrated so that intrinsic and extrinsic parameters of both devices are known, and the gold-standard 6-DoF transform is obtained by backprojecting corresponding 2D fiducial pairs (midpoint of the shortest segment between the non-intersecting rays) then point-based rigid registration to the CT fiducials, RMS-minimising. TRE evaluated over every voxel in a box bounding the vertebra. This is a genuine fiducial-based clinical gold standard — the claim holds. None of it is obtainable.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes — genuinely real human X-rays, not DRRs. Two ceiling-mounted kV sources with two floor-mounted Flashscan 20 flat-panel amorphous-silicon detectors (dpiX LLC, Palo Alto), 512x512, 0.4 mm pixels, 12-bit, acquired in-room on living patients during CyberKnife spinal radiosurgery treatment. DRRs appear in the papers only as the moving/synthetic side of the registration. This attribute of the candidate is fully confirmed.
corrections: Subject count is wrong: the primary text says FOUR patients, not '4-5'. All four follow-up papers (Acad Radiol 2005, ICCV 2003, TMI 2005, Med Phys 2005) re-use the identical four.

Anatomy is wrong: the cohort is C3, C5, T1, T8 — cervical and upper thoracic only. There is NO lumbar case. The candidate's 'cervical to lumbar spine' conflates the general CyberKnife spine programme with the four cases actually obtained.

'n_images: counts not public' is wrong — the counts ARE published. WBIR 2003 §2 states ~20-30 orthogonal pairs per patient at ~60 s intervals, 512x512, 0.4 mm, 12-bit, plus that only ONE randomly chosen pair per patient was used in the reported work. What is not public is file sizes and a manifest.

The candidate's primary URL is not a repository record or a data page — it is the authors' self-archived preprint PDF. There is no record to open. Framing it as the PRIMARY record overstates what exists.

'The only route is the authors: C.R. Maurer (now at Accuray) and T. Rohlfing' — Maurer at Accuray is corroborated, but Rohlfing is no longer at SRI International (he is at Google); the archived contact [e-mail withheld] is 22 years stale. More importantly, I could find no primary source establishing that an author route EXISTS at all: no paper, page or archived site offers one. Report this as 'no route found', not as an author route.

Access should be graded harder than 'unreleased no route' implies to a reader skimming: this is not a dataset whose release lapsed — it was never announced, never named, never given an identifier, and the papers contain zero data-sharing language. There is nothing to chase.

Cannot verify any claim about the ~20 additional patients (including lumbar) beyond the single WBIR future-work sentence; no publication ever used them, so their existence in usable, fiducial-annotated form is unestablished.

The two DOIs are correct and resolve (Crossref): 10.1007/978-3-540-39701-4_16 = Russakoff, Rohlfing, Ho, Kim, Shahidi, Adler, Maurer, WBIR 2003, LNCS 2717, pp. 151-160; 10.1016/j.acra.2004.09.013 = Russakoff, Rohlfing, Adler, Maurer, Acad Radiol 12(1):37-50, 2005. Note the Acad Radiol author list is four, not the WBIR seven.

Relevant comparator the candidate omits: the publicly downloadable 3D/2D spine gold standards exist elsewhere (Tomazevic/Pernus, Comput Aided Surg 2005, doi 10.3109/10929080500097687, explicitly motivated by the lack of public gold-standard data — cadaveric lumbar, CT+MR+X-ray). If the project needs a 2D-3D spine gold standard it should go there, not here.

verdicts.real_xray: CONFIRMED real acquisitions. Acad Radiol 2005 and WBIR 2003: "Approximately 20-30 pairs of orthogonal projection x-ray images obtained at intervals of approximately 60 seconds for the duration of treatment with the two Flashscan 20 flat-panel amorphous silicon detector (ASD) x-ray cameras (dpiX, LLC; Palo Alto, CA). The x-ray images have 512 x 512 pixels with pixel size of 0.4 mm and 12-bit intensity values (stored as 16-bit integers)." These are live intra-treatment projections of patients, not DRRs -- DRRs appear in these papers only as the computed floating image rendered from CT for the similarity measure. NOT MV portal: the imaging chain is two ceiling-mounted diagnostic x-ray sources firing onto two floor-mounted aSi flat panels, physically separate from the 6 MV x-band treatment LINAC. CAVEAT: none of the four papers states a tube potential. "kV setup radiographs" is an inference from the CyberKnife design, not a primary-sourced number, and the imaging is not "setup" radiography in the linac sense -- it is periodic intra-fraction tracking imaging.
verdicts.paired_ct: CONFIRMED, CT (not CBCT), same subject, same treatment episode. Acad Radiol 2005: "A pretreatment CT image with slice thickness of 1.25 mm and a field of view sufficiently large to image the entire cross-section of the body." It is a contrast planning CT of the lesion region, acquired AFTER percutaneous fiducial implantation so the markers are visible in it. Because it is a lesion-region scan (C3, C5, T1, T8), the CT craniocaudal coverage also excludes lumbar spine and pelvis. No CBCT anywhere in this system or these papers.
verdicts.anatomy: REFUTED as stated. Not "cervical to lumbar". Three independent primary sources give the identical cohort: ICCV 2003 -- "We obtained four archived data sets of patients... Two of the patients have tumors near cervical vertebrae (C3 and C5), and two have tumors near thoracic vertebrae (T1 and T8)"; WBIR 2003 -- "Two of these patients have cervical vertebrae lesions (C3 and C5) and two have thoracic vertebrae lesions (T1 and T8)"; Acad Radiol 2005 -- same sentence. So: cervical and upper/mid thoracic ONLY. ZERO lumbar, ZERO sacrum, ZERO pelvis. The word "lumbar" in these papers appears only in descriptions of the general CyberKnife clinical protocol ("Thoracic and lumbar spine patients rest in a conformal alpha cradle"), never in the cohort. For a lumbar/sacral/pelvic fluoroscopy project this dataset contains no usable anatomy.
verdicts.counts: 4 patients, not "4-5". The "four to five" figure in the MICCAI 2004 progressive-attenuation-fields paper is markers per patient ("These patients had four to five metal fiducial markers implanted percutaneously"), not patients -- that paper used only TWO of the four. Image counts ARE public, contrary to "counts not public": ~20-30 orthogonal stereo pairs archived per patient over the treatment (so roughly 80-120 pairs / 160-240 frames across the cohort), but WBIR 2003, ICCV 2003 and Acad Radiol 2005 all state "Only one randomly chosen pair of x-ray images per patient is used for the work reported here." The actual gold-standard working set in the literature is therefore 4 stereo pairs = 8 X-ray images against 4 CTs. Only the TMI 2005 markerless-tracking paper appears to have used frame sequences (its abstract reports per-frame tracking percentages); I could not retrieve its full text to confirm counts.
verdicts.pose_or_labels: Pose, no anatomical labels. Per case the authors held: (1) camera calibration model plus intrinsic and extrinsic parameters for both cameras, obtained by scanning a QA calibration phantom; (2) 3D positions of the four fiducials in the CT; (3) 2D positions of the four fiducials in both projections. Gold-standard 6-DoF rigid transform = backproject each 2D pair, take the midpoint of the shortest segment between the non-intersecting rays as the 3D point, then RMS-minimising point-based rigid registration to the CT fiducials. Markers are 2 x 6 mm stainless-steel self-retaining tacks in lamina or facet. NO segmentations, NO vertebra-level labels, NO landmarks beyond the fiducials. The authors themselves caveat the gold standard: MICCAI 2004 attributes patient #2's ~1.6 mm residual to "inaccuracy of the gold standard transformation rather than errors of the intensity-based registration method," because "fiducial markers in actual patients cannot be implanted in mathematically optimal locations."
verdicts.access_now: No route found; "unreleased" holds as far as I can check. No data-availability statement, data page, repository record or download link in any of WBIR 2003, ICCV 2003, MICCAI 2003, MICCAI 2004 or Acad Radiol 2005. Wayback CDX of stanford.edu/~rohlfing (full prefix crawl) shows only /publications/, /research/{bee,dbm,fly,igs,nir}/ and a dead /software/ -- no data directory. igl.stanford.edu has 280 archived URLs total and no data page (only a copy of the same PDF under ~torsten/references/). ai.stanford.edu/~russakof is a stale 2003 PhD-candidate page with papers and no data. Nothing on Zenodo or NITRC (the Zenodo hit "gold standard dataset for non-rigid 2D/3D registration" is Jin/Xia/Gao, a Suzhou THORAX dataset -- unrelated). I cannot prove a negative, but there is no public route. Author contact is the only conceivable one and both first authors left this line of work (Russakoff's entire post-2005 Europe PMC record is ophthalmology deep learning; Rohlfing moved to SRI International). Note: the publicly downloadable spine 3D/2D gold standard is the Ljubljana cadaveric L1-L5 phantom (Tomazevic/Likar/Pernus, lit.fe.uni-lj.si) -- a DIFFERENT dataset, which Acad Radiol 2005 explicitly contrasts as "only vertebraes L1-L5, with very little soft tissue."
verdicts.licence: None. No licence, terms of use, or data-sharing statement in any primary source. Copyright notice on the WBIR preprint explicitly restricts even the PAPER to one personal copy.
corrections: ANATOMY IS WRONG. Candidate says 'Cervical to lumbar spine'. Three primary sources (ICCV 2003, WBIR 2003, Acad Radiol 2005) all state the same four cases: lesions at C3, C5, T1 and T8. No lumbar, no sacrum, no pelvis in any case. The only 'lumbar' text in these papers describes the generic CyberKnife immobilisation protocol, not the cohort.

SUBJECT COUNT IS WRONG. Candidate says '4-5 living patients'. Every primary source says exactly four. The 'four to five' in MICCAI 2004 refers to fiducial markers per patient, not patients; that paper used only two of the four.

'n_images: counts not public' IS WRONG. Acad Radiol 2005 and WBIR 2003 both publish the counts: ~20-30 orthogonal pairs per patient at ~60 s intervals, 512x512, 0.4 mm pixel, 12-bit. What is small is the USED set: 'Only one randomly chosen pair of x-ray images per patient is used for the work reported here' -- i.e. 4 pairs / 8 frames with gold-standard transforms.

'xray_kind: kV setup radiographs' is UNSOURCED on the kV part. No paper states a tube potential. What is stated is that the sources are separate ceiling-mounted x-ray tubes and the detectors are dpiX Flashscan 20 aSi panels, distinct from the 6 MV LINAC -- which supports 'not MV portal' but does not source 'kV'. They are also intra-fraction tracking images, not setup films.

DEVICE ATTRIBUTION IS IMPRECISE. Candidate credits 'Accuray CyberKnife orthogonal amorphous-silicon kV cameras'. The system is Accuray CyberKnife but the detectors are named as Flashscan 20 flat panels from dpiX, LLC, Palo Alto.

THE LUMBAR DATA THE CANDIDATE IMPLIES WAS NEVER PUBLISHED. WBIR 2003 discussion: 'We have access to clinical gold-standard image data from at least twenty additional patients and plan to analyze this data in the future. These patients have spinal lesions at vertebral locations distributed throughout the spinal column, including the lumbar region.' I can find no publication by this group that ever analysed those cases and no release of them. Treat the ~20 lumbar-inclusive cases as an unfulfilled 2003 plan, not as an existing dataset.

'ct_or_cbct_same_subject: true' is CONFIRMED but the CT is a lesion-region planning scan (1.25 mm slices, full body cross-section in-plane), so its craniocaudal coverage also excludes lumbar and pelvis.

'institution: Stanford University Image Guidance Laboratories' CONFIRMED (Image Guidance Laboratories, Dept. of Neurosurgery, Stanford), and the data is stated as archived CyberKnife clinical data from patients treated under an extended FDA protocol at Stanford.

DOIs CONFIRMED via CrossRef: 10.1007/978-3-540-39701-4_16 = Russakoff, Rohlfing, Ho, Kim, Shahidi, Adler, Maurer, WBIR 2003, LNCS, pp. 151-160; 10.1016/j.acra.2004.09.013 = Russakoff, Rohlfing, Adler, Maurer, Academic Radiology 12(1):37-50, January 2005. (The Acad Radiol running header prints '2004; 12:37-50'; the issue is Jan 2005.) Two further papers use the same data: ICCV 2003 light fields, and MICCAI 2004 / Med Phys 2005 progressive attenuation fields.

'C.R. Maurer (now at Accuray)' IS UNSOURCED HERE. In the primary sources Maurer is Stanford Neurosurgery ([e-mail withheld]). The WBIR paper acknowledges three Accuray employees for technical assistance, which establishes a corporate relationship but not his current affiliation. I did not verify the current-employer claim.

SERVES 'A' SHOULD BE DOWNGRADED for a lumbar/sacral/pelvic fluoroscopy project: even if obtained, the four cases contain no lumbar, sacral or pelvic anatomy in either the X-rays or the CTs, and the usable gold-standard set is 8 frames.

ACCESS: no data page, licence or sharing statement exists in any primary source or on either author's archived site, and no repository record exists. Confirms 'unreleased, no route' to the extent a negative can be checked.

candidate.name: UCLA / Brainlab multi-institution ExacTrac spine setup X-rays with planning-CT DRRs (Petragallo, Lamb et al., Med Phys 2023)
candidate.why_relevant: New counts in the known UCLA lineage: stereoscopic ExacTrac kV setup X-rays with planning CT for 429 spine radiotherapy patients (1,592 fractions) from six or more institutions, with a Brainlab co-author. The sites include UCLA, UCSF, Beth Israel Lahey, UAMS, UT Health San Antonio, Piedmont and Kaiser. This is larger than the 254-patient Charters 2024 set. The data statement could not be read (Wiley returned 403), and no deposit was found.
candidate.institution: UCLA (lead) plus 6 institutions, with Brainlab AG
candidate.device: Brainlab ExacTrac stereoscopic kV
candidate.anatomy: Spine (radiotherapy targets)
candidate.pose_or_labels: Physician-approved clinical 6-DoF alignments; simulated off-by-one-vertebra shifts
candidate.is_update_of_known: UCLA Charters 2024 kV setup radiographs of thoraco-lumbar spine + planning CT (254 patients)

verdicts.access_now: NOT downloadable. On request only, and doubly gated. The primary record's DATA AVAILABILITY STATEMENT reads, verbatim: "Research data will be shared to the extent allowed under Institutional Review Board approval and institutional data-sharing agreements, upon request to the corresponding author." (aapm.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mp.16359, section mp16359-sec-0190; Wiley returns 403 to WebFetch/curl and to a Googlebot UA — I read it with curl_cffi impersonating Safari, HTTP 200, 282,500 bytes.) That is a promise, not a release, and it is conditioned twice: on IRB approval and on six separate institutional data-sharing agreements. Corresponding author Rachel Petragallo, UCLA Radiation Oncology (she has since finished her PhD, 2024, so the contact is likely stale). NO deposit exists anywhere I could search: Crossref `relation` is empty (no linked dataset DOI); Zenodo q=ExacTrac returns 3 hits, all unrelated Italian/phantom publications; figshare search returns 0; Dryad returns 0; DataCite has no record for this work; TCIA has no ExacTrac/setup-radiograph collection (only the unrelated Spine-Mets-CT-SEG). The group's own lab page rosaml.net publishes code only ("Stereoscopic DRR generator for the ExacTrac image-guidance system", github.com/jcharters-mp/DRR; ARL_repo; hdrpac) and lists no datasets. The article itself is also closed: OpenAlex oa_status "closed", Europe PMC isOpenAccess N / not in PMC, Semantic Scholar openAccessPdf empty. The only files you can actually download from the record are the Supporting Information (mp16359-sup-0001-SuppMat.docx 28.3 KB, -0002-SuppMat.doc 33 KB, -0003-FigureS1.jpg 89.5 KB, -0004-FigureS2.jpg 253.9 KB, -0005-FigureS3.JPG 62.3 KB — ~467 KB total, behind the same paywall), and they contain no imaging data.
verdicts.licence: No data licence, because no data are released. The article carries Wiley's standard subscription terms (Crossref license URL http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/termsAndConditions#vor, © 2023 American Association of Physicists in Medicine); the site footer asserts "All rights reserved, including rights for text and data mining and training of artificial intelligence technologies". The candidate's "licence: Unknown" is better stated as "none — closed article, unreleased data". Note also a declared interest: "Daniel Saenz reports a research agreement with Brainlab ending in March 2020 for projects unrelated to the current manuscript."
verdicts.counts: Confirmed from the abstract and expanded from the author's dissertation (Petragallo 2024, UCLA, escholarship.org/uc/item/5896r7bn — chapter 2 is this paper): 429 patients, 1,592 treatment fractions, 3,184 clinical x-ray images (two stereoscopic x-rays per fraction) with matching DRRs. After simulating one superior and one inferior off-by-one shift per pair, 9,552 two-channel (x-ray + DRR) arrays. The candidate's "5,700–9,372" is the size of the TRAINING set in each leave-one-institution-out fold, not a per-fold pair count; test sets ranged 180–3,852 arrays. Per-institution table (dissertation Table 2.1, patients / fractions / clinical images / date range): UCLA 87 / 330 / 660, 6/2014–12/2017; Inst 2 72 / 246 / 492, 10/2017–10/2021; Inst 3 45 / 228 / 456, 4/2015–7/2021; Inst 4 38 / 116 / 232, 7/2020–11/2021; Inst 5 174 / 642 / 1,284, 7/2020–11/2021; Inst 6 13 / 30 / 60, 12/2013–1/2021. Note the skew: one unnamed institution contributes 40% of the patients and UCLA only 20%.
verdicts.real_xray: Yes — real clinical kV setup radiographs of living patients, not renders. Brainlab ExacTrac stereoscopic kV system, two oblique x-rays per fraction, acquired in routine radiotherapy between 12/2013 and 11/2021 at six institutions, anonymized and pooled at UCLA under a UCLA IRB protocol. The final x-ray/DRR pair of each fraction was kept. The paper's own DRRs are renders, but the x-ray half of every pair is real film-equivalent clinical acquisition.
verdicts.anatomy: Thoracic spine. The abstract says only "spine radiotherapy patients", but the methods (dissertation §2.2.1) say each institution "searched their own internal database to identify thoracic spine patients". The candidate's "Spine (radiotherapy targets)" is too broad — do not expect cervical or lumbosacral coverage, and in particular do not expect the lumbosacral junction this project cares about.
verdicts.paired_ct: Overstated in the candidate. There is a planning CT per patient in the clinic, and the DRRs are rendered from it by the ExacTrac system — but the CT VOLUMES were never part of the assembled corpus. The dissertation is explicit: "ExacTrac x-ray/DRR pairs from each treatment fraction were anonymized and collected into a central image database at UCLA." What exists is 2-D x-ray + 2-D DRR. So `ct_or_cbct_same_subject: true` should be qualified: paired CT-derived DRRs, yes; paired CT, no — and getting the CTs would be a separate and larger ask of six institutions.
corrections: NOT A RELEASE. The DAS is 'Research data will be shared to the extent allowed under Institutional Review Board approval and institutional data-sharing agreements, upon request to the corresponding author.' Set access from 'unknown' to 'on request only, IRB + six institutional data-sharing agreements'. No repository deposit exists (Crossref relations empty; Zenodo/figshare/Dryad/DataCite/TCIA all negative; the lab's own site publishes code only).

The article is closed-access, not just the data (OpenAlex oa_status 'closed', not in PMC, no OA PDF anywhere). Wiley serves 403 to normal clients; the page is readable only with a browser TLS fingerprint.

'six or more institutions' is wrong — the paper says exactly six. The candidate's site list (UCLA, UCSF, Beth Israel Lahey, UAMS, UT Health San Antonio, Piedmont, Kaiser) names SEVEN clinical centres and is an inference from author affiliations, not a stated mapping. The dissertation anonymizes the contributors as UCLA plus 'Institution 2-6'. I could find no primary source naming which six contributed, so treat the site list as unverified.
Brainlab AG (Munich) is an author affiliation (Pascal Bertram), not a contributing imaging site. A competing-interest note also discloses a Brainlab research agreement for a co-author.
'planning-CT DRRs' with ct_or_cbct_same_subject=true is misleading: only 2-D x-ray/DRR pairs were collected centrally. The CT volumes themselves are not part of the corpus.
Anatomy is THORACIC spine, not spine generally (dissertation methods). No cervical or lumbosacral coverage should be assumed.

pose_or_labels is overstated. The labels actually attached to the data are BINARY ('no-error' vs 'shift') per two-channel array.
